Millions of households will face a squeeze from soaring energy bills this winter with prices set to hit a three-year high from October.

Regulator Ofgem increased the price cap to a three-year high on Wednesday, raising it by 4 per cent from October 1 for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales.

Ofgem said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the average household using both electricity and gas if this level was sustained for a year.

It serves as a major blow for the Labour government, as the energy secretary admitted the prime minister’s formerly announced help on energy bills will not cover the price hike.

Andy Burnham has vowed to continue to look for ways to get prices down in the long term, but faces criticism from political opponents and calls to do more to help households.

open image in gallery Regulator Ofgem increased the price cap to a three-year high on Wednesday, raising it by 4 per cent from October 1 for a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales ( PA )

Speaking to reporters from a supermarket in London, the prime minister said: “It’s difficult for people and I recognise that.

“But it’s why, within days of taking office, I announced that we would remove VAT off electricity bills to give people that little bit of help.

“That kicks in from October. We know the price cap will have an impact, but it is what we can do right now.

“And we’ll continue to look as we go forward at how we get energy prices down in the long term, and that’s what we need to do too.”

Reacting to the energy price cap rise, Miatta Fahnbulleh said: “Families will be understandably concerned about the cost of energy bills this winter, which is being driven up by the Iran war.

“Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.

open image in gallery It serves as a major blow for the Labour government, as the energy secretary admitted the prime minister’s formerly announced help on energy bills will not cover the price hike ( Sky News )

“This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.”

But she admitted the prime minister’s energy measures won't cover price cap increase, telling Sky News: “It doesn't, but it helps.

“So it's £45 lower than it would have been had we not acted. But look, we know that there is more that we need to do.”

It comes after the Middle East conflict affected wholesale prices. The ongoing heatwaves across Europe have added further pressure by increasing gas demand for power generation to meet air conditioning and cooling demand.

Asked if she was frustrated about the impact of Donald Trump’s war on Iran had raised prices, Ms Fahnbulleh said: “ I am frustrated that global events are having an impact on households, businesses in this country.

“Of course I am, and you know when you're working to do things like increasing the amount of clean power to drive down bills, and then you've got shocks like that that then increase bills. That is massively difficult for families, but it's hugely frustrating for government as well.”

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has vowed to continue to look for ways to get prices down in the long term, but faces criticism from political opponents and calls to do more to help households. ( PA )

However, she denied the government’s drive to net zero had pushed up energy bills, and said: “Well, so it's simply not true, and when I talk about clean power, it is, yes, good for the environment - but it's absolutely critical to our strategy to delivering bills that are more affordable because it breaks that link to global fossil fuel markets.”

The increased October cap, which will remain in place for three months, will come into force as households start to increase their energy usage further by using their heating more regularly, adding to bills.

In a further blow for households, analysts Cornwall Insight released their latest forecast on Wednesday for a further 9% increase to the price cap in the New Year.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK.

“We welcome the government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter.

“Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap, and many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for electricity consumed out of peak times.

“It’s also worth considering different payment methods, with prepayment customers paying the lowest price cap rates, and could save consumers an average of about £45 compared to direct debit.”

The Conservatives have accused Labour of failing to deliver on its promise to cut energy bills, with Claire Coutinho, shadow energy secretary, having said: “Labour promised to cut energy bills by £300, but they have gone up by nearly £400 instead.

“Our cheap power plan would cut energy bills for households and businesses by scrapping Government taxes and levies on bills, and it wouldn’t cost the taxpayer a penny. We have to put cheap energy first.”

The Resolution Foundation think-tank urged the government to take more action on energy bill.

“This underscores the need for the government to have targeted support with energy bills designed, costed and ready to switch on as soon as January, in order to protect households from another cost of living crunch,” Jonathan Marshall, Principal Economist at the Resolution Foundation said.

The energy price cap was introduced by the government in January 2019 and sets a maximum price that energy suppliers can charge consumers in England, Scotland and Wales for each kilowatt hour (kWh) of energy they use.

It aims to ensure that prices for customers on default energy tariffs are a fair reflection of the cost paid by suppliers for wholesale energy, and that the profit firms make is capped.

Ofgem sets its cap every three months as the average amount paid by the typical household.

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round takes place this week as more teams from the Premier League, including current cup winners Manchester City, enter the competition and learn who they will face.

Most top-flight clubs, such as Chelsea and Tottenham, entered the tournament in the second round with those who are competing in European competitions this season now involved as well.

Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United are among those to enter at this stage.

Their participation also means that the third round will be played across two midweeks in order for the teams involved in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League to juggle their match schedules.

Here’s everything you need to know about the draw:

When is the Carabao Cup third round draw?

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round will take place today, Wednesday 26 August. It will follow the conclusion of the second round tie between Preston and Everton which kicks off at 8pm BST, meaning the draw could start at around 10.15pm BST.

How will the draw work?

Pre-draw

Before the main draw, there is a pre-draw to decide if the eight Champions League and Europa League clubs will be at home or away. This part is before Preston North End’s Round Two tie against Everton on Sky Sports.

Main draw

The main draw will take place following the conclusion of Round Two tie, the first eight ties will involve those Champions League and Europa League clubs. Their home or away position will have already having been decided. They will then be drawn against a team in a separate bowl with the remaining teams in the competition – so cannot meet one another at this stage.

Following the conclusion of those eight ties being drawn, the final eight ties will be drawn as normal.

From Round Three onwards, there is no longer a divide between the Northern and Southern sections.

How can I watch the Carabao Cup draw?

The Carabao Cup third-round draw will be shown live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Football following the conclusion of Preston v Everton.

Sky Sports subscribers will also be able to watch the draw live online via the Sky Go app.

Which teams are involved?

32 teams are involved in the draw including 23 winners of second round ties and nine additional Premier League clubs who are also competing in European competitions this season.

Those teams in Europe and entering the competition for the first time this season are: Arsenal, Aston Villa, Bournemouth, Brighton & Hove Albion, Crystal Palace, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Sunderland.

Of those, Brighton can be in Europe through the Conference League, but that competition does not begin until October, so it does not affect the Round Three schedule.

Carabao Cup draw ball numbers

The ball numbers will be confirmed on this morning ahead of the draw.

Norwich

Middlesbrough

When will the Carabao Cup third round be played?

The third round of the Carabao Cup is scheduled to take place across consecutive weeks, starting on 7 September and 14 September. The ties will be played midweek as single-leg fixtures with the winners progressing to the fourth round.

Immigrant visa interviews at U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide have been temporarily suspended as President Donald Trump's administration continues a broad immigration enforcement push during his second term.

A U.S. State Department representative said Tuesday that the pause stems from a newly launched global training program for diplomatic missions worldwide, requiring adjustments to scheduled visa service appointments.

The measure forms part of a wider immigration policy overhaul under Trump, who maintains that stricter measures are required to enhance national security.

open image in gallery A U.S. State ​Department spokesperson said on Tuesday that it launched a global training initiative at ​all U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide ( Reuters )

The administration's efforts have included canceling visas and permanent residency status, as well as turning down applications linked to political views, such as participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations targeting Israel's military actions in Gaza.

These initiatives have encountered legal hurdles in federal court. On Friday, a U.S. judge blocked a policy that would halt immigrant visas for individuals from 75 nations, ruling that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had exceeded his legal authority by issuing the suspension.

While the State Department provided few details on the schedule or full scope of the staff training, it said the program is designed to teach consular staff to identify individuals who might rely on U.S. public assistance, while ensuring applicants are assessed "comprehensively and consistently."

Applicants affected by the decision have already begun receiving notices that their interview dates have been canceled and will be rescheduled later, according to an initial report by the Financial Times.

open image in gallery Trump has pursued an aggressive deportation drive and immigration ​crackdown that includes revocations of visas and green cards and rejection of applications ( Reuters )

Human rights organizations have strongly criticized the administration's actions, calling the measures discriminatory and alleging violations of constitutional guarantees to free expression and due process.

Critics further warn that the enforcement push fosters an unsafe climate within the country, raising particular concerns among ethnic minorities regarding potential racial profiling.

Although Trump's 2024 presidential campaign focused primarily on curbing unauthorized border crossings, his administration has simultaneously introduced hurdles for lawful entry, including steep fee increases for specific employment-based visa categories.

News.title: ‘I just hope I leave something good behind’: Dolly Parton reflects on her legacy in resurfaced interview
News.content:
The late Dolly Parton reflected on her legacy before her death at 80, saying she hoped to “leave something good behind”.

Dolly Parton, who was born in a two-room log cabin and rose to become the world’s wealthiest country music star with timeless hits including “9 to 5” and “Jolene,” passed away after a brief battle with cancer on Tuesday (25 August).

Speaking to CBS Mornings in 2024, the iconic singer contemplated how she wanted to be remembered, adding: “I'd like to be thought of as a decent human being. When I'm gone, I'd like you to smile and think, 'Oh, she was funny.'

“I would just like to be known for what I think I am, which is just a regular person.”

Everyone from Taylor Swift and Beyoncé to Eminem and Linda Ronstadt have paid tribute to Parton, describing her as “the gift that kept on giving” and saying her legacy would be “an everlasting one”.

A Chinese artist was sentenced to three years in prison on Tuesday for “infringing upon the reputation of heroes” through satirical works of art, including statues of the country’s former leader Mao Zedong.

The US-based Gao Zhen, who was part of an artistic duo known as the Gao Brothers, was arrested while visiting family in China in August 2024. He has been in custody ever since.

He was sentenced by the Sanhei People's Court court in northern Hebei province, according to his wife Zhao Yaliang.

The charges against Gao relate to artistic works that China considers insulting to revolutionary figures. One such piece of work is a 2009 statue called Mao’s Guilt which shows the founder of modern China kneeling in repentance. Another is the Miss Mao series of caricatures depicting Mao with breasts and an engorged nose.

Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders, who has been advocating for Gao's case, described the sentence as “a very clear case of a violation of a person’s freedom of expression.”

Yi said the artist planned to appeal the sentence and noted that the artworks in question were created before the law Gao was sentenced under had been passed.

The court did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Amnesty International criticised the court sentence, which it described as a deterrent against artistic expression.

“The lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offense illustrate the authorities’ determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression,” Amnesty's China director Sarah Brooks said.

“No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history.”

Zhao said she hoped to be reunited with her husband, and be able to return to the US, where the family had immigrated. “I felt two years was my limit and I was really disappointed and sad,” she said. “I haven't been able to catch my breath.”

She had prepared clothes for her husband hoping he would be released. Chinese courts often count pretrial detention as time served in a sentence.

The Gao Brothers, whose works addressed themes of authoritarianism and censorship, became famous during a time of relative openness in China and were exhibited both inside the country and abroad.

In recent years, however, Beijing has increased scrutiny of certain aspects of expression, especially in regards to political figures. In 2018 the legislature passed a law banning any criticism of the country’s heroes.

Plans for Dolly Parton’s funeral are already in place following the country icon’s death at 80 on Tuesday.

“At Dolly’s request, a small, private service will be held for immediate family,” the singer’s team shared in a statement.

However, Parton did reveal one major detail about her funeral arrangements to fans more than a decade before her death.

“I’m sure they’ll be playing “I Will Always Love You” when I die, just like they did with Whitney Houston,” she told Entertainment Weekly in a 2014 interview.

“When they picked her coffin up and started in on that song, I started to cry, and I thought, ‘Oh my Lord.’ That’s when it hit me that she was really gone.”

open image in gallery Dolly Parton shared the song she wanted played at her funeral in an interview more than a decade ago ( AFP/Getty )

Houston’s cover of “I Will Always Love You” played as pallbearers carried her casket out of the church at her 2012 funeral. The song was originally written and recorded by Parton in 1973; however, it was Houston’s 1992 cover — recorded for her acting debut opposite Kevin Costner in The Bodyguard — that turned the track into a global hit.

But that wasn’t the song Parton herself wanted at her own funeral.

“There’s a song called ‘If We Never Meet Again.’ It’s an old country-gospel church song that talks about if we never meet again this side of heaven, I will meet you on that beautiful shore,” she told EW.

“‘Where the charming roses bloom forever and where separations come no more.’ That was my daddy’s favorite. We did sing it at his funeral, and I would like it to be sung at mine.”

open image in gallery Parton wanted the country-gospel church song ‘If We Never Meet Again’ to be played at her funeral, as it was at her father’s ( PA Archive )

It is unclear whether there will be a live rendition of the song at her funeral; however, Parton has duetted with her goddaughter, pop star Miley Cyrus, on a number of occasions in the past.

Asked in a previous interview what her funeral song would be, Parton famously replied: “I don't know — but I won't be singing it!”

Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the news of her death on behalf of the family, saying: “Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus.”

Seaver also revealed that his aunt requested to be laid to rest in a “beautiful bed of plush cotton.”

“After a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest,” Seaver said.

According to TMZ, the singer will be buried in the mausoleum at Woodlawn Memorial Park in Nashville, Tennessee, next to her husband Carl Dean, who died last year.

Her representative later confirmed that she had died at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, “after bravely facing a brief battle with cancer,” surrounded by loved ones.

Everyone from Taylor Swift and Beyoncé to Eminem and Linda Ronstadt has paid tribute to Parton, describing her as “the gift that kept on giving” and saying her legacy would be “an everlasting one.”

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump ordered flags to fly at half-staff in the U.S. to honour the singer, writing: “This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will.”

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest
News.content:
Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He said: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo fumes as Ange Postecoglou subs him – but ex-Tottenham boss masterminds amazing comeback
Sports.content:
CRISTIANO RONALDO was fuming with Ange Postecoglou after subbing him off for Al-Nassr – but his decision was justified following their comeback win against Al-Ettifaq.

Al-Nassr completed a stunning turnaround to beat their rivals 3-2 after going 2-0 down with ten men.



Former Tottenham boss Postecoglou – who only took over the Saudi side last month – took the very bold move of hooking the legendary forward at half time.

Ronaldo, 41, was visibly angry with the Australian’s decision and was seen shrugging and holding out his arms as he trudged towards the dugout.



But Postecoglou knew he needed a quick response after Ondrej Duda and Alvaro Medran had put the hosts into a commanding lead.

Al-Ettifaq had capitalised on Al-Nassr keeper Bento being sent off after just 12 minutes.

Ronaldo was already fuming with the team’s back-up goalkeeper Abdulrahman Al-Otaibi for his mistake in fumbling Medran’s shot for 2-0.

At half time, Postecoglou opted to bring on midfielder Abdullah Al-Khaibari instead of ex-Real Madrid superstar Ronaldo as he looked to shift the momentum.

His changes didn’t have an immediate impact as he later introduced Abdullah Al-Hamdan and Sami Al-Najei.

But in the 74th minute Al-Nassr pulled one back through ex-Liverpool star Sadio Mane, before Abdulelah Al-Amri made it 2-2 three minutes later.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

And in stoppage time, Mane raced clear before calmly slotting home to seal their comeback win.

Postecoglou defended his decision to sub off the five-time Ballon d’Or winner after the game and said he was simply looking for “a different approach”.

He said: “When I made the substitutions, including taking Ronaldo off, I believed the players coming on could make an impact.

“I came here to help the players, so as I said, I’m proud of them because every substitute made a positive contribution.

“I’m here to help the team with what I see, and everyone knows that Ronaldo hasn’t played in a long time.



“He performed exceptionally well in the first half, and we opted for a different approach.”

This isn’t the first time Ronaldo has reacted poorly to being substituted in his career.

He stormed down the tunnel after being hooked by ex-boss Stefano Pioli during a win over Al-Kholood in March 2025.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

And Ronaldo also fumed at ex-Manchester United boss Ralf Rangnick for subbing him during a win over Brentford in January 2022.

Ronaldo threw his jacket while sitting on the bench and was accused of being “too emotional” by Rangnick.

Sports.title: Former Premier League star ‘goes missing and hasn’t been seen for a week’ as police launch search
Sports.content:
POLICE in Hungary have launched a search for former Premier League footballer Akos Buzsáky.

The 44-year-old starred for Queens Park Rangers in the English top flight in the 2011/12 season, scoring two goals.



He also starred for The Hoops and Plymouth in the Championship before ending his career at Portsmouth in League One in 2013.

However, the ex-midfielder has been missing for over a week now.



Official police records say they have been trying to find the Hungary international since August 18.

His father, Ákos Buzsáky Sr., was contacted by news outlet Blikk about the search, but was not aware of his son being missing.



He said: ” I didn’t know that the police were also looking for my son.

“He basically spends a lot of time in Greece, where he works as a construction contractor.

“He spent almost the entire last year there.

“Since we don’t live under the same roof, it’s not surprising that we only speak less often.



“The last time I spoke to him was last week, when he was at home.”

The report adds Buzsaky no longer lives with the mother of his two daughters.

His mum has also been looking for him in recent days and it is possible she is the one who reported him as missing to the police.

Sports.title: Premier League’s top spenders this summer with promoted minnows splashing more cash than Tottenham and Man Utd
Sports.content:
CHELSEA are the Premier League’s top spenders this summer having splashed £347million on new players.

Tottenham are next on £322m… although actually have a lower net spend than newly-promoted Ipswich.



The record for Prem summer spending is £3.3bn, set in 2025.

That figure could be exceeded ahead of next Tuesday’s transfer deadline, with Valuball reporting that £2.73bn has so far been splashed by Premier League sides.



TRANSFER NEWS LIVE: ALL THE LATEST FROM THE SUMMER WINDOW

Chelsea bought Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for a club-record £117m, with Maxence Lacroix, Marco Palestra, Geovany Quenda, Valentin Barco, Emmanuel Emegha, Pep Chavarria and Danny Welbeck also coming in for decent fees.

The Blues have a net spend of £187m, with their £347m splurge offset by sales of the likes of Andrey Santos, Marc Cucurella, Trevoh Chalobah and Tyrique George.

Tottenham, meanwhile, twice smashed their transfer record in buying Mateus Fernandes for £85m and then Sandro Tonali for a fee potentially rising to £100m.

With Savio and Jan Paul van Hecke also coming in for hefty fees, Spurs’ summer spending has topped £320m.

Following the Savio deal, announced yesterday, the North Londoners’ net spend stood at £139m, with Luka Vuskovic, Cristian Romero, Djed Spence and Will Lankshear among several departures.

Tottenham have raised eyebrows with their summer spree, although their net spend is only the Prem’s fourth highest.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Aforementioned Chelsea are top, with Arsenal and IPSWICH also topping Spurs.

The Gunners have bought Bruno Guimaraes, Ezri Konsa and Christos Tzolis, while making Piero Hincapie’s initial loan permanent.

With Gabriel Martinelli having not yet departed for Saudi Arabia, Arsenal have only brought in £46m from player sales, having flogged Leandro Trossard, Jakub Kiwior, Christian Norgaard and Karl Hein.

Ipswich have spent £165m on new players including the likes of Julio Enciso, Emersonn, Abdul Fatawu, Abdoul Ouattara, Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic as they look to stay in the Prem this time around.



Gary O’Neil’s side have only brought back £16m in player sales, with George Hirst and Arijanet Muric the most high-profile departures, giving them a net spend of £149m.

Seven teams have so far brought in more in player sales than they have spent; Sunderland, Manchester City, Crystal Palace, Brighton, Newcastle, Nottingham Forest and Aston Villa.

City have brought in an astonishing £289m, having flogged the likes of Savio, Tijjani Reijnders, Rodri, James Trafford, Manuel Akanji and Nathan Ake.



Villa, meanwhile, have a net spend of minus-£102m, having brought in £257m from the sales of Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans, Donyell Malen, Enzo Barrenechea, Lewis Dobbin and Lucas Digne.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Manchester United‘s acquisition of Carlos Baleba took their net spend to £100m.

Michael Carrick‘s men have brought in £63m from selling Rasmus Hojlund and Radek Vitek, helping to fund splashes for Baleba, Tielemans and Santos.

Sports.title: Premier League stars’ top cars this season revealed, from a £209k Lamborghini Urus to a £140k electric Porsche
Sports.content:
ITS a new Premier League season, which means its stars will be upgrading their motors.

But, unlike you and me who might shop at AutoTrader or take a walk through an Arnold Clark showroom, footballers go to a more exclusive source.



Football’s elite get in touch with Richard Clark, founder and CEO of Premier Sports Solutions, who supplies some of the most expensive cars in the world.

Their showroom in Bournemouth is filled with supercars from Lamborghini, Audi, Mercedes, and Porsche worth hundreds of thousands of pounds.



Clark told SunSport: “We’ve been selling cars to footballers for over 20 years and for a long time the trends have been pretty obvious.

“It’s always been very SUV heavy. Urus, G63, Range Rover, that sort of thing. But this season we’ve definitely noticed things starting to change.”

Here’s what are the most popular…

Porsche 911, from £139,400

Making a comeback is the Porsche 911, with the GTS and GT3 models proving to be popular.

“This has probably been the biggest surprise,” Clark explained.

“Sports cars traditionally haven’t been that popular with footballers. Most want something big, comfortable and practical that they can use every day, but suddenly we’re getting loads of interest in the new 911.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“The GTS has been especially popular and we’re also getting plenty of interest in the GT3. It definitely feels like sports cars are having a bit of a comeback.”

Lamborghini Urus, from £190,000

Since its release in 2018, the Lamborghini Urus has remained a favorite among Premier League footballers.



And it’s only going to continue when they can get their hands on the new Urus SE Performante, which is slated for late 2026 and is expected to cost around £209,000.

“The Urus is still massive,” Clark revealed.

“It’s been one of the biggest footballer cars for the last few years and the new hybrid versions have got everyone interested again.

“We’ve already had a lot of interest in the new Urus SE Performante, even before the car was announced, which probably says everything about how strong the demand still is.”



Mercedes G63, from £184,595

The G-Wagon is car regularly seen at training grounds all over the country.

It is still a go-to for football’s biggest stars.

Clark said: “The G63 is just one of those cars that never seems to go out of fashion.

“Footballers have loved them for years and every time Mercedes updates it we get existing customers wanting the latest one.



“A lot of the lads still like to personalise them too with Urban kits, wheels and carbon fibre.”

Audi RS5, from £89,400

Audi’s RS5 has always been attractive to footballers, but now as a hybrid and electric it is really cottoned on.

“The new RS5 is proving really popular as well,” Clark told us.



“It’s now hybrid, it’s seriously quick and it still works perfectly as an everyday car.

“We’re definitely seeing players becoming more open to hybrids and electric cars now too.

“Part of that could be the tax benefits if they have a company they can put the car through, but the cars themselves are also getting much better.”



Porsche Cayenne Electric, from £83,200

The speedy Porsche Cayenne Electric, which manages 0-62 mph in 2.5 to 4.8 seconds, is also proving to be a hit off the pitch for players.

“The new electric Cayenne is seriously impressive,” Clark purred.

“We’re already seeing a lot of interest in it from footballers and it’s got all the quality and refinement you expect from a Porsche, but the performance is ridiculous.

“The Turbo accelerates about as quickly as a Bugatti, except you can put the family in it and use it every day.

“I think cars like this are going to make a lot more footballers seriously consider going electric.”



Big in 2027

While those cars are all impressive, Clark is already confident what motor footballers will be desperate to add to their garages NEXT season.

No surprises, it’s a Range Rover Sport, but their Electric version which is slated for release in 2027.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Clark revealed: “I think the new electric Range Rover is going to be huge.



“It basically looks like a normal Range Rover, which is probably exactly what people want. It just happens to be silent and electric.

Sports.title: Julian Alvarez situation ‘very tense’ as Atletico issue devastated star a transfer ultimatum with Arsenal circling
Sports.content:
JULIAN ALVAREZ has been told to get his head down at Atletico Madrid or accept a move to Arsenal, according to reports.

The Argentine striker faces an uncertain future after demanding an exit and failing to seal a dream move to Barcelona this summer.



He was jeered by fans after coming on as a sub in their 2-2 draw against Villarreal on the opening day of La Liga.

The 26-year-old was not in the squad for 2-0 win over Malaga days later and the situation is now “extremely tense”, Sky Sports have reported.



Alvarez is said to be “devastated” by both the hostile reception from supporters and being told he will not be allowed to join Barcelona.

Arsenal are the only other option for Alvarez but the Gunners are not hopeful of sealing a seismic move for the player, the reports.

However, Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta – who helped negotiate Alvarez’s switch from Man City in 2024 – has been in contact with his former employers in recent days.

And Atletico chief Miguel Angel Gil Martin is ready to listen to an offer of £130million from Arsenal if it arrives, the report adds.

Some figures at Atletico believe it is “increasingly impossible” for Alvarez to stay at the club given the toxic situation.

Should Arsenal complete a mega deal for Alvarez, it would be only their second £100m+ arrival after Declan Rice‘s £105m move in 2023.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Spanish journalist Ruben Uria told Sky: “Julian and his agent believe that everything that’s happening is the fault of Gil Marín, Atletico Madrid‘s CEO, who publicly asked them to say they wanted to leave Atletico.

“We are waiting to see how events unfold regarding Julian, waiting to see how Arsenal reacts, and if they have genuine interest in the Argentina player. Atletico Madrid will not sell to Barcelona.”

Alvarez is seen as one of the world’s best forwards after netting 49 goals in 107 outings for the Spanish club.

He joined in an £81m move from Man City, where he scored 36 times in 103 games but became second fiddle to Erling Haaland.



This week, Atletico boss Diego Simeone backed the club’s stance on Alvarez after leaving him out of the Malaga game.

But he opened the door to Alvarez returning to the squad once he had been given more time for his head to clear.

He said: “Miguel Angel is the club’s owner. Nothing is more definitive than the club’s owner, it’s crystal clear.

“It’s like when a judge hands down a ruling: ‘Dismissed’.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“What he said is crystal clear. From a sports perspective, we want to look out for the person, the player, so he can continue to uphold his reputation.

“We don’t see him playing in this game. I hope that over the next four days, he’ll be closer to where we want him to be.”

Sports.title: Former England star Dion Dublin launches new business venture alongside presenting Homes Under The Hammer
Sports.content:
PREMIER LEAGUE icon Dion Dublin has taken on another shock role away from football – after becoming the co-owner of a spirits producer.

The former England striker, 57, has been among Match of the Day’s star-studded pundits for a number of years since hanging up his boots.



And Dublin raised eyebrows when he was announced as the surprise new co-presenter of BBC property show Homes Under the Hammer in 2015.

But the one-time Premier League title winner has launched a fresh business venture.



Dublin – who featured for the likes of Manchester United, Coventry City and Aston Villa before retiring 18 years ago – now co-owns 52North.

The former marksman is set to combine his role with his existing on-screen gigs at the BBC.

Cambridge United club director Dublin said: “What attracted me to 52North was the ambition behind it.

“They have built something really exciting and I could see the potential straight away.

“This isn’t about putting my name on a bottle. I’m becoming part of the business because I believe in the brand, the products and where we can take it.

“We’ve got big ambitions and I’m looking forward to getting stuck in.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Gemma Taylor, who co-founded the Surrey-based spirits producer two years ago, hopes Dublin will help to grow the brand with his network of contacts in sport and broadcasting.

She said: “We’ve always wanted to build 52North for the long-term. We’ve worked incredibly hard to get the brand to where it is today, and bringing Dion on board gives us an opportunity to take that ambition even further.

“Dion and I bring very different experiences to the table, which is exactly why we make a great partnership.

“He genuinely believes in what we’re building and I’m really excited about what we can achieve together.

“We’re now at the stage where we’re looking for the right distribution partner to help us take that next step and make 52North more widely available across the UK.



“It’s important to us that any partner shares our passion for the brand and our ambitions for where 52North can go.”

The award-winning company specialises in producing triple-distilled rum and liqueurs.

Dublin, who won four England caps, notched 111 Premier League goals during his stunning career and bagged the top-flight’s Golden Boot in 1998.

Sports.title: Carlos Baleba is final piece of Man Utd’s midfield jigsaw – now he needs to ‘do a Carrick’ and guide them to the title
Sports.content:
CARLOS BALEBA need look no further than his new manager for the inspiration to be a title winner at Manchester United.

It is 20 years since Michael Carrick joined the Red Devils from Tottenham in an £18.6million deal.



And current boss Carrick’s most consequential signing this summer is another deep-lying midfielder.

Baleba, 22, has arrived from Brighton for an initial £65million — a year since United first enquired about the Cameroonian.



It begs the question why United waited until the final week of the transfer window to sign him.

But their midfield overhaul is now complete — with Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos also arriving at Old Trafford this summer.



Towards the end of last season United also tied down England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo, 21, on a contract until 2031.

No player in Baleba’s position has proved such a game-changer in terms of helping United to fulfil their ambitions since Carrick’s arrival in 2006.

Sir Alex Ferguson needed to strengthen his midfield at the time with United having been unable to win the Premier League title in three successive seasons.

Carrick proved the final piece in the jigsaw as United were crowned champions in his first season.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

And along with Owen Hargreaves who arrived the following summer, Carrick was pivotal in the Red Devils finishing top of the pile in five of Fergie’s final seven seasons in charge — as well as winning the Champions League in 2008 — before his retirement in 2013.

United have made headline signings for their engine room since those two – Marouane Fellaini, Paul Pogba, Fred, Casemiro and Manuel Ugarte among them.

But none have them have been able to help United to their former Premier League heights. Pogba was Baleba’s idol.

But hopefully there will be none of the constant problems Pogba caused in trying to force an exit during his second six-year stint at United.

Baleba’s arrival is perhaps recognition that Santos — signed from Chelsea for £50m — does not offer all of the solutions to the Red Devils’ problem No 6 position,



Santos does not have Baleba’s physicality and United’s need for a specialist defensive midfielder saw them make a fresh enquiry to Real Madrid for Frenchman Aurelien Tchouameni last month.

Baleba commanded a cheaper fee and salary than Tchouameni would have done — and has the benefit of three years of Prem experience.

Director of football Jason Wilcox said: “Carlos’ determination to join Manchester United and his confidence we will achieve our shared ambitions mean he’s the perfect signing.”



Baleba was impressed by United’s vision for his development and was made to feel wanted.

He had briefly spoken with Carrick and been deep in conversation with Matheus Cunha after United’s 3-0 win at Brighton on the final day of last season.

Even though Brighton had just qualified for the Conference League, Baleba had set his sights higher.

He will get Champions League football at United and believes he is an ideal fit having adapted to the Prem’s speed and physicality over the past three season.

Baleba completed United’s rebuild for the new season.



Bruno Fernandes’ future has been a point of discussion for months and was this week crowed United’s first PFA Player of the Year since Wayne Rooney in 2010.

While the Portuguese midfielder has enough individual accolades to fill a skip, he has found team medals harder to come by.

He was won just two trophies in nearly seven years with United — although they have also lost two European finals in that time.

He can no longer complain that the squad is lacking.



United may be unconvincing in defence but they have nine fit senior defenders and Baleba’s arrival gives the squad greater balance.

Fernandes was close to Casemiro, the predecessor in Baleba’s position before his departure in the summer.

While Baleba does not quite have the presence of five-time Champions League winner Casemiro, he is more athletic and dynamic.

Fernandes turns 32 in September and his contract expires next year.



United will almost certainly trigger a one-year extension until 2028 — unless they furnish Fernandes with a new deal before then.

United have targeted 2028 — the 150th anniversary of the club — to end their long wait for a title.

Sealing a 21st United title would not only be the perfect send-off for Fernandes, it would seal his status as a legendary figure at the club.

Even before Saturday’s horror show at Hull — that saw them start the season with a shock 2-0 defeat — this season has felt too soon for United to be crowned champions.



But they should have little trouble in convincing Fernandes to agree to new terms.

He will have some leverage in terms of his salary however — particularly with the return of Marcus Rashford, the club’s highest wage earner despite having made his last start for United in December 2024.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

United have made no secret they want their salary structure to ensure their best player is also their highest earner. The PFA award underlines Fernandes’ status.

But he is another man who can be inspired by Carrick in his quest for a Prem title.

Sports.title: Mayer: I feel unbeatable - Cameron fight won't be close!
Sports.content:
Mikaela Mayer says she feels "unbeatable" and that her blockbuster unification fight against Chantelle Cameron for the world super welterweight titles won't be close.

British WBO title holder Cameron (22-1, 8 KOs) faces American Mayer (22-2, 5 KOs) at the bp pulse LIVE arena on Saturday - live on Sky Sports - with every bout on the MVPW-06 main card pitting a UK fighter against a US opponent.

WBA and WBC champion Mayer has no shortage of respect for Cameron - who has won her last four fights since a rematch defeat to Katie Taylor in 2023 - but has backed her own ability to unify the titles in front of what is set to be a hostile Birmingham crowd.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer says she and Chantelle Cameron are at the peak of their powers and that the super welterweight showdown can only lead to 'an action-packed' fight.

"I feel better than ever," Mayer told Sky Sports. "I just know I just feel unbeatable right now. I feel in a great position and I can't wait to get out to the UK and do my thing.

"[Cameron] is good at what she does. She's an aggressive fighter. She lets her hands go.

"She fights at a fast pace and so do I. So that's going to make for a very exciting fight for the fans.

"But I just don't think it's going to be as close and as much of a war as everyone thinks.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chantelle Cameron can't wait for her unified world super welterweight title fight with Mikaela Mayer in Birmingham on 29 August.

"There's probably a handful of people who think I'm stupid for coming to the UK and going onto Chantelle's turf, but I'm just confident in myself right now.

"I'm fighting better than I've ever fought, smarter than I've ever been. And I just believe in myself.

"I feel like no matter where I go, I'm still going to kick butt. So it could be here. It could be there. I'm taking the win."

Mayer pointed to her "versatility" as a defining factor come Saturday, insisting nothing can prepare Cameron for the new and improved version of the 36-year-old that awaits.

"I'm really hard to train for because I've developed so much these last 10 months of being in the gym," Mayer told Sky Sports.

"I know I haven't fought since last October but the things I'm doing now, it's really impossible for Chantelle to have trained for me at this point.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer, Chantelle Cameron, Caroline Dubois and Amelia Moore face off ahead of their MVP 06 clashes on Saturday.

"I'm going to do everything I can to make it a very obvious win, maybe a stoppage, we'll see, but I know I'm coming out with my hand raised.

"I've worked on making sure that my inside game and when I do press forward that my defence is tighter and I'm the one landing my shots. I'll definitely be using a little bit of everything I've got, but knowing mine and Chantelle's styles there will definitely be moments where it will be a dog fight."

Mayer vs Cameron - fighter records

Mikaela Mayer Wins 22 Losses 2

Chantelle Cameron Wins 22 Losses 1

'A win would be one of the best moments of my career'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer is supremely confident she'll beat Chantelle Cameron when the pair clash on 29 August, live on Sky Sports.

The 35-year-old Cameron won the WBO super welterweight title - a belt Mayer had vacated just months after beating Mary Spencer for it - with a dominant victory over Michaela Kotaskova in April.

The significance of the chance to become unified world champion by reclaiming the WBO crown is not lost on Mayer, with the American describing the prospect of victory as a career-defining moment.

"[A win would be] definitely up there with one of the best [moments].

"I've had a pretty awesome career. Even though I've gone through some ups and downs, I think that's what makes my career even more special and what makes these big fights that are ahead of me extra special.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chantelle Cameron says she has been waiting a long time for a big name clash with Mikaela Mayer and put their super welterweight world titles on the line.

"I've had to go through trials and tribulations - I've had to adjust, I've had to make changes in my team and keep continuing to get better - and I've done that.

"Going in there and having a dominating performance against someone like Chantelle Cameron, who is very highly respected - the only person to beat Katie Taylor - that's going to definitely be one of the best moments of my career thus far."

The upcoming bout may not be the last between the two, with Mayer revealing that a rematch clause has been included in the contract of both fighters:

"Well, Chantelle and I do have a rematch clause on both of our ends, which is unique, but if it's the type of fight that everyone expects, then why not do a rematch?

"Why not give it to the world again? I have no problem giving a rematch when it's, when it's justified.

"Do I want to kick her butt so bad that she doesn't even want to activate that rematch clause? Of course. But if she does, we can go again."
