World.title: Joao Fonseca Pulls Out of 2026 US Open With Abdominal Injury
World.content:
Brazilian tennis star Joao Fonseca has withdrawn from the 2026 US Open after failing to recover from an abdominal injury suffered during the Cincinnati Open. Fonseca announced his decision on Monday, August 24, less than a week before the men’s singles competition begins at Flushing Meadows.

The 20-year-old underwent medical tests and began treatment after returning to Brazil, but he and his team determined that he needed more time before competing again. “Unfortunately, this means I won’t be able to play in the US Open,” Fonseca said. “It was not an easy decision to make, as it is a very special tournament for me.”

Fonseca first felt discomfort on the left side of his abdomen during a practice session in Cincinnati. He had defeated Botic van de Zandschulp in his opening match but withdrew before facing Christopher O’Connell in the third round. The initial hope was that Fonseca would recover in time for New York. Further examinations, however, showed that attempting to play a best-of-five-set Grand Slam tournament would come too soon.

His absence removes one of Latin America’s leading players from the final major tournament of the season. Fonseca entered the week ranked No. 26 in the world and owns a 19-13 record in 2026. His biggest result came at the French Open, where he reached his first Grand Slam quarterfinal after beating Novak Djokovic and two-time finalist Casper Ruud.

The Brazilian eventually lost to Jakub Mensik in the quarterfinals, but his run in Paris strengthened his reputation as one of the most dangerous young players on the men’s tour. The US Open also holds special meaning for Fonseca. He won the boys’ singles title in New York in 2023 and made his men’s main-draw debut two years later. He reached the second round in 2025 before losing to Tomas Machac.

Injuries have interrupted Fonseca’s season more than once. A lower-back problem forced him to withdraw from tournaments in Brisbane and Adelaide at the beginning of the year and also kept him out of Brazil’s February Davis Cup series. Fonseca has not announced a firm date for his return. Brazil is scheduled to face Switzerland in the Davis Cup on September 18 and 19 in Rio de Janeiro, but his participation will depend on how quickly the abdominal injury heals.

The men’s singles draw will be held on August 27, with first-round matches beginning August 30.

World.title: Costa Rica Relies on One Machine for Key Cancer Treatment
World.content:
Costa Rica’s public health system depends on a single machine at Hospital México to provide an important form of cancer treatment, leaving patients vulnerable if the equipment stops working, according to the internal auditors of the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS).

The machine provides brachytherapy, a type of radiation treatment used particularly for cervical cancer. Instead of directing radiation at the tumor from outside the body, doctors place a small radioactive source inside or very close to the affected area. This allows doctors to deliver a strong dose directly to the tumor while limiting radiation exposure to nearby healthy tissue. Brachytherapy can also be used for prostate, breast and other cancers.

The CCSS Internal Audit raised the concern in an advisory issued on July 21. It warned that the institution’s entire ability to provide the treatment is concentrated in one unit at Hospital México. That means a mechanical failure, maintenance problem, shortage of specialized supplies or difficulty with the hospital’s infrastructure could interrupt brachytherapy across the public health system.

The risk is not theoretical. The previous machine failed beyond repair in December 2021, leaving Costa Rica without the equipment needed to continue the treatment. The CCSS responded by providing financial assistance for some patients to travel abroad for care. That arrangement increased costs, created additional paperwork and placed patients at risk of delays during treatment.

A replacement machine has since been installed, but Costa Rica still has no second public unit available as a backup. The concern is especially serious for patients with locally advanced cervical cancer. Brachytherapy is often used alongside chemotherapy and radiation delivered from outside the body. For some patients, ordinary external radiation is not considered an equal substitute.

Timing also matters. Cancer treatments are planned in a specific order and within a recommended period. An interruption can make it harder for doctors to complete the treatment as intended. The auditors said Costa Rica will continue to need brachytherapy for decades, even as vaccination against the human papillomavirus, commonly known as HPV, and improved screening help prevent more cervical cancer cases.

HPV causes most cervical cancers. Vaccination and early detection can greatly reduce the risk, but they do not remove the immediate need to treat people who already have the disease.

The audit urged CCSS authorities to examine ways to reduce the Costa Rica’s dependence on the Hospital México machine. Possible solutions would need to be considered as part of the institution’s plans for equipment purchases, hospital infrastructure, maintenance and emergency preparation.

The available information did not include a deadline for obtaining a backup machine or expanding the treatment to another public hospital. The warning comes as the CCSS is carrying out wider changes to Costa Rica’s radiotherapy services. Hospital México is replacing aging radiation equipment, while additional treatment capacity is planned for other hospitals.

However, those projects involve several types of radiation technology. A new external-radiation machine does not automatically provide the same treatment as a brachytherapy unit. For patients, the audit’s main point is that Costa Rica once lost access to this treatment because its only machine failed, and the public health system remains exposed to the same basic risk.

World.title: 19-year-old man remanded for allegedly stabbing brother in the eye; come to court with his eye black
World.content:
19-year-old man remanded for allegedly stabbing brother in the eye; come to court with his eye black

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being accused of attacking his older brother with a knife during a family dispute.

Brenton Conrad Archer, a construction worker of Iguana Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument upon his 22-year-old brother.

Archer pleaded not guilty.

Police allege that Archer and his brother became involved in an altercation at a residence on Iguana Street on Friday, August 21. The confrontation reportedly escalated into a fight during which Archer’s brother was stabbed several times.

Police later visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where the brother was observed with lacerations to both sides of his mouth as well as stab wounds to his left eye and cheek.

The prosecution did not object to bail for Archer; however, the Magistrate expressed concern that the brothers may live at the same residence or in close proximity to each other.

Archer told the court that his brother does not live in the same yard, but the Magistrate opted to temporarily withhold bail while the prosecution verifies their living arrangements.

The court said the precaution was necessary to avoid another confrontation between the siblings once Archer is released.

Archer, who also appeared in court with visible injuries to his eye and a bandaged right hand, was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

He is due back in court on September 2, 2026, when the issue of bail is expected to be revisited.

World.title: Sheffan Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza remanded over alleged armed burglary and theft of $46,000 pickup
World.content:
Sheffan Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza remanded over alleged armed burglary and theft of $46,000 pickup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A member of the Belize Coast Guard and a salesman/manager were remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday after being charged with aggravated burglary in connection with an alleged armed home invasion in Hattieville.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sheffan Devan Hemmans, a member of the Belize Coast Guard, and 46-year-old Alberto Arreaza, a salesman, manager and farmer from Teakettle Village, appeared before a Magistrate in Court #5, where they were jointly charged with aggravated burglary.

Police allege that on Thursday, August 20, the men, while armed with a firearm, entered a home in the Mile 17 area of Hattieville and stole a pickup truck.

The vehicle is valued at $46,000.

Both men pleaded not guilty to the charge.

The Magistrate informed Arreaza and Hemmans that, because the alleged offence involved a firearm, the lower court could not grant them bail at this stage. They were advised that they may apply to the High Court for bail through an attorney if they wish to secure their release before becoming eligible for bail consideration in the Magistrate’s Court.

Both men were subsequently remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Arreaza and Hemmans are due back in court on October 20, 2026, when they are expected to receive disclosure in the case.

World.title: Man accused of stealing cousin’s bicycle remanded after court rejects guilty plea
World.content:
Man accused of stealing cousin’s bicycle remanded after court rejects guilty plea

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 27-year-old Belize City construction worker accused of stealing his cousin’s bicycle was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after telling the court he was considering pleading guilty simply because he had no one to bail him.

Israel Anthony Usher appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with theft.

Police allege that on August 13, 2026, Usher stole a 24-inch Hurricane Beach Cruiser bicycle valued at $500 from a female relative at a Benbow Street address.

Before entering a plea, Usher told the Magistrate that if he pleaded not guilty he had no one to secure bail for him, and asked whether pleading guilty would result in a fine instead.

The Magistrate told Usher that a guilty plea could only be accepted if he was actually admitting that he stole the bicycle.

Usher then denied stealing it, telling the court that the owner is his cousin and had allowed him to borrow the bicycle. According to Usher, police later stopped him while he was riding the bicycle against the flow of traffic and confiscated it after he was unable to produce proof of ownership.

He claimed his cousin later believed he had stolen or disposed of the bicycle and made a theft complaint against him.

After hearing his explanation, the Magistrate refused to accept a guilty plea merely for convenience and entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf.

Usher was offered bail in the sum of $500 plus one surety of the same amount, but was unable to secure bail by the end of the day and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

He is due back in court on October 6, 2026, when the theft matter will continue.

World.title: Belize City man ordered to stay 100 yards from brother after allegedly pulling knife on him
World.content:
Belize City man ordered to stay 100 yards from brother after allegedly pulling knife on him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City businessman accused of assaulting his brother, including allegedly threatening him with a knife, is out on bail but has been ordered by the court to stay at least 100 yards away from his sibling while the case remains active.

Thirty-two-year-old Alexander Elvis Jones, a resident of the Conch Shell Bay area, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with common assault and aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument upon his brother.

The charges stem from an alleged dispute on August 5, 2026.

Jones pleaded not guilty to both counts.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail in the sum of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

As conditions of his bail, Jones must have no contact with his brother or any other prosecution witnesses and must remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant. He is also required to attend all court dates or risk having his bail revoked.

Jones met bail and is due back in court on October 5, 2026, for disclosure.

World.title: Woman granted $800 bail after allegedly threatening to burn down her sister’s home with sister and children inside
World.content:
Woman granted $800 bail after allegedly threatening to burn down her sister’s home with sister and children inside

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 38-year-old Belize City woman has been granted bail after being charged with threat to damage property following an alleged family dispute in which she is accused of threatening to burn down her sister’s home.

Shantae Robateau, a customer care representative, appeared in court unrepresented and pleaded not guilty to the charge. Police allege that during an incident on July 31, 2026, Robateau threatened her sister, saying she would burn down the house while she and her children were inside.

According to the police report, the sister told investigators that she was at her Ebony Street home at around 9:15 p.m. when Robateau allegedly arrived outside the residence carrying a piece of 2-by-4 wood, shouting and demanding that Jones come outside.

The complainant reportedly contacted their older brother, who lives nearby, and asked him to intervene. Police say that as efforts were made to remove Robateau from the property, she allegedly threatened to physically harm her sister and later threatened to burn the house down with her sister and her children inside.

The woman subsequently made a report to police, prompting an investigation. Robateau later turned herself in to police and was charged.

At her arraignment, the prosecution did not object to bail but requested that conditions be imposed. The Magistrate granted Robateau bail in the sum of $800 with one surety of the same amount.

As part of her bail conditions, she must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Friday between 6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. and attend all scheduled court appearances.

The case was adjourned until October 13, 2026.

World.title: Justin Goff rejects 1 year sentence for guilty plea in ammunition case
World.content:
Justin Goff rejects 1 year sentence for guilty plea in ammunition case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Justin Stephen Goff, 38, has decided to maintain his not guilty plea and proceed toward trial on a charge of keeping unlicensed ammunition, two days after asking the Belize City Magistrate’s Court for an indication of the sentence he could receive if he pleaded guilty.

Goff appeared in court Friday morning and told the Magistrate that, after considering the matter, he would not plead guilty.

On Wednesday, August 19, Goff had requested a sentence indication as he considered changing his plea. He was reportedly informed that, after consideration of an early guilty plea and other mitigating and aggravating factors, he could face a sentence of approximately one year and four months’ imprisonment.

Goff, however, rejected that option on Friday and will instead contest the charge.

His case was adjourned until September 4, 2026, when he is expected to receive disclosure from the prosecution.

Goff was first arraigned on April 7, 2026, after police alleged that he was found three days earlier in possession of three live rounds of ammunition — two S&B rounds and one Aguila round — without a licence.

At his arraignment, Goff pleaded not guilty and alleged that the ammunition had been planted on him by a police officer. He told the court that he had been asleep beneath a shed when officers approached and questioned him about a firearm.

Goff claimed that an officer later produced three rounds of ammunition and falsely attributed them to him.

He remains on remand while the case proceeds.

World.title: Protecting Belize’s Children: UNHCR and UNICEF train social workers to handle high-risk cases
World.content:
Protecting Belize’s Children: UNHCR and UNICEF train social workers to handle high-risk cases

By Zoila Palma: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, and UNICEF are working to strengthen Belize’s child protection system by training social workers and child protection professionals to better respond to vulnerable children, including those affected by displacement, abuse, neglect and family separation.

The Best Interest Procedure Training brings together frontline professionals from across the country to develop practical skills for making decisions that prioritize the safety, rights and well-being of children.

Participants are taking part in case studies, interactive discussions and practical exercises focused on assessing risks and developing appropriate protection responses.

The training is especially important for cases involving violence, exploitation, neglect, abuse, displacement and family separation, where decisions can have lasting consequences for children.

The Best Interest Procedure provides a structured, child-centered approach to help social workers determine what course of action is most appropriate for each individual child.

The initiative forms part of continued collaboration between UNHCR, UNICEF and the Department of Human Services within the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs.

UNHCR Officer-in-Charge in Belize Mariya Voloshkevich said strengthening the capacity of social workers is an important investment in Belize’s child protection system, while UNICEF Representative Sajid Ali emphasized that every child has the right to protection, care and support.

Department of Human Services Director Shawn Vargas stressed that family separation must be approached with particular care. He noted that children have a fundamental right to family life and, whenever it is safe and appropriate, should remain with or maintain meaningful contact with their families. He emphasized that separation should not be treated as an easy or automatic solution, and that any decision to separate a child from their family must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, while considering both the immediate and long-term impact on the child.

UNHCR and UNICEF say they will continue working with Belizean officials and partners to strengthen child protection services and safeguard the rights and well-being of children across the country.

World.title: Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October
World.content:
Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Fresh Pond resident Imari Young, who is before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a burglary charge, was allowed to remain on bail Friday after being brought before the court on a bench warrant for failing to attend a previous court date.

Young appeared unrepresented before Magistrate Neeshad Rohammad, who asked him to explain why his bail should not be revoked after he failed to appear in court on July 22.

Young told the court that he had been sick at the time. He also said his mother is hospitalized and that his father recently died. Young claimed that he had obtained a doctor’s document explaining his absence, although the court reportedly had no record of receiving it.

Despite the missed appearance, the Magistrate did not revoke Young’s bail and allowed him to remain free while his case continues.

Young is charged with burglary and is now scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on October 14, 2026, when his trial is expected to begin.

World.title: Unhealthy trend: Student obesity surges to 15.3%
World.content:
The Global School-based Health Survey confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight. (Photo: Adobe stock)

MORE than three in every 10 students captured in a recent survey by the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) were overweight while 15.3 per cent of them were obese.

The Global School-based Health Survey (GSHS), which was conducted between January and March this year, had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools.

It confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight, while underweight remains a concern.

According to the survey, obesity moved from six per cent in 2010 to 15.3 per cent in 2026, while the number of overweight students jumped from 21.7 per cent in 2010 to 31.7 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, there was an uptick in underweight students, from 2.1 per cent in 2010 to 3.4 per cent in 2026.

The survey also found a dip in physical activity from 23.2 per cent in 2017 to 19.6 per cent in 2026, while 70.2 per cent reported less than eight hours of sleep, which can be attributed to the long hours students spend on the Internet as sedentary behaviour — sitting down for more than three hours per day increased from 56.4 per cent in 2017 to 68 per cent in 2026.

“Students [who are] less active, more sedentary, and many not getting enough sleep means that there is an increased risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems,” said the NCDA.

It called for more physical activity, greater promotion of recreation and sports, and encouragement for students to adopt healthy sleep habits.

The NCDA blamed unhealthy eating patterns for the rise in obesity among students, and recommended the promotion of healthy school food environment, expansion of nutrition education, and promotion of balanced diets.

But despite the increase in obesity and overweight, the survey found that in the 30 days before it was conducted there was a drop in consumption of one or more sodas per day by students.

In 2010 the NCDA found that 72.5 per cent on the respondents had consumed one or more sodas in the 30 days before the survey, while this year only 49.7 per cent of the respondents said they had done so in the past seven days.

The survey said underweight was highest among grade nine boys, 6.4 per cent, and grade 11 girls, 4.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the highest rate of obesity was among grade seven girls, 43.2 per cent, and grade seven boys, 40.5 per cent.

The Global School-based Health Survey, noted the NCDA, provides high-quality data to inform decision-making and action for school and youth health.

In his reaction to the survey findings, Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton urged parents and guardians to ensure their children eat healthy foods at home and school.

He said it is always a better choice to take a meal from home to school if the school does not have facilities for the preparation of hot meals.

Tufton also urged parents and guardians to encourage their children to participate in more physical activities if they want to ensure that they do not fall victim to diabetes, heart disease, and other non-communicable diseases.

“Parents and guardians must insist that their children become more health conscious. Fast food and sugary beverages are not healthy, and I want to remind you parents that, should these young ones get diagnosed with a non-communicable disease, it will follow them into adulthood and put more stress on your resources as well as the health system,” said Tufton.

The NCDA said the survey has shown that healthy eating, regular physical activities, and adequate sleep are essential for the well-being, learning, and long-term health of Jamaica’s children and adolescents.

It added that the lack of physical activity increases the risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID); and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: ‘Baddies build furniture too’
World.content:
Carpenter Sydonie Miller at her shop in DunKirk, Kingston (Photo: Garfield Robinson).

With work hard to find and financial constraints mounting during the coronavirus pandemic, one Jamaican woman discovered a hidden talent that opened an unexpected livelihood for her in a labour-intensive trade not often pursued by local females – carpentry.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sydonie Miller had been finding it difficult to secure a job in 2020, during the heights of COVID-19, despite having a bachelor’s degree in business management and secretarial skills.

Miller, who was a new mother at the time, said her husband, a taxi operator, was the only one working and she was determined to find a way to contribute to her family.

Her journey to carpentry began with a desire to own a padded bedhead and being quoted what she considered an exorbitant price to have one made.

“At the time, it was padded bed did run the place. When I go to ask the price, them a give me an arm and a leg for it. Me say me nah pay that,” Miller told Observer Online.

So, she decided to build it herself.

Seeking the guidance of a carpenter friend on Charles Street and gathering the necessary materials, Miller went on to make her first bedhead.

After completing the project, Miller’s curiosity and determination pushed her to learn more. She eventually made her way to Oxford Street, where veteran carpenters such as Chucky, Paul, Max, Abi Doll and Warren took her under their wings and taught her how to build a wider range of furniture, including dressers, chests of drawers and beds.

But for Miller, learning the trade was not difficult because she has always been a practical learner. She quickly grasped the skills being taught to her.

“If you’re going to do something, I see what you’re doing. If you show me one time, you don’t have to show me again. Just the one time, I know what to do,” she explained.

But the mother of three said her entry into carpentry was about more than simply learning how to build furniture. She believes the skill was placed in her path for a reason.

“At the time, I was at work and I can’t forget the day. The almighty say I give you a skill, go and use it. I have business management, secretarial skills. I thought it was that skill but I never knew it was this skill. So when him say I give you a skill, go and use it, me just say alright me ago just go deal with the bed head. Me see say me can build dresser and me just a build. Me go under the wings of the veterans,” she said.

Miller, who now owns her very own furniture business, Luxurious Furnitures by Syd, said her client base now ranges from individual customers to stores in the downtown Kingston area.

When Observer Online visited her shop on Banana Street in the McIntyre Villa community of East Kingston, Miller was seen working on a bedhead and bed bottom for one of her customers.

While her skills have helped her build a business, Miller said being a woman in a male-dominated trade has presented its own challenges.

“Some of them, when them see a woman come and say you know say me build this, them don’t believe it” she explained.

Miller said some customers only become convinced that she builds the furniture herself after seeing a male carpenter deliver one of her pieces.

Despite the doubters, Miller said she has also encountered customers who appreciate the fact that she is a woman in the trade and are willing to give her the time needed to complete their furniture.

“To be honest, it’s a bittersweet moment, but at the end of the day there are some people that really love me, who are really happy that I’m a woman and I do this. You have some patient ones, big up on unu self. Them say alright then, I’ll give you time,” she added.

The carpenter said each piece of furniture requires patience and attention to detail, with the process involving several stages before a finished product is ready.

“For me its patience, to really put in the work, because remember, furniture building takes time. It has different layers, different processes to build. So to build a bed head like this, it takes time. I have a lot of different grades of sanding to do,” she said.

She further explained: “I have to start the sanding from, like, 80, and I go down to 180. Then I go down to 200. Then I go down to 220. It’s patience. And you have to get all the nooks and crannies. You can’t just sand off just the bigger parts. You have to sand from the corners, from underneath, behind, everything. So it’s just patience.”

Of all the furniture she has made since entering the trade, Miller said one particular piece remains her favourite, a king-size mahogany bed set. She said the piece holds special significance because it challenged her skills when she was still new to furniture building.

Miller is now encouraging other women not to allow traditional perceptions about certain professions to prevent them from pursuing their interests.

“Don’t follow the stigma say a man work. Woman can do it, too. Once you see something that you want to do just do it. Learn the skill, do it, because at the end of the day, it’s not who do it. It’s really how you set your mind to do it or if you have the determination to do it,” Miller said. “So don’t follow them a man work. Baddies build furniture too. Baddies build furniture too.”

World.title: Fewer students drunk or high
World.content:
(Photo: Adobe stock)

THE National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) is reporting that fewer teenagers are using illegal drugs or drinking alcohol across Jamaica, but the numbers remain concerning.

According to the NCDA, its recent Global School-Based Health Survey (GSHS) conducted January to March 2026 — which had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools — showed that the consumption of alcohol by students in grades seven to 11 dropped from 52.5 per cent in 2010 to 38.8 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, the number of children who started consumption of alcohol before age 14 has decreased from 80.2 per cent in 2010 to 71.5 per cent this year. Also, teenagers who get drunk after the consumption of alcoholic beverages dropped from 35.5 per cent in 2010 to 21.5 per cent in 2026.

But 10.3 per cent of adolescents still attend school under the influence of alcohol, and 10.6 per cent are exposed to s about alcohol.

The NCDA — an agency of the Ministry of Health and Wellness — believes the overall message for positive trends has been working; however, it says continued action is needed to strengthen early prevention programmes, enforce underage drinking laws, reduce youth exposure to alcohol marketing, and increase parent and school engagements.

The survey also found that the use of ganja among adolescents declined from 21.5 per cent in 2017 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, a trend welcomed by the NCDA.

However, the organisation says it is concerned that 24.3 per cent of adolescents have easy access to the weed, while it noticed an emergence in the use of ecstasy, also known as molly.

Ecstasy is a synthetic psychoactive drug with both stimulant and psychedelic effects. Teens use it at parties and other gatherings, but it can cause dangerous spikes in body temperature, dehydration, high blood pressure, and heart failure.

With some students still attending school under the influence of substances because of the easy access to ganja and ecstasy, the NCDA says it will be expanding its substance-use prevention programme, aimed at strengthening prevention, delaying initiation, reducing access, and providing timely support for young people.

It also plans to improve the monitoring of emerging drugs.

In the meantime, the GSHS found that physical fights among students declined from 50.1 per cent in 2010 to 27 per cent in 2026, while injuries from fights dropped from 59.6 per cent in 2010 to 49 per cent in 2026.

In addition, the survey says bullying dropped from 40.2 per cent in 2016 to 27 per cent in 2026.

However, the survey found that 15 per cent of teenagers faced cyber bullying in the past year but there was no comparative figure with 2010. Another 16.9 per cent experienced bullying off school compounds.

The NCDA said despite a drop in physical fights among students, it will be strengthening its violence-prevention programme as it seeks to maintain safe school policies.

“Safe environments are essential for academic success and healthy development,” said the NCDA.

“Violence and injuries impact students’ physical and mental health, learning and well-being. Bullying and cyberbullying can lead to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and social isolation,” the NCDA added.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: More vacancies than advertised
World.content:
Numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts.

With the new academic year just days away numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts. But Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS) President Anniona Jones says the influx of s across various media do not reflect the full picture of the staffing needs.

According to Jones, while some vacancies have been caused by teachers embarking on well-earned vacation breaks, others are the result of educators leaving the system, some without proper notice.

“Some of these resignations do not reach the regional office, and sometimes we fill [vacancies] based on old resumes and not necessarily place all of it in an ad because not every school has the fiscal position to even run an ad. So what you’re seeing in the paper is the tip of the iceberg of the actual gaps in schools because many of us do not place in the national papers the s for teachers. We use a lot of social media, word of mouth, our teachers’ groups, Jamaica Teachers’ Association groups, and so on. That’s what’s happening. So we really don’t have a good picture nationally on what is really happening on the ground,” Jones told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The educator, who was responding to queries by the Observer about what accounts for the almost perennial influx of s yearly during the summer break, explained that the system itself is partly accountable.

“The education system asks all members of the academic staff to apply for their leave by November of the first term, for the following academic year. So leave applications are made almost a year in advance. Usually, by June we would get notification from the Ministry of Education indicating which teachers’ leave application is approved. This year it came a little later in July, and we see where a priority was placed on approving leave applications, certainly in Region One, which is Kingston and St Andrew, for persons who would have applied for eight months,” Jones outlined.

She said while the leave amounts might seem staggering, a little known fact is that “it takes a regular classroom teacher or vice-principal five years of service in order to qualify for four months of leave”.

“So, unlike many people’s workplace where they will get two weeks’ vacation leave, we don’t do that in education, and there are a lot of reasons for that. However, that’s how the system is set up. So teachers will get leave of four months or eight months. They’d apply for study leave, and they would know at that period of time,” she said.

Jones noted that because of the late approvals, principals were not made aware, until July, of how much their staffing levels would be affected for September.

“Usually that’s when many principals know how many of the teachers who have applied for leave have had their leave approved, and whether or not it is for four months, eight months, a year study leave, two years, or so on. So that means that July and August of every year, obviously, you’re going to see a large number of applications in the media, and we will have to fill these positions for smooth start of school for September,” Jones said.

She noted that teacher migration and not just vacation entitlements have also influenced the s of vacancies.

“There are several factors causing teacher migration. It’s not a national problem only, it’s not a regional problem only, it’s an international problem; and if you look at many of the international bodies, such as Education International, some projections go as high as 40 million teachers may be needed within the next decade globally. There are lots of reasons why teachers are leaving the education system: terms and conditions of service, salary, moving on to other interests, and so many other reasons. But we do have a significant shortage in some areas, the industrial arts [for example]. Obviously, persons can earn far more money in the private sector than in teaching,” she told the Observer while noting that Jamaican educators are in high demand by other territories.

The recruitment, she said, is also driven by the fact that there are “shortages in some areas that are undersubscribed like history, geography, the foreign languages like French, Spanish” in addition to the fact that some schools are located in remote areas, or in communities where Zones of Special Operations are in force, or areas that experience high levels of crime or violence, therefore “not many people may want to work in some of those areas”.

According to Jones, the discontinuation of a special hazard allowance — a grant that made to teachers who worked in very remote or rural situations, or in high-risk areas — as an incentive is also a contributor to some schools finding it difficult to fill vacancies.

“So there are many factors that would influence how fluid the system is. And then, of course, if we only have four months available, and that teacher gets a position that is potentially permanent, a teacher may go in that regard. So the short-term vacancies may also be difficult to fill,” the JAPSS president stated.

She said it is difficult to provide a total number of all schools with unfilled vacancies.

“If you look in the papers you will find that even schools that would have advertised before, they may have conducted interviews and even made an offer to a teacher. A teacher may rescind that offer from one school and move to another school where they did interviews because teachers are applying for multiple jobs, they’re doing many interviews, and then they’re picking once they’re offered. So, because of how fluid the system is, you may also find that you may think that you have filled a vacancy, and a teacher calls back to say, ‘I am so sorry. Instead of working at your school for four months or eight months, I’ve just been offered a position for a year, or a clear vacancy at another school, and so I’m going to take that offer instead’. So even though you may think that you filled the vacancy, it now becomes available again because the teacher is moving in the direction of what is best for them and their families,” Jones said.

Asked to say whether this meant the association still has no clear picture as to readiness for the new school year Jones said, “We have filled most of the vacancies… but many schools will have at least one or two positions that they’re hoping to fill this week, with some schools having as many as six or eight positions that are yet to be filled”.

Jones, in the meantime, had this message for parents, guardians, and students: “Every Jamaican child deserves high-quality education, and conditions of work for the teacher are conditions of learning for the children. So if it is that we want the best for our children, then it means we should want the best for the teachers. So, please help us to advocate for the conditions that will be required for us to be able to attract the best and the brightest, retain the most experienced teachers, so that our children can ultimately benefit.”

Added Jones, “Let’s celebrate those who have gone on their well-earned leave; [working] five years to get four months is a lot [and working] 10 years to get eight months is a lot. So let’s celebrate with those who are taking well-deserved breaks. But let us work together to advocate for a better education system.”

World.title: Celene Hall takes Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 crown
World.content:
Celene Hall makes her first walk as Miss Universe Jamaica 2026.

Despite winning five sectional prizes, the newly crowned Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 titleholder, Portland native Celene Hall said she had no idea that she would have emerged the winner.

Hall competed with 32 other ladies for the coveted title and to represent Jamaica at the Miss Universe finals in Puerto Rico in November.

he coronation show took place on Sunday night inside a jam-packed ballroom at AC Hotel Kingston.

“I know I received a lot of sectional awards, but honestly, it wasn’t until the crown was placed on my head that I really knew that I was Miss Universe Jamaica 2026,” Hall told the

Jamaica Observer shortly after she was crowned.

This marked the start of a new journey and the end of countless days and nights of practice, rehearsals, and training.

Hall first entered the Miss Universe Jamaica Portland pageant, which she won a few months ago.

According to Parish Director Shanique Rogers, Hall was transformed during the process.

“From the beginning, she listened, she understood what the crown represented, and, most importantly, she was willing to learn… She is not the same woman who entered the competition in Portland. The Miss Universe Jamaica Portland platform challenged her, developed her, and helped shape her into the queen she is today,” Rogers, a former Miss Universe Jamaica finalist, told the Observer.

She added: “Seeing Celene win makes me incredibly proud, because I know the amount of hard work, dedication, and behind-the-scenes effort that went into preparing her for this moment. To see that hard work pay off is truly rewarding.”

Hall concurred that the pageant challenged her.

“I knew the space would challenge me more to grow into the absolute best version of myself, and that is the reason why I entered in the first place,” she shared.

From Passley Gardens in Port Antonio, she attended Titchfield High School.

Her beaming parents, three sisters and two brothers were on hand to witness her success.

“She started modeling from primary school and she just kept going, and we have been supportive of her,” said her mother, Sonia Hall.

Father Victor said, “Celene has been a queen from ever since. I told her mother from the beginning that Celene had what it takes.”

The coronation show started more than an hour late, and once it got going there was no turning back. The 33 contestants opened the show but they were quickly reduced to a top 20.

The ladies then moved into swimwear before the top 14 were announced.

The evening gown competition resulted in the final six spots being filled.

After being interviewed, the final three were revealed to be Kadejah Anderson, Celene Hall, and Tianna McDaniel.

Hall won the Essence of Style Award, Best in Swimwear, Best in Evening Gown, Most Aware, and the Altruism Award.

Tianna McDaniel was adjudged Most Photogenic; Andrea Hill – Most Congenial; Marcie Lee Smith – Best Personality; Alanda Newman – Runway Star Award; and Marsha Roberts, Alanda Newman and Channon Smith made a three-way tie for Spirit of the Pageant award.

At the end of the night second runner-up was determined to be Anderson, while McDaniel, a medical practitioner, finished in the first runner-up position, as Hall snagged first place.

World.title: ‘Cricket isn’t dead!’
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen opener Kirk McKenzie hits the ball during the Caribbean Premier League T20 match against Trinbago Knight Riders at Sabina Park in Kingston on August 15, 2026.

JAMAICA Cricket Association President Dr Donovan Bennett believes the Jamaica Kingsmen have already made a strong impression on the island is optimistic they can play a key role in developing grassroots cricket locally.

The Caribbean Premier League (CPL) returned to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019 as the new Jamaica franchise hosted four games which concluded last Tuesday.

Tens of thousands of Jamaicans turned out for the four matches against the Barbados Tridents, Trinbago Knight Riders, Guyana Amazon Warriors and St Kitts and Nevis Patriots with some of the Caribbean’s top players on display including the Kingsmen’s own Rovman Powell and Andre Russell as well as regional stars Nicholas Pooran, Shimron Hetmeyer and Sunil Narine.

It continued the trend of growing crowd interest shown by local fans following last summer’s series between the West Indies and Australia, as well as Sri Lanka’s visit in June.

Bennett believes the Kingsmen’s home leg is a good reflection of the state of cricket in Jamaica.

“I have heard many persons who are or were cricket fans saying that cricket is dead in Jamaica but what both the Sri Lanka tour and the CPL that followed have clearly said is that cricket is not dead in Jamaica,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“In fact, cricket is still one of the most popular sports in the country and that as long as the people are fed the right diet, they get what they want to see, they will come out and support us and it was clear to everybody from the crowds. It was a fantastic atmosphere, not just the numbers, but the participation because the crowds were a behind the team with almost every ball that was bowled. It was really something electric and really a pleasure to sit and observe.”

Although pleased with action on the pitch, Bennett says he was impressed by the Kingsmen’s early investment in youth cricket.

The team’s ownership sponsored the All-Grace Shield and All-Headley Cup exhibitions tournament in July, which saw some of the best high school cricketers from the urban and rural areas go head to head in a 50 over match and a T20 match over two days. The

Observer understands the Kingsmen handed over $3.1 million to the JCA to execute the matches.

“As I made a presentation to them, it was a yes and I can tell you, the amount that was literally given to us for the two games is a significant amount of money which comfortably put both games on,” Bennett said. “I think it is something that should encourage the schools to participate on a wider basis and for players to have something substantive to look forward to at the end of the season. It should be the responsibility of ISSA but in a situation where ISSA does not have an interest, then I think the JCA has got to take up the responsibility and get those games on a yearly basis.”

While happy with the progress the Kingsmen have made, Bennett wants them to do more to help develop the next generation of Jamaican cricketers.

“As soon as the CPL is concluded, hopefully we can sit down with the Kingsmen to discuss other development programmes because I am not one of those who sees development from above downwards. I think that is one of the problems with West Indies Cricket over the years is that a lot of money has been spent at the top and very little at the bottom,” he said.

“We have had initial discussions, we haven’t had any decisions as yet. But certainly things like our under-13 programme has got to be put on the table because we really want to do an extended, comprehensive under-13 programme. Every year, we need to have an Under-13 Jamaica team and then from that, we need to extract the best players out of that group every year and put them into a specialised, continuous programme so that in a couple of years’ time, we can have a large cadre of players who, from an early age, have been taught the right things, the right attitudes and also the seriousness at which they should take the cricket, both representing Jamaica and the West Indies.”

The Kingsmen, who have four games remaining in the league stage, are currently just outside the play-off spot in fifth on four points. They return to action on Thursday against the Patriots at Warner Park in St Kitts.

World.title: Before You Book: Questions You Should Ask Your Hotel Wedding Venue
World.content:
Finding a beautiful hotel venue is exciting. You can already picture the décor, the guests arriving, the food being served and everything coming together perfectly.

But before you sign the contract or pay that deposit, there are a few important conversations you need to have.

When planning a wedding at a hotel, what you don’t ask can sometimes cost you just as much as what you do. A venue may look perfect during a walkthrough, but the details behind the scenes — from additional fees and set-up times to catering restrictions and technology — can have a major impact on your event.

Here are some things you should know before saying yes to a hotel venue.

What Exactly Is Included in the Venue Cost?

Never assume that everything you see during your tour is included in the quoted price. You should also ask about taxes, service charges, overtime charges and any additional fees that may appear on the final bill. The goal isn’t simply to know the rental price; it’s to understand the true cost of hosting your event there.

Will the Space Really Work for Your Wedding?

Capacity is about more than the maximum number of people allowed in a room. A ballroom might accommodate 300 people theatre-style but significantly fewer once you add banquet tables, a stage, dance floor, buffet stations, décor and audiovisual equipment.

Explain exactly what you’re planning and ask the hotel how many guests the space can comfortably accommodate with your preferred layout.

Think Beyond the Start and End Time

Your invitation might say 6:00 pm, but your event begins long before the first guest arrives. Decorators, florists, entertainers, photographers and production teams may need several hours to prepare. Ask when vendors can access the venue, where they can load and unload, and how much time is allowed for breakdown afterward. If additional set-up or breakdown time comes at an extra cost, that’s something you want to know well in advance.

Understand the Food and Beverage Details



If the hotel provides catering, don’t stop at choosing a menu. Ask about food-and-beverage minimums, service styles, what’s included in the per-person price and how dietary requirements and allergies are handled. If you’re hoping to bring a special cake, outside caterer or another food or beverage item, confirm whether it’s permitted and whether additional fees apply.

These small details can have a surprisingly big impact on both your plans and your budget.

Ask About Vendors, Technology and Entertainment

If you already have a favourite decorator, DJ, photographer or production company, confirm that they’re allowed to work at the hotel. Some properties have preferred or exclusive vendors, while others may require outside suppliers to provide insurance or meet specific requirements.

Technology deserves the same attention. Ask what’s available for microphones, speakers, screens, projectors, lighting, electrical connections and Wi-Fi. And before planning candles, elaborate installations, confetti, hanging décor or late-night entertainment, ask about the hotel’s restrictions. There may be rules around open flames, wall or ceiling installations, amplified music and the time entertainment must end.

Consider the Guest Experience

Walk through the experience from your guests’ point of view. Where will they park? How easy is it to find the event space once they enter the hotel? Accessibility matters too. Ask about ramps, elevators, accessible restrooms and step-free access for guests who may need them.

A beautiful venue means very little if getting into it — or moving around it — is difficult for your guests.

What Happens When Plans Change?

Guest counts rarely remain exactly the same from the day you book until the day of your wedding. Find out when the final guaranteed number is due and what happens if attendance increases or decreases.

If your wedding booking includes overnight accommodation, discuss room blocks, booking deadlines and any commitments attached to those rooms.

You should also understand the hotel’s cancellation and rescheduling policies. Are there cancellation charges? And what happens if circumstances outside your control affect the event?

Is there a back-up location secured for you if you are outdoor and it rains?

These aren’t the most exciting questions to ask, but they’re some of the most important ones to have answered in writing.

Know Who Will Be Looking After You



The person who shows you the ballroom and prepares your proposal may not be the person managing your event on the day. Ask who your main contact will be throughout the planning process and who will be responsible for your function once event day arrives. Knowing exactly whom to call when you need an answer or something changes can make the planning process considerably easier.

And Finally, Ask the Question People Often Forget



After you’ve gone through everything on your list, ask your hotel representative: “Based on the type of event I’m planning, is there anything else you think I should know before I book?”

It’s a simple question, but an experienced event professional may immediately identify something you haven’t considered.

Before You Sign



Choosing a hotel event venue isn’t only about finding the prettiest ballroom or the most attractive package. You’re choosing a partner that will play a significant role in your guests’ experience.

The right venue shouldn’t just look good in photographs. It should have the space, team, policies and resources to help your event run smoothly — from the first vendor arriving for set-up to the final guest heading home.

Because when it comes to wedding planning, the questions you ask before you book can save you from the surprises you don’t want later.

World.title: 11 years after decriminalisation, ganja use complicating mental health care
World.content:
AI image of a young man smoking marijuana. (Adobe stock)

Eleven years after Jamaica decriminalised ganja, the use of the substance features heavily among patients presenting with psychosis and schizophrenia. While there is currently no data establishing whether use of the herb is causing or contributing to the mental health problems, its prevalence is complicating treatment.

This is against the background of data from the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) pointing to an increase in high-risk usage of cannabis and the potency of the substance in Jamaica, as well as an increase in admissions for psychosis and schizophrenia over the last decade.

“What we do know is that the majority of psychiatric admissions in our public hospitals are coming from psychosis or schizophrenia. And the majority of those persons do use cannabis. So, we can look at that relationship and see that it is strong,” said Director for Treatment Services at the NCDA, Dr Kristen Robinson Barrett.

Still, Robinson Barrett noted that there is little data specifically exploring cannabis-induced psychosis.

Psychiatrist at Bellevue Hospital, Dr Brian Kazaara concurred that cannabis use has a striking presence among patients presenting with mental issues, but suggested that the substance rarely causes psychotic disorders.

“We don’t have official studies performed at Bellevue Hospital regarding cannabis use among patients, but from a cursory observation I can safely say the vast majority of patients admitted to the hospital also use cannabis,” he said.

Kazaara, who previously worked at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), pointed to a survey carried out by UHWI that revealed that the majority of persons admitted to the institution’s psychiatric ward smoked cannabis.

“What studies show is that persons with common psychiatric conditions like major depressive disorder or anxiety disorders use cannabis far more frequently than persons who do not have mental illnesses,” he said.

Despite this, Kazaara explained, “Cannabis-induced psychosis is not the norm. It is rare. At Bellevue we very, very rarely see that diagnosis. I also worked at UHWI for seven years [and] rarely saw it, almost never.”

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug and can affect the way that people perceive the world, leading to relaxation, paranoia, or other effects.

“It binds to our cannabinoid receptors around our body, but particularly in our brain, and that’s how we get the effects. It tends to create effects as it relates to emotions and feelings,” Robinson Barrett said. “They might experience changes as it relates to their time perception, so things might feel slowed down… issues with their concentration, so their attention and their awareness, their reaction time will change.”

Kazaara cautions that cannabis use can muddle the treatment of mental health issues.

“Cannabis definitely complicates psychosis, because for persons who use cannabis, they are more likely to develop an earlier onset of psychosis. So it may happen earlier than if they didn’t use it. It makes symptoms worse. It makes it harder to treat,” he explained.

Jamaica has a strong culture of recreational cannabis use, and Research Analyst at the NCDA Uki Atkinson explained that while overall population use has not necessarily changed over the last decade following decriminalisation of the drug, the potential for high-risk use has.

She supported her assessment with results from the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) which was used during surveys in 2016 and 2023.

“We were able to compare the levels of high-risk use from 2016 to 2023. In 2016, 50 per cent of the people who used cannabis in the past year were deemed to be at high risk for misusing it,” Atkinson said, noting “this has increased by 16 per cent in 2023. So, it shows not necessarily that more people are using ganja… But there’s a significant increase in high-risk patterns of use.”

In addition to high-risk usage, the potency of cannabis being consumed in Jamaica is also a concern.

According to a European study, using high-potency cannabis with a tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration over 10 percent, significantly increases the risk of developing psychotic symptoms or disorders, especially with daily use.

Robinson Barrett expressed serious concern about current potency trends worldwide compared to a potency of around four per cent in the 1990s.

“As of 2024, we’re looking at potencies of 15 to 20 per cent,” Robinson Barrett indicated.

“The potency trends of cannabis in Jamaica measured between 2014 and 2020, were showing that over that decade, the cannabis potency would have moved from about one per cent to over 10 per cent across 12 parishes,” she continued. “So, we’re concerned… because we have a culture of heavy use in young age groups…it’s a very concerning picture as it relates to all young people and any other vulnerable group.”

Outside of general risks, Robinson Barrett noted that there are some who may be particularly susceptible to the effects of cannabis use, including youth.

“Generally speaking, the earlier the age of onset for any substance is going to increase your risk for addiction, and it’s going to increase your risk for its effects…for the cannabis, we’re looking at increased risk for development of psychosis, increased risk for cognitive impairment,” Robinson Barrett said.

She also highlighted people who are genetically vulnerable, or have a family history of mental illness as well as heavy users who smoke regularly.

While cannabis has many cannabinoids, Robinson Barrett explained that the main ones are Delta-9-THC, which most people know as a psychoactive component, and CBD, which can have a calming or relaxing effect.

Kazaara agreed that cannabis misuse can complicate mental health treatment.

“Yes, it does. Cannabis complicates the treatment of psychiatric conditions. For example, in the case of schizophrenia, it can worsen symptoms and also make the medication we use for it, less effective,” he explained.

In the meantime, Atkinson stressed that the NCDA was not demonising cannabis, highlighting the medicinal benefits and scope for a medicinal industry.

“We recognise the value, but we see the downside in our clients and in some of the young people who we have to treat,” she explained.

She urged that use must be balanced with ensuring that the population, especially youth and those with a predisposition to mental illness, understand the risk of use, particularly in a problematic manner.

World.title: Musk receives Ukraine’s Order of Freedom from Zelenskyy
World.content:
Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service has helped Ukrainian forces maintain communications and coordinate operations since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. | Imen Ben Youssef/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

The honor comes as Kyiv tries to persuade the tech mogul to let its army use Starlink inside Russian territory.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded his country’s Order of Freedom to Elon Musk Wednesday, amid efforts to persuade Musk to expand access to his Starlink network.

Zelenskyy’s presidential decree praises Musk for “protecting people’s lives and freedom, and developing relations between the peoples of Ukraine and the United States of America.”

Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service has helped Ukrainian forces maintain communications and coordinate operations since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In February 2026, SpaceX disabled thousands of Starlink terminals used by Russian forces, weakening their military capabilities.

Ukraine is trying to convince the tech mogul to allow its army to use the Starlink network within Russian territory. Doing so would allow Ukraine to improve the accuracy of missile and drone strikes deep inside Russia. “For now, Musk has said that this would be an escalation. But he may change his mind when he sees more arguments,” Zelenskyy told journalists last Saturday.

The Order of Freedom is often awarded to foreign leaders for their support for Ukraine — recent recipients include French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda.

World.title: France and Germany collide over Europe’s industrial future
World.content:
France and Germany are clashing over how far the EU should go to protect European industry — with Paris pushing stronger “Made in Europe” rules and Berlin warning against provoking new trade fights.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart look at what that battle says about Europe’s struggle to go green, stay competitive and keep its markets open at the same time.

Then, Brussels is rattled by another wave of shootings. We look at the drug trade behind much of the violence, the Antwerp connection, and the political fight over whether the capital has enough police resources — or whether Belgium’s fragmented system is part of the problem.

And on a much lighter note: Eurostar may finally get some serious competition. New operators are lining up to run through the Channel Tunnel, raising the prospect of more trains — and maybe cheaper tickets — between Brussels and London.

World.title: Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives wish they could be as popular as she is
World.content:
“Kemi is popular. We are trying to promote the rest of the shadow Cabinet to make sure that popularity rubs off on the rest of the party,” said one Badenoch staffer, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record.

So far, it hasn’t worked.

“Badenoch’s success has still failed to translate into any meaningful movement in the polls for her party,” said Scarlett Maguire, founder of independent polling firm Merlin Strategy. “The Conservatives’ mediocre polling numbers, still worse than when they lost the 2024 election, shows the extent to which they have lost trust in their brand.”

New look conference

The party’s first big set piece moment this autumn will come when the Conservative Party meets for its annual conference in Birmingham at the beginning of October.

Badenoch’s performance at last year’s gathering marked the beginning of her transformation as party leader, and her team is hoping to repeat the trick by making this year’s conference more Badenoch-focused.

There will be less policy this year, according to one shadow minister familiar with the plans and also granted anonymity to speak freely.
