World.title: Comment “le mur de fer” promis contre l’immigration clandestine à Mayotte s’est enlisé
World.content:
Un plan opérationnel “avant fin 2029, voire 2030”

Un appel d’offres, publié par le ministère de l’Intérieur le 12 août et repéré par POLITICO, dévoile l’ampleur du retard pris par le programme “mur de fer”. Celui-ci vise à recruter un prestataire extérieur, dont le rôle sera justement d’accompagner l’administration dans la mise en place globale du dispositif. Selon le phasage détaillé dans le règlement de consultation de l’appel d’offres, le plan “Uhura wa shaba”, dans toutes ses composantes, pourrait ne pas être pleinement opérationnel avant fin 2029, voire 2030.

En effet, une fois le prestataire sélectionné — fin 2026, au plus tôt, d’après les délais fixés dans ce document — celui-ci devra s’engager dans la préparation, puis l’organisation d’un “dialogue compétitif” pour choisir les industriels susceptibles de fournir les équipements et technologies nécessaires, pour une période de 33 mois au total. S’en suivra la phase “d’exécution” de ce chantier, pendant 51 mois.

“Si l’on fait les comptes, cela renvoie la mise en place du rideau de fer à 2030-2034, ce n’est pas acceptable”, s’agace Saïd Omar Oili. “J’y vois le signe que le gouvernement veut sous-traiter au privé la réflexion globale de la lutte contre l’immigration à Mayotte, un sujet de souveraineté, fustige Estelle Youssouffa. Lancer un tel chantier maintenant, c’est aussi un constat d’échec sur ce qui a été fait ces dernières années”.

Les radars actuels moins performants que les précédents

Dans l’appel d’offres, le ministère reconnaît lui-même que la “couverture des radars installés au début des années 2000 est significativement incomplète”. Celle-ci s’est retrouvée d’autant plus fragilisée par la tempête Chido qui a détruit une large partie des moyens de surveillance et d’interception.

“Des mesures de rattrapage ont été déployées : quatre radars légers et des caméras longue portée ont été achetés”, affirme le ministère de l’Intérieur, sollicité par POLITICO. Mais “ces radars ne disposent toutefois pas d’une portée de détection équivalente à celle des anciens radars”, pointe un rapport sénatorial publié en avril 2026 sur Mayotte et la Réunion. Le programme “rideau de fer […] n’a pas tenu ses promesses”, conclut ce document.

Selon les projections inscrites dans le marché public, le rideau de fer devait rendre “atteignable” l’interpellation de 20 000 étrangers en situation irrégulière en mer par an, contre 4 584 en 2025, d’après le bilan de la préfecture de Mayotte. Cette année-là, un total de 23 421 personnes ont fait l’objet d’un éloignement du territoire.

World.title: Belgium awards scholarships to Palestinian students — but gives them no way to leave Gaza
World.content:
The obstacles facing them are partly procedural, mostly political. POLITICO spoke to four of the scholarship recipients, who were told visas could only be obtained in person at a Belgian diplomatic post, such as the one in Jerusalem. Two of them have been able to successfully obtain visas with the help of lawyers in Belgium, suggesting solutions can be found even in Belgium’s rigid immigration system.

But visas on their own are of little help. None of the students and researchers offered funded places in Belgium currently have any way to actually get there.

In a written statement, Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories said it facilitates and encourages the evacuation of students and researchers from Gaza at the request of a third country.

Anneleen Van Bossuyt speaks during a plenary session at the Belgian Federal Parliament in Brussels on June 5, 2025. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images

But a spokesperson for Belgium’s foreign ministry, led by Prévot of the centrist Les Engagés party, said there was currently no decision in the coalition government to organize any more evacuations. The department said it was “actively investigating” what could be done to help the students but that any decision on new evacuations would be the “responsibility of the government as a whole.”

Two Belgian government officials, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the coalition was divided on just about everything related to Palestine. While Prévot’s foreign ministry says it is looking for solutions, the French-speaking centrist Reformist Movement party (MR), whose leader Georges-Louis Bouchez is known for his pro-Israeli positions , and De Wever’s New Flemish Alliance (N-VA) are said to be against further evacuations.

“It’s common knowledge that if something gets stuck [on this issue], it’s going to be those two parties that are against it,” one of the officials said. MR and De Wever’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

World.title: Andy Burnham has to shape the UK’s social media ban. Australia and France could show him how.
World.content:
MPs return to Parliament next week after the summer break, and Burnham’s government will need to decide how the ban — which is supposed to come into effect in spring — will work.

Australia

Australia was the first country in the world to introduce a social media ban for kids in December last year. Last month, the Australian government published its first wave of findings on the experiences of more than 4,000 children and families since the ban took effect.

The numbers do not show a huge drop in kids accessing social media. The proportion of under-16s holding at least one social media account fell from 52.4 percent to 42.3 percent at the three-month follow-up. Meanwhile, the proportion who reported using a social media platform (with or without an account) fell even less, from 85.9 percent to 81.5 percent.

Australia only requires age-restricted platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent under-16s from creating or keeping accounts. Access via logged-out experiences, for example, is permissible.

The rationale is that account-based access — and the data harvesting that comes with it — increases the likelihood of exposure to potentially harmful design features, such as algorithmic suggestions or infinite scroll.

But the U.K. could go further than Australia by casting a wider net to cover both account ownership and access. That could implicate not just the social media platforms, but internet service providers too. The previous Starmer government has already laid the groundwork by handing itself powers, via the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, to force ISPs to keep kids out.

World.title: Nigel Farage wants to scrap GDPR for the UK
World.content:
“[T]he GDPR has strangled small businesses and tech firms alike in a web of unnecessary regulation ... Ten years after the Brexit referendum we should not still be following ridiculous EU privacy laws that hurt British businesses,” Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said in a statement.

The EU GDPR provides for a wider set of individual rights around personal data (including the “right to be forgotten”) than New Zealand's Privacy Act does.

However, Reform UK stressed in its press release that following the New Zealand model would preserve the U.K.'s EU data adequacy status, meaning personal data would still be allowed to flow freely between the U.K. and EU.

The European Commission only grants adequacy to countries that provide an essentially equivalent level of data protection to that of the EU.

The U.K. has already diverged from Brussels on privacy laws with the passage of the Data (Use and Access) Act last year, which relaxed some aspects of the U.K. GDPR in a bid to boost economic growth.

World.title: Frankfurt Airport employee dies after contracting malaria, operator Fraport says
World.content:
An employee at Frankfurt Airport has died of malaria, a spokesperson for the facility’s operator Fraport said on Wednesday.

 

A further five employees at the airport also contracted the infectious disease and are receiving medical treatment.

The cause of the infections is believed to be a mosquito that travelled by plane from a malaria-endemic area to Germany, likely in July.

Fraport says its focus is now on information and prevention. Employees are being advised to see a doctor if they experience any malaria-like symptoms and to tell medics they work at the airport.

Mosquito traps have also been set up at the airport to catch the insects so they can be taken to a lab for examination.

Lufthansa aircraft parked at Frankfurt Airport, 12 March, 2026 AP Photo

Rare transmission

The federal agency for disease control and prevention, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), said such cases are "very rare."

Malaria is transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes if they have previously become infected themselves.

The RKI says there are some Anopheles species in Germany that can transmit malaria pathogens under suitable environmental conditions, but such cases have been extremely rare.

According to the Frankfurt Health Department, so-called "airport malaria" is a very rare transmission route outside of a malaria-endemic area.

A health worker shows a bottle of the malaria vaccine R21/Matrix-M before administering it in Yenagoa, 9 December, 2024 AP Photo

"Human-to-human transmission plays no role in airport malaria," a spokesperson said.

A study aiming to record all cases of airport and baggage-borne malaria in Europe from 1969 to 2024 identified a total of 145 cases, nine of which were in Germany.

Malaria can be life-threatening and according to the World Health Organisation symptoms include fever, headaches, breathing difficulties and seizures.

“The disease can lead to coma and death, especially among high-risk groups,” the German Foreign Office said.

Protection against mosquito bites can help prevent the spread of the disease.

World.title: Zelenskyy awards Elon Musk Ukraine’s ‘Order of Freedom’ despite years of criticism
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded tech billionaire Elon Musk the Order of Freedom, one of Ukraine’s most prestigious state honours, months after the SpaceX founder worked with Kyiv to block Russia’s illegal use of Starlink — a move that disrupted Moscow’s battlefield communications and helped slow the Russian advance.

 

The decree, published on Ukraine's presidential website on Wednesday, cited Musk’s “outstanding personal merits in protecting human life and freedom” and his contribution to relations between Ukraine and the US.

The award marks a striking turn in the complicated relationship between Musk, Ukraine and the country’s leadership, as Kyiv is critically dependent on his satellite technology amid repeated disagreements over the war and Musk’s increasingly sharp criticism of Zelenskyy.

Musk's Starlink has been crucial to Ukraine since the first days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, providing communications for civilians, government institutions and the military after conventional networks were damaged or destroyed.

Musk activated the service over Ukraine in February 2022 after an appeal from then-Digital Transformation Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

Tens of thousands of terminals have since become central to Ukrainian battlefield communications and increasingly to the operation of drones.

But Russian forces also found ways to obtain Starlink terminals illegally, despite SpaceX saying it did not sell the service in Russia or do business with the Russian government or military.

By early 2026 Kyiv officials said Russian forces were increasingly mounting the terminals on attack drones, giving operators a resilient connection that allowed the UAVs to fly at low altitude, resist electronic warfare and be controlled over longer distances.

Kyiv appealed directly to SpaceX in February, and Musk responded publicly to Fedorov as Ukrainian and SpaceX engineers worked on measures to prevent Russia’s unauthorised access.

The intervention underscored the extraordinary role Musk and his companies have come to play in a war in which satellite communications are deeply integrated into military operations.

Musk’s turbulent relationship with Ukraine

Although Musk provided Starlink to Ukraine at a critical moment in 2022, disagreements soon emerged over how far the technology should be used in Ukrainian military operations.

Musk repeatedly argued that Starlink was intended to provide communications rather than facilitate long-range attacks and has repeatedly said that its use in strikes on Russian targets could escalate the war.

His restrictions had direct consequences on the battlefield.

According to the 2025 media investigation, Musk ordered Starlink coverage shut down in parts of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory during Kyiv’s 2022 counteroffensive, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.

A separate controversy surrounded Crimea. Musk rejected a Ukrainian request to activate Starlink around Sevastopol for Ukraine’s operations against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, saying he feared SpaceX would otherwise become “explicitly complicit in a major act of war and conflict escalation”.

The disagreements later became increasingly political.

Musk repeatedly questioned continued Western support for Ukraine and argued that Kyiv should seek a negotiated end to the war.

He also criticised Zelenskyy directly and backed calls for Ukraine to hold elections despite martial law, under which national elections have been suspended since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The issue became particularly explosive after US President Donald Trump returned to the White House and began pressing Kyiv over elections while seeking to negotiate an end to the war with Moscow.

New Starlink requests from Kyiv

Kyiv has continued to work closely with SpaceX despite Musk’s criticism.

Starlink remains deeply embedded — and irreplaceable — in Ukraine’s military communications, while its integration into drones has given Ukrainian forces a more resilient means of controlling unmanned systems in areas where conventional radio links are vulnerable to Russian electronic warfare.

The technology has become particularly important for strikes in Russian-occupied Ukraine, where Ukrainian forces have increasingly used drones to attack logistics routes, command positions and other military targets far behind the front line.

Ukraine is now seeking Musk’s approval to extend the use of Starlink-equipped drones for strikes deep into Russia’s territory.

Kyiv believes the technology could allow its forces to hit mobile Russian and North Korean ballistic-missile launchers when they move into firing positions, potentially giving Ukraine another means of countering one of the most difficult threats facing its air defences.

Musk has refused to approve it so far.

World.title: Second arrest over deadly sword attack at Swedish school
World.content:
A second man has been arrested over a sword attack at a school in central Sweden that left a 17-year-old girl dead and three other students wounded, prosecutors said on Wednesday.

 

The man is suspected of assisting murder and attempted murder over the attack at Brinell School in Fagersta, northwest of Stockholm, on August 21.

Prosecutors have not disclosed his age or said how he is suspected of being involved. They are expected to decide by noon on Thursday whether to ask a court to detain him or release him.

An 18-year-old student at the school is already in custody on suspicion of murder and attempted murder after allegedly carrying out the attack while classes were under way.

Two boys, aged 12 and 17, were seriously injured, while a third boy under 18 suffered minor injuries and was later discharged from hospital.

Police fired shots during the operation to arrest the suspected attacker but he was not hit.

Investigators initially said they had no reason to believe more than one person carried out the attack and have not publicly identified a motive.

Police are also investigating whether the 18-year-old had links to online communities that glorify school violence.

A TikTok account reportedly belonging to the suspect was taken down after the attack. Before it was removed, it contained videos glorifying school attacks and an image of a sword apparently taken inside a bathroom at Brinell School.

Sweden's Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, left, and Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson visit the memorial. 22 August, 2026. AP Photo

Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson visited Fagersta on Saturday and joined opposition leader Magdalena Andersson at a memorial to the victim.

“What must never happen has happened again,” Kristersson said.

Sweden has suffered several deadly attacks at schools in recent years.

Eleven people, including the gunman, were killed in a mass shooting at an adult education centre in Örebro in 2025, the deadliest mass shooting in Sweden's history.

In 2022, two female teachers were killed in an attack involving a knife and an axe at a school in Malmö.

Three people were killed in Trollhättan in 2015 when a 21-year-old man armed with a sword attacked a school in what authorities described as a racist hate crime. He was shot dead by police.

World.title: Nvidia earnings preview: The report the entire market is waiting on
World.content:
The most consequential corporate event of the quarter lands tonight.

 

Nvidia will drop its figures after the US close at around 22:00 CET, and while the past quarter is expected to be enormous, what will move markets is what CEO Jensen Huang says about the months ahead.

Four times a year, listed companies open their books and tell investors exactly how much money they made and how much they expect to make next quarter.

These earnings reports move share prices, pension funds and ultimately, the wider economy.

Nvidia's matters more than most because it makes the chips that power the artificial intelligence boom. If its outlook disappoints, the shockwaves will not stay in Silicon Valley.

The company has become a proxy for the entire AI rally.

The report will land on the back of a difficult run for Nvidia's stock, having lost ground for seven consecutive sessions, its longest losing streak since 2022. Shares rebounded roughly 3% since Monday ahead of the earnings report but are still down over 6% from last week's open.

European chipmakers have as much riding on tonight's guidance as Wall Street.

ASML, the Dutch group whose lithography machines underpin Nvidia's entire supply chain, has raised its own 2026 sales forecast twice this year on the back of AI demand, and its shares — along with those of Dutch chip-equipment maker BE Semiconductor and German optics group Jenoptik — tend to move in step with Nvidia's outlook.

For the month of August, Nvidia is still up around 8% and year-to-date performance is solid with the stock increasing over 13% since the yearly open.

Analysts polled by Bloomberg expect adjusted earnings of $2.09 a share on revenue of roughly $92 billion (€78.8bn), which would represent growth of 96% on the same quarter last year.

Nvidia itself had forecast $91 billion (€78bn), give or take 2%, meaning consensus sits less than a percentage point above the company's own midpoint. That narrow gap raises the bar as a modest beat may not be enough to satisfy investors.

As for data centre revenue, it is forecast to top $85.4 billion (€73.1bn), up around 105%.

Investors will get a clearer look at where that money comes from, because Nvidia changed its reporting last quarter to separate sales to hyperscalers and AI clouds, expected at $43.5 billion (€37.2bn), from industrial and enterprise customers, projected at $41.7 billion (€35.7bn).

The company has beaten Wall Street estimates in 22 of the past 24 quarters.

The question hanging over Nvidia's quarter

The main concern regarding Nvidia is concentration.

The firm still draws the bulk of its revenue from Amazon, Google and Microsoft, each of which is designing its own chips to reduce reliance on the company, and the new disclosure will show precisely how large that dependence remains.

Huang's commentary on demand into 2027 therefore carries more weight than any single figure.

The question has grown sharper since July, when markets fell on doubts about whether vast AI investments will generate returns.

Nvidia's answer has been to help finance the buildout itself, assembling a $500 billion (€433bn) capital pool with Wall Street firms this month and backing an eight-gigawatt data centre in Ohio alongside OpenAI.

A week stacked with market catalysts

Nvidia is not the only major test for the markets this week.

July's personal consumption expenditures index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, is due at 14:30 CET on Wednesday alongside a second estimate of second-quarter GDP.

Economists expect headline prices to have risen 0.1% on the month and the core measure 0.2%, leaving the annual core rate at 3.3%.

Attention then shifts to Wyoming, where the Kansas City Fed's Jackson Hole symposium opens on Thursday.

Kevin Warsh delivers the keynote on Friday, his first as Fed chair, 19 days before a September policy meeting that markets currently price as roughly a one-in-three chance of a rate rise.

The ECB's Isabel Schnabel joins a panel the same day.

World.title: In pictures: The world pays tribute to country music queen Dolly Parton
World.content:
Tributes are pouring in from around the world following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton.

 

“After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” her publicist, Marcel Pariseau, said in a statement on Tuesday.

The American singer-songwriter-actress-philanthropist was one of the most influential figures in country music, writing hundreds of songs and creating some of the most enduring hits in popular music, including 'Jolene', '9 to 5' and 'I Will Always Love You'.

Tributes have already begun appearing across the US. In her home state of Tennessee, landmarks and institutions have been illuminated in pink in honour of the star, while fans have gathered to lay flowers and celebrate her extraordinary life.

Here's a look in pictures at some of the tributes already pouring in for the deeply beloved queen of country music.

World.title: ICE arrests hit nearly 50,000 in July, highest of Trump's mass deportation agenda
World.content:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested nearly 50,000 people in July, the highest monthly total since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, according to new figures.

 

ICE made 49,571 arrests in July, up 15% from 43,021 in June and 70% from 29,241 in February, according to government data analysed by the Associated Press news agency.

The surge in immigration arrests comes as the Trump administration continues to pursue its mass deportation agenda, shifting from high-profile operations in major US cities to less visible enforcement actions.

As arrests have surged in recent weeks, boosted by increased hiring, ICE has detained people during traffic stops and increasingly relied on state and local law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration enforcement duties.

ICE officers have also begun arresting Haitians who have lost protections from deportation.

The new arrest numbers show the administration “didn’t stop the enforcement,” said Mark Krikorian of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for more immigration restrictions.

“They changed the tactics and are, if anything, being more effective.”

ICE agents aim at protesters outside the Delaney Hall detention center during a protest against the transfer of detainees in Newark, 29 May, 2026 AP Photo

State partnerships become key to immigration enforcement

The number of arrests made by state and local police departments who partner with ICE has dramatically increased over the last year.

Those partnerships, which ICE has grown with the help of generous financial incentives for participating agencies, accounted for 6,500 arrests in July, or about 13% of the total, the data showed. A year earlier, they accounted for less than 5% of ICE’s monthly arrests.

Texas and Florida accounted for nearly 20,000 arrests in July, highlighting the growing role of the two states in the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda.

Both states have expanded cooperation with ICE through so-called 287(g) agreements, which allow state and local law enforcement officers to carry out certain federal immigration enforcement duties.

A sign at a vigil in Lewiston lists some of the people killed by federal agents, 14 July, 2026 AP Photo

Over half of immigrants arrested had no criminal history

The Trump administration has repeatedly said its immigration enforcement operations target people who have committed crimes in the US as part of efforts to improve public safety.

However, the data shows that more than half of those arrested in July had no criminal convictions and were not facing criminal charges. Less than a quarter had been convicted of a crime.

Half of the arrests were non-custodial, meaning ICE agents detained people in the community rather than taking custody of those already held in prisons or by local police.

At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration agents since Trump returned to office and launched his immigration crackdown.

World.title: 'Unique and irreplaceable': Dolly Parton tributes from public figures and celebrities
World.content:
For many music fans, the fabric of the universe feels noticeably weaker following the news that country music legend Dolly Parton has died aged 80.

 

The American singer-songwriter-actress-philanthropist, best known for her hit songs ‘I Will Always Love You’, ‘Jolene’ and ‘9 to 5’, died in Nashville, Tennessee, after a “brief battle” with cancer.

Her death comes just days after sharing a health update, following the cancellation of her Las Vegas residency and the death of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025.

"I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn't pay attention to when I was watching over Carl," she told People. "It's not like I haven't been through hard times with my health. But I think because we live in a 24/7 world with social media, everything gets magnified in ways it wasn't years ago.”

She added: "I used to joke that I was the Queen of the Tabloids, but now I guess I can say I'm the Queen of Social Media AI! Seriously, though, even though I'm still healin', I’m still workin'."

Tributes paid to Dolly Parton AP Photo

The family’s official obituary said: “A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family. Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place. Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact.”

Inspire, she did. Countless public figures and celebrities have paid tribute to the Queen of Country, who was voted the most beloved public figure in America following a recent academic poll.

Showing that art can bridge divides by fostering empathy, several politicians have paid their respects to Parton.

Donald Trump ordered flags to be lowered at half mast to honour the artist, and wrote on Truth Social: “This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM.”

American flag lowered for Dolly AP Photo

Both senators from Tennessee, where Parton was born on 19 January 1946, reacted on social media and called her death a great loss to the state.

"Tennessee has lost one of its greatest legends - a woman who never lost sight of her faith, her roots, or the Volunteer Spirit. [Dolly Parton] was a true Tennessee treasure, and her legacy will forever be defined by her love of faith, family, and the place she proudly called home," said Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty.

Sen. Marsha Blackburn posted: "There are no words to adequately express the sorrow our family and indeed, all Tennesseans, feel in the loss of Dolly Parton. An iconic leader who loved our great state and nation. Her passing leaves a void that no one can ever fill. Dolly, we will always love you."

Sen. Bernie Sanders highlighted Parton's accomplishments beyond her music career as a philanthropist.

"She was not only a talented musician & songwriter, but a lifelong philanthropist and advocate for literacy, education, LGBTQ+ rights, healthcare and disaster relief," Sanders said. "Her music and humanity touched millions. She will be sorely missed."

Former US President Joe Biden stated: "Simply put, Dolly Parton was an American original. She was an inspiration to millions.” He added that the singer was "a relentless advocate" for women and for equality and praised her charity work of providing books to children around the world.

"She lived her values with a flair and vitality for life that was uniquely her own," Biden added, describing her as "a trailblazer in every sense of the word".

Kamala Harris shared that Parton was “a true American icon”, while former President Barack Obama wrote on X: “It’s hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton. Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and - as if that wasn’t enough - helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna COVID vaccine. What a life. Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly’s family and her many, many fans.”

In 2020, Parton memorably played a key role in funding the research that aided the development of one major COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna), donating $1 million of her own money to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

Former US president Bill Clinton also paid tribute to Parton, recalling that he and Hillary Clinton were longtime fans and first saw her perform in 1974.

“Dolly Parton was one of a kind – a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart,” Clinton wrote. “And she always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy. Hillary and I were big fans and first saw her in 1974, and will always be grateful for the music and the memories.”

Parton’s work beyond music and acting included the Dollywood Foundation, the non-profit organisation founded in 1988 which champions the education of children in her home state of Tennessee.

The Dollywood Foundation has said it remains "honoured to carry the mission she entrusted to it."

Foundation president Jeff Conyers said in a statement: "Dolly often said that she had been blessed far beyond anything she ever dreamed possible, and she believed deeply that those blessings came with a responsibility to give something back. That belief is woven into everything we do at The Dollywood Foundation. While we are heartbroken by her loss, the mission she gave us is as clear today as it has ever been, and we will carry it forward for generations to come."

Then there’s Parton’s literacy initiative, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, which has distributed more than 300 million books globally since 1995. Inspired by her father’s inability to read or write, the programme sends one free book every month to children from birth to five - regardless of family income – in the US, Canada, UK, Australia and Ireland.

Her family has requested that donations may be made to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library at imaginationlibrary.com.

Following the news of her death, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has also vowed to continue the singer’s work, saying her vision was always to build something that would “last for generations”.

It recalled how proud Parton was of the programme, particularly because of its connection to her father, quoting her as saying: “My Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done.”

In a statement, the organisation said: “The world grieves with us today. And yet we find ourselves just as certain about what comes next. For decades, Dolly & the team at The Dollywood Foundation – home of Dolly Parton's Imagination Library – worked to build something that would last for generations. So it will. The work ahead has never felt more meaningful, and we will carry it forward as she lifts us all up. Dolly, we will always love you.”

Hundreds of celebrities from the muisc world have also paid tribute to Parton, from Paul McCartney and Céline Dion to Taylor Swift, Eminem and Elton John.

Sir Paul McCartney has said it is "difficult" to take in the news of her death, knowing her as a woman who was so "full of life".

He said: "The magnificent star Dolly Parton has died and it is so sad. She was such a wonderful woman."

"She was so bubbly and full of life it is difficult to take in the news that she has passed," he said. "Her songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music and it is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly. She was a very clever business woman who understood the value of her music and, most importantly, the effect that she had on the people of the world."

McCartney added there was "no greater honour" than when she sang ‘Let It Be’ on her 2023 album, Rockstar, and added: "Even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honoured that she did it."

Céline Dion paid tribute to Parton on Instagram, describing her as "pure light, with a kind heart and a generous spirit", while Fleetwood Mac drummer Mick Fleetwood described her energy as "personable" and said her "positive approach to life and the amazing songs she wrote is her legacy that will live on in a world that so needs healing".

Superstar Beyoncé described Parton as the "barometer" and the "north star" for the music industry. In a statement on her website, Beyoncé says she is grateful for Parton's "art, heart, generosity, humour and entrepreneurship", adding that she was "honoured" to work with the country icon. The two worked on Beyoncé's 'Cowboy Carter' album, where they recorded a reworked cover of ‘Jolene’.

Sir Elton John said Parton was "a giant of an artist – unique and irreplaceable, with the kindest heart", while Joan Jett referred to the country icon as “a one of a kind, altruistic, down to earth, musical genius”.

Eminem joined the chorus of tributes by sharing a note he received from the country legend following his induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. The rapper, who says he never got the chance to meet the "icon" and "superstar in every sense", says the note really had an impact on him.

As for Jack White, who once covered ‘Jolene’ with his band the White Stripes, he kept his tribute short and sweet. “Instant Sainthood,” wrote the musician on social media.

Taylor Swift also paid her respects, describing Parton as “the gift that kept on giving”. Here is her statement in full:

"A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real, or right. But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one.

She was truly the gift that kept on giving. Dolly gave us someone to look up to while encouraging us to be who we are as individuals. Somehow she was able to give us her lessons about the world gently and honestly, simultaneously, and oftentimes hilariously. She managed to give the world the ultimate mystery and fantasy in some corners of her life, but to give full transparency in the ways that counted. Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self worth as an artist.

Along with her other fans, I am so grateful for all of it. For the melodies and lyrics she wrote that thawed even the coldest hearts. For the millions of books she provided children all over the world so that they might fall in love with stories the way she did. For the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too.

Dolly, I’ll think of you each step of the way."

Dolly Parton AP Photo

RIP Dolly Parton 1946 – 2026. You will be missed.

World.title: Deadly flash flood wipes away villages in Nepal, Tibet
World.content:
Rescue helicopters have been unable to land in affected areas due to high flood waters. The leaders of Nepal and China ordered major rescue operations.

Numerous people were killed a a flash flood in Nepal that swept away villages and damaged bridges in the Himalayas.

At least 8 people were killed in Nepal while Chinese authorities also reported that a mudslide caused "major casualties" on the other side of the border in Tibet.

"There could be heavy casualties or loss ​of property," regional Nepali official ‌Narendra Pariyar told Reuters. "But I cannot say for sure now."

Villages in Rasuwa district were swept away by the deluge of water and mud Image: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

Major rescue operations underway

Nepal dispatched rescue helicopters to the mountainous Rasuwa region, but floodwaters were too high for the helicopters to land.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the military and police were assisting with rescues.

"Instructions have been given ... to move ​the people living in the lower areas ⁠to safer places," he said. "People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert."

Helicopters were unable to land due to the high flood waters Image: REUTERS

Chinese President Xi Jinping also ordered an "all out" rescue effort.

He said "the most urgent task is doing everything possible to search for and rescue the missing people... quickly treat injured people and minimize casualties to the greatest extent possible", according to Chinese state media.

More to follow...

World.title: Germany: Carnivalgoers rescued after being trapped on ride
World.content:
Passengers became stranded high up in the air after a swing carousel malfunctioned in Hamburg.

Nearly two dozen carnivalgoers were rescued after a 90 minute ordeal in central Hamburg late on Tuesday, having been stuck 25 meters (82 feet) in the air on a swing carousel ride.

The Hamburger Dom carnival is held in the St.Pauli area of the city three times a year, and is one of Germany's longest-running and most well-visited fun fairs, attracting some 10 million guests annually.

On Tuesday evening, 23 passengers become stuck partly up the 70-meter (230-foot) ride when it malfunctioned and stopped moving.

The 23 passengers were stuck for over an hour Image: Bodo Marks/dpa/picture alliance

Firefighters arrived at the scene, erecting ladders to bring down each guest individually.

Authorities said that no one needed medical attention, but that the ride would remain closed through Sunday when the carnival concludes.

Basic first aid was administered, but no one needed to go to the hospital, authorities said. Image: Bodo Marks/dpa/picture alliance

World.title: Germany news: Sugar tax plan leaves sour taste
World.content:
Skip next section Which products could be subject to the sugar tax?

08/26/2026 August 26, 2026 Which products could be subject to the sugar tax?

Despite being called a sugar tax, the levy only applies to drinks and not confectionery Image: Yona Elsner/photothek.de/picture alliance

Despite being widely described as a "sugar tax," the proposal is aimed at drinks containing sugar or sweeteners, rather than sweets or other sugary foods.

A Finance Ministry paper suggests the levy could apply not only to soft drinks but also to:

Juices

Milk-based drinks

Iced tea

Beer-based mixed drinks

Oat and soya drinks

Ready-made coffee drinks

Alcohol-free beer and wine

The paper also floated taxing zero- and light drinks containing artificial sweeteners. But Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has now ruled that out.

"I won't do that. It won't happen," Klingbeil said on Instagram, adding that a "sugar tax on sugar-free drinks" made no sense.

He stressed that the leaked paper was only an internal working document and had neither been politically agreed nor approved by the coalition.

Pure milk and 100% fruit juice were listed as exempt in the draft. The final scope of any tax therefore remains unsettled.

World.title: NYC: Mamdani opposes rally with Hindu nationalist leader
World.content:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced opposition to an upcoming event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, calling the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" while acknowledging the city can't block a private event.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it.

Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK.

What did Mamdani say?

When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event."

Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from."

His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India."

"It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision."

Who is organizing the event?

The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity.

Bhagwat is visiting several countries in a bid to reform the RSS's global perception [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled.

"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity."

What is the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and how is it related to PM Modi?

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.

The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.

In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.

100 years of the Hindu nationalist RSS movement To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rights organizations decry rise in abuses against religious minorities

However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.

India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities.

The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

World.title: Pakistan: Islamabad hospital fire kills at least 14 infants
World.content:
A fire broke out in the third floor of a maternity ward in Islamabad. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for an immediate investigation into the tragedy.

A least 14 infants were killed after a fire broke out at the maternity ward of a hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Wednesday.

"A fire broke out on the third floor of the MCH Ward at PIMS Hospital," the district office of Islamabad said, referring to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences.

The blaze broke out at around 6:45 a.m. (0145 UTC) when an air conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, rescuers said.

Distraught parents gathered outside the hospital Image: Aamir Qureshi/AFP

Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time, adding that one was rescued.

Outside the hospital, a nurse read out the names of babies who had perished as their families gathered around.

"I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," one father told the AFP news agency.

"My wife was in the ward. They took everyone out. We were sitting on the road waiting for help."

Investigation underway

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," he said in a statement.

"Those ​responsible should be identified, and ​the strictest action should be taken."

The incident is one of the deadliest hospital fires in recent memory in Pakistan, where healthcare is subsidized but public hospitals are often are under-resourced and overburdened.

World.title: Despite international bans, landmines are back in force
World.content:
It was considered a major achievement when most countries in the world agreed to ban anti-personnel mines in the 1990s. But given the Russia-Ukraine war, the situation in Europe is changing.

Raheela Bibi was outside playing with her siblings when a landmine exploded. It was August 2020 and she was 12, living in Pakistan. Both her hands were amputated after the incident. Her sister suffered a serious leg injury, while her brother's eye was hurt. Bibi told DW in 2023 that though it was extremely difficult for her to do her homework, she was determined to continue with her education.

In 2025, more than 5,000 people, mainly civilians, were killed or injured by landmines or unexploded ordnance according to a preliminary analysis by the NGO Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor. In South Sudan, 90% of the victims last year were children.

Landmines are actually designed to injure adults not kill them. This is because an injured soldier is more of a strain on an enemy country's resources than a dead soldier. But in peacetime, landmines continue to pose a deadly threat not only to soldiers but to civilians and particularly children, who often die.

Decades after the brutal conflicts from 1991 to 2001 that were Yugoslav wars, people continue to be killed and injured by landmines in former Yugoslavia, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Landmines are not designed to kill adults but to maim them Image: Mast Irham/dpa/picture alliance

Ottawa Treaty in force since 1999

In 1999, there were approximately 25,000 landmine casualties per year. This prompted pressure to ban the use of anti-personnel landmines. In 1997, representatives from more than 120 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty, which became legally binding in 1999. In total, 166 countries ratified the treaty, but not China, India, Russia or the US.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty. Ukraine has also withdrawn though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.

"This is a dangerous precedent that European states, of all countries, have set," Simone Wisotzki from the Frankfurt-based Leibniz Peace Research Institute (PRIF) told DW. "Other parties to the Ottawa Treaty, which could also face equally extreme situations in times of conflict, could take the same step. We would then have to deal with more withdrawals, which would, of course, undermine the legitimacy of the entire treaty."

Last year, Ukraine withdrew from the treaty and justified the move citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines in Ukrainian territory. "We cannot remain bound under conditions when the enemy has no restrictions," said Roman Kostenko, the secretary of the Ukrainian parliament's committee on national security, defense and intelligence.

If a country isn't at war, its withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty is supposed to take effect six months after its announcement. If it is at war, however, withdrawal should take effect only after a peace treaty has been signed. Despite the legal uncertainty, Ukraine is reportedly already using mines, albeit on a much smaller scale than Russia.

A quarter of Ukraine affected by landmines

According the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), as of mid-2025 approximately 25% of Ukraine was affected by landmines and explosive ordnance. This applied not only to Ukrainian-controlled territories but also to Russian-occupied areas in the east and southeast of the country.

"Since February 2022, over 1,150 civilians have been killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW)," UNMAS writes on its website, pointing out that the cost of full demining is estimated at just under $35 billion (approx. €30 billion) over 10 years.

Poland, Finland (which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine), Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, which have all suffered from Russian aggression and occupation in the past, also decided to withdraw from the Ottawa Treaty last year.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has stated on several occasions that his country wants to be able to mine its eastern borders with Russia very quickly if need be. The state-owned Polish defense company Belma has been contracted to produce anti-personnel mines in large quantities. Lithuania has also announced that it will resume the manufacture and purchase of landmines.

The Finnish military has said that if mines are necessary, they should be laid responsibly, accurate maps of their position must be created and there should be precise plans for demining.

Wisotzki from PRIF said that this is progress compared to the past but that modern anti-personnel mines often have integrated sensors and smart technologies that make it difficult to remove and destroy the mines.

"That's why I'm very critical of this and say that even new technologies present problems that, in turn, make mine clearance more difficult. In practice, mines are always laid in areas that are also used by civilians. They then remain in those territories and then injure civilians disproportionately."

In its reports, the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor has pointed out that while mines that were laid during past conflicts continued to be cleared, mines continue to be laid in Ukraine or in other countries such as Myanmar.

Decades after conflicts people continue to demine territories, such as here in Cambodia Image: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP

Less arms control in the world

This comes at a time when there is increasingly less arms control. In the past few years, three major agreements between the United States and Russia have expired or been terminated: the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty that banned all nuclear and conventional ground-launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and missile launchers with intermediate range; the New Start Treaty which is a nuclear arms reduction treaty; and the Treaty on Open Skies, which set out the framework for a regime of observation flights over the territory of participating states.

In 2023, Russia's withdrawal also effectively put an end to the CFE treaty that aimed to create a secure and stable balance of conventional armed forces in Europe and to remove the capability to launch surprise attacks or large-scale offensives

"Humanitarian arms control — which includes the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention — was in effect the only area that could still be said to be working," Wisotzki said. "And that is no longer the case."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: US military kills 4 in Caribbean boat strike
World.content:
The US military killed four people in a strike on a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean, the latest in a campaign that has killed more than 200 people and drawn condemnation from rights groups.

The US military struck a boat in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, US Southern Command said.

It's the latest action in a nearly yearlong controversial campaign by President Donald Trump's administration targeting alleged drug traffickers in Latin America.

What do we know about the latest US strike in the Caribbean?

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southern Command said in a post on X, accompanied by a video showing what appeared to be a boat in motion, followed by a flash.

The command did not identify those killed or give a precise location, saying only that the boat was operating along established smuggling routes in the Caribbean.

No evidence was released showing the vessel carried drugs.

Fishers in Colombia worry as US strikes alleged drug boats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to a count by AP news agency, the strike brings the death toll to at least 227 people across 68 strikes since the campaign began about a year ago. Reuters news agency, tracking Caribbean and Eastern Pacific strikes together, put the total above 210.

Tuesday's strike followed another one in the Eastern Pacific over the weekend that killed two people. The weekend strike was the first by the US military in more than two months.

Rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and independent United Nations investigators, say the strikes violate international law and amount to extrajudicial killings.

Why is the US conducting these strikes?

Trump says the United States is engaged in an "armed conflict" with drug cartels operating in the region and has framed the strikes as necessary to clamp down on the drug trade and its toll on American lives. But his administration has not made public the evidence behind its claims that those killed were trafficking narcotics.

The campaign is also expanding, with Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth saying this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow joint US military operations against criminal groups within their borders. Guatemala has disputed that any such agreement was reached.

Ecuador began similar joint operations with the US in March.

World.title: China: Dissident artist jailed for satirical Mao sculptures
World.content:
Sculptor Gao Zhen was charged under China's "Law on the Protection ⁠of Heroes ​and Martyrs." His supporters have called for his immediate release.

A court in China has reportedly sentenced a dissident artist to three years in jail for sculptures which satirized former Chinese revolutionary leader Mao Zedong.

Sculptor Gao Zhen, 70, became famous in the 2000s for addressing sensitive topics in China such as the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre through artworks he produced with his younger brother Gao Qiang.

Zhen, who is based in New York, was arrested during a visit to Beijing in August 2024. He was tried this year ⁠in a ⁠one-day behind-closed-doors trial and found guilty of "infringing upon the reputation of heroes."

"We feel outraged," Gao's wife Zhao Yaliang told the Reuters news agency. "Ever since I learned of the ​verdict, I haven't been able to recover from it. It's devastating."

Zhao also said she and her son, who is a US citizen, had been barred from leaving China since Zhen's detention two years ago.

Which Mao sculptures were deemed illegal?

Zhen was charged under China's "Law on the Protection ⁠of Heroes ​and Martyrs," legislation which came into effect in 2018 and was strengthened in ​2021.

The artworks found to have broken the law, however, date to 2005 and 2009, according to Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders who has been advocating for Gao's case.

"The court has now sentenced him to three years ... for artwork he made as far back as 2005, some 16 years before the law he was charged under even existed," Yi told Reuters, calling the punishment "a very clear case of a violation of a person's freedom of expression."

The artworks in question are reported to be "Mao's Guilt," a 2009 bronze statue of the former leader kneeling remorsefully, and the "Miss Mao" series of caricatures which depict Mao with breasts and a Pinocchio-like nose.

Calls for Zhen to be released

"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks told the Associated Press.

"The lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offense illustrate the authorities' determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression."

Researcher Yi said: "The only outcome that respects Gao Zhen's rights is his immediate, unconditional release."

There has as yet been no official statement from the court.

World.title: Última hora de la entrada de  inmigrantes a Ceuta, en directo | Pedro Sánchez comparecerá el 3 de septiembre en el Congreso para abordar la crisis en Ceuta
World.content:
Elma Saiz regresa a la Ciudad Autónoma para supervisar la ampliación de los recursos de acogida a migrantes | Feijóo exige convocar la Comisión de Secretos Oficiales para que el CNI aclare las “versiones” del Gobierno

La Junta de Portavoces ha acordado este miércoles fijar la comparecencia del presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, para abordar la gestión de la crisis en Ceuta el próximo jueves 3 de septiembre. La fecha ha sido decidida por los grupos de la Cámara en una reunión celebrada esta mañana después de que el propio Sánchez pidiera comparecer para ofrecer explicaciones por la entrada de unos 80.000 inmigrantes el pasado 30 de julio en la ciudad autónoma. La Diputación Permanente iba a debatir también a partir de las 12 la comparecencia urgente del presidente. Este miércoles el BOE ha publicado además el real decreto que declara la “situación de interés para la seguridad nacional” en Ceuta, con un mando único vigente hasta el 31 de diciembre, liderado por el ministro Ángel Víctor Torres, que ha respaldado la versión de Marlaska sobre los avisos del CNI. Por su parte, el presidente del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha exigido convocar la Comisión de Secretos Oficiales para que el CNI aclare las “versiones” del Gobierno, ante el “desbarajuste” entre Robles y Marlaska, y ha reprochado al Ejecutivo que “alguien miente”. Además, este miércoles la ministra de Migraciones, Elma Saiz, regresa a Ceuta para seguir los trabajos de ampliación de los recursos temporales de acogida, donde ya se ha reubicado a más de un millar de personas que permanecían acampadas en la playa de El Trampolín.
