World.title: GCash and PSA pioneer use of National ID for digital financial inclusion
World.content:
Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by GCash and was produced by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the production of this piece.

Financial technology has broadened access to payments and digital services across the Philippines, but bridging persistent gaps in inclusion and reach remains a pressing priority due to a lack of official documentation, a requirement for joining the digital economy.

A study by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) shows that 40% of adult Filipinos remain unbanked due to lack of documents, including IDs. As such, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) and GCash teamed up to expand National ID registration nationwide, especially in underserved communities.

Through a joint effort between PSA co-location and GCash barangay outposts, a mobile, on-demand initiative for ID and e-wallet registration, more than 2,000 Filipinos across over 25 barangays nationwide have been able to secure their National IDs and open verified GCash accounts since July 2025.

“Because of GCash’s financial services, more people will register for the National ID to access features like the e-wallet.” said Ronnie Mallillin, a PSA registration officer in Cavite.

With their National IDs, Filipinos can start their financial journey, access essential services, and build a secure and empowered future.

Financial services within reach

Danielle, 19, is among the National ID registrants assisted by the PSA and GCash. Forced to pause her studies to support her family, she worked as a street vendor to cover daily needs while saving for her eventual return to school.

A STEP TOWARDS FINANCIAL INCLUSION. Danielle gets her photo taken as part of her National ID registration.

Achieving her goals required access to digital financial services, but having no valid government ID prevented her from opening formal accounts. With her new National ID, Danielle can now open a GCash account, unlocking opportunities to grow her business, including loans for expansion.

Through the lending arm of GCash, Fuse Financing Inc., Filipinos can quickly access digital loans with flexible options and fair terms, covering expenses, investing in opportunities, or scaling small businesses. Fuse has disbursed P362 billion in loans to 10.5 million unique borrowers as of end-2025.

For now, Danielle focuses on helping her mother, who earns a living doing laundry, after her father passed away. She also hopes to enroll again by next year.

Building businesses with GCash

Just like Danielle, Alma is looking at GCash to boost her income. The housewife from Bulacan wants to build a business offering bill payment services in her neighborhood.

She was referring to the GCash Pera Outlet Plus, a separate app for nano, micro, small, and medium enterprises that allows them to provide cash-in and bill payment services in their communities. Through the app, they can serve both GCash users and unbanked customers with services like Send Money, Cash In, Cash Out, Bills Payment, and Buy Load.

This reflects the rising demand for digital financial services and the opportunities they create, highlighting the role of GCash in supporting and strengthening Filipino livelihoods.

Alma’s interest in opening a GCash account began during the pandemic. Many friends and relatives wanted to help her financially but could not because she lacked a valid government ID. With her new National ID, thanks to PSA, she is now ready to maximize financial opportunities.

Helping loved ones

GCash also aims to simplify sending money, a service often out of reach for those without a valid ID. This routine transaction can profoundly impact families separated by distance, as seen in the stories of Eldie and Mutya.

Eldie, a construction worker who suffered a stroke, would travel to stores to send funds to his family. With his own GCash account, he can now transfer money for his loved ones.

OPENING THE DOOR TO DIGITAL TRANSACTIONS. Eldie registers for a National ID through GCash and PSA.

For Mutya, family is also a key motivation. The laundrywoman from Quezon regularly sends money to her mom in another town.

She notes that when it rains, it becomes a hassle to go to a store just to send money to her mother or pay for other transactions. Indeed, digital platforms now provide convenience for both sender and recipient.

REACHING THR GRASSROOTS. Mutya (right) sets up her GCash account with help from a staff member (left) after completing her National ID registration.

Joining the digital economy

GCash continues to prioritize financial inclusion, helping more Filipinos access digital financial services and participate in the digital economy. This comes as digital payments now account for more than half of all retail transactions in the Philippines, according to the BSP, which aims to raise this share to 60 to 70 percent by 2028.

“We want every Filipino to maximize the opportunities offered by the digital economy, and it all starts with having a valid ID. Accessing digital financial services opens doors to education, entrepreneurship, and better ways to manage their finances,” said Ren-ren Reyes Jr., president and CEO of G-Xchange Inc., the mobile wallet operator of GCash. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kai Sotto, AJ Edu back together again for Gilas Pilipinas after 3-year wait
World.content:
TWIN TOWERS. Kai Sotto (right) and AJ Edu in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the 2023 FIBA World Cup.

The fourth window of the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers where Gilas Pilipinas will host Iran and Jordan marks the first time that Kai Sotto and AJ Edu are both available since Tim Cone took over as head coach

MANILA, Philippines – Good friends and longtime frontcourt partners Kai Sotto and AJ Edu link up for Gilas Pilipinas for the first time in three years.

And their reunion could not have come at a more crucial time as the Nationals face a must-win situation in back-to-back home games against Jordan and Iran in the fourth window of the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers on August 28 and 30, respectively, at the Mall of Asia Arena.

Sotto, 24, and Edu, 26, last played together in the national team during the Philippines’ co-hosting of the 2023 FIBA World Cup before injuries sidelined them out one after the other.

Lingering knee issues kept Edu out of national team action for much of 2024, and just as he was set to return, Sotto suffered a knee injury in 2025.

“It’s been a while. The last time was the World Cup that we played together, that’s three years ago,” said Edu. “Thankful we’ve both kind of overcame our injuries and we’re both healthy now. Definitely excited to share the court with Kai again.”

But even if it has been years since they last donned the national colors together, Sotto and Edu — who both play as imports in the Japan B. League — have kept in touch.

When Sotto sustained his injury, he reached out to Edu for advice, turning to his close pal who knew what it meant to endure the long, difficult road back.

“It was a huge challenge when I got injured, but I’m incredibly thankful to God for guiding me through it and to all the people who helped me along the way. AJ was one of them. He was one of the people I often turned to after I got injured because he went through the same thing,” said Sotto in Filipino.

For head coach Tim Cone, having Sotto and Edu back together is a big relief, especially after an initial shortage of big men forced veteran June Mar Fajardo to delay his planned retirement from the national team.

Cone tapped Fajardo for what could be his last two Gilas Pilipinas games as the team is without Quentin Millora-Brown and Mike Phillips.

“I’m real excited about that. Those guys, they complement each other, I think, very well. I think it’s fun,” said Cone, who will have both Edu and Sotto available for the team for the first time since he took over as head coach in 2024.

“You add June Mar to the mix and we’ve got a real good big man rotation. AJ and Kai are both versatile enough to play the four position, so it gives us a little bit of versatility in our frontline.” – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No Batangas-Mindoro undersea tunnel exists; video is AI-generated
World.content:
While there was a proposal to link the two provinces, it was not intended to be an undersea tunnel; the circulating video uses images that resemble a bridge in China

Claim: A video shows the Batangas-Mindoro undersea tunnel, which is already nearing completion.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user “Herbert Aquino Lucendovlogger” posted a video featuring an aerial shot of the alleged Japan-made structure and footage of the inside of the undersea tunnel.

The video’s narrator says, “Wow malapit na pala matapos ang Batangas-Mindoro undersea tunnel. Napakagandang daanan ito ng mga motorista. Gawang Japan talaga, napakatibay.”

(Wow, the Batangas-Mindoro undersea tunnel is nearly complete. This is an excellent road for motorists. It’s made by Japan, very sturdy.)

The post has 7.4 million views, 97,300 reactions, 7,600 comments, and 10,000 shares as of writing.

The facts: There is no Batangas-Mindoro undersea tunnel in the Philippines. The video is AI-generated.

AI detection tool HiveDetect analyzed the video frame by frame and labeled it as 99.9% likely to be AI-generated. It also flagged the speech in the video as 99.1% likely to be AI, with SightEngine scoring a screenshot of the post at 95% AI probability.

Fact-checking outlet VERA Files also flagged a similar post on April 10 as fake and AI-generated.

Inspiration from China: Reverse image search results showed that the AI-generated bridge seemed to take inspiration from the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge in China.

It is the world’s longest sea crossing, running 55 kilometers across the Pearl River Delta and connecting three of the country’s prominent cities through a bridge-tunnel system. It also has several artificial islands, which appear similar to the images shown in the AI-generated video.

Mindoro-Batangas Super Bridge: While there is no undersea tunnel in the Philippines, there was a proposal in 2015 to construct a “super bridge” linking the two provinces.

It was envisioned as a 15-kilometer floating bridge covering an 8.5-kilometer distance from Mindoro Island to Verde Island, then a 6.5-kilometer stretch from Verde Island to Batangas, to be constructed under the public-private partnership framework.

The administration of former president Rodrigo Duterte included the proposed bridge into its “Build, Build, Build” infrastructure program. Data from the National Economic and Development Authority showed that the project was retained up until 2019.

In 2023, San Miguel Corporation expressed interest in taking on the project. However, there have been no reports or public records regarding the bridge’s construction to date. – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: What Will Drive Next Wave of Investment in Central Asia
World.content:
TASHKENT – Investors increasingly want predictable policies, credible financial regulation, functioning capital markets, digital infrastructure, a talent pool and transparent governance, as Central Asia seeks to strengthen its position as an attractive and resilient investment destination. According to experts, Central Asia now has an opportunity to attract a larger share of global investment flows, but doing so will require not only financial innovation and regional connectivity, but also stronger institutions, transparent regulation and deeper capital markets.

Over the past few years in Central Asia, several factors have been positive for the countries, including high gold prices and very high income flows supporting current account deficits. The question is whether this will last long. External risks also include rising fuel and food prices, as well as climate factors.

The experts agreed that macroeconomic stability is the foundation for attracting investors during the panel session at the Silk Road Forum on Aug. 24.

Central Bank of Uzbekistan Governor Timur Ishmetov said the country will continue reducing inflation toward the 5% target by next year to ensure macroeconomic stability. The exchange rate remains flexible and market-oriented.

“The IMF reclassified our exchange rate regime to floating, and we are keen to continue on that. We will continue on capital account liberalization, but in a gradual and rightly sequenced manner. We drafted the roadmap for sequencing of those reforms. Our aim is, while providing more flexibility, to improve institutions, safeguard requirements, risk management, to make sure that we will not harm our stability issues and to improve our regulation,” he said.

Uzbekistan also reduced the state share in the banking sector from 85% to close to 60% in the last few years, and we will continue this trend.

Foreign investors are looking for growth but also predictability.

“Uzbekistan saw a 6% average growth since 2017 in real terms. There is obviously a demographic dividend, which is pretty high in Central Asia overall and Uzbekistan in particular, which will help the market to grow. We have seen consistent policy making in Uzbekistan. In fact, our upgrade of the sovereign credit rating in 2025 was very much linked to this consistent track record of policy making and coordination between the authorities on that front,” said S&P Global Ratings Director Roman Rybalkin.

The country’s first major international equity transaction is being presented as a signal of investor confidence. The National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan (UzNIF) was listed on both the London Stock Exchange and the Tashkent Stock Exchange. The transaction raised $692 million, with demand exceeding $2.9 billion. The fund was trading at a significant premium to its net asset value.

“We continue to bring companies to the market from our portfolio, because through the successful listing of the UzNIF, it shows the global interest in Uzbekistan, and we want to take advantage of this window of opportunity over the next few years and list a few of our assets including Uzbekistan Airways, UzTelecom, the hydropower business, and I think our successful IPO should also pave the way for very attractive private businesses that will be coming to the market over the next few years,” said Marius Dan, Chief Executive Officer for Central Asia at Templeton Global Investments.

Uzbekistan is also advancing its fintech ecosystem. UzCard and Humo are successful examples of networks that build fintech ecosystems around their payment networks. The country has 100 fintech startups, and the government seeks to double that number by 2030 and attract 1 billion investments in this sector.

Tashkent is hosting the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum 2026. The Central Bank of Uzbekistan and Singapore-headquartered Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN) support the event, which Ant International co-hosts on Aug. 24-26.

The event connects more than 4,000 participants from 74 countries in Tashkent. The forum focused on five key themes: digital payments and infrastructure; Islamic finance and new economic corridors; AI and emerging technologies; tokenization and digital assets; and cross-border finance and regulation.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Transport Sector Is Diversifying as Growth Moderates, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s transport sector maintained positive growth in January-July 2026, with the physical volume of transport and warehousing services increasing 7.4% year on year, down from 22.5% a year earlier. The slower pace of expansion, alongside diverging trends across transport modes, may signal a gradual shift in the structure of the country’s logistics system, experts say.

The latest figures from the Bureau of National Statistics’ Aug. 12 report show that Kazakhstan’s transport sector is still expanding, with freight transportation up 0.9% and freight turnover increasing 1.0%. Passenger transportation grew 4.5%, while passenger turnover rose 6.1%.

However, the slower pace of growth does not necessarily indicate a weakening of the sector, according to financial economist Rassul Rysmambetov. He said the comparison with last year’s 22.5% growth should be viewed in the context of a high base effect.

“The slowdown from 22.5% to 7.4%, if calculated correctly, can’t be explained as a crisis in transportation. Partially, it is a higher base effect, because last year’s high growth rate cannot be sustained for long,” Rysmambetov told the Astana Times.

He described the current rate as still representing “robust expansion,” with the sources of growth becoming more diversified.

“Now we have domestic trade, road transportation, and Caspian shipping growing instead of high-volume transit and pipeline,” he added.

Different modes reflect different parts of the economy

The overall figures conceal significant differences between individual segments. Road freight transportation increased 6.2% year on year, accounting for 37% of the sector’s total freight volume. Freight turnover in the segment rose 6.5%.

Maritime freight transportation increased 7.2%, while freight turnover grew 18%. Inland waterway transportation recorded particularly rapid growth, with freight volumes increasing 68.5% and freight turnover more than doubling, rising 109.6%.

At the same time, railway freight volumes declined 1.7% to 190.1 million tonnes. Despite the decrease in physical volume, railway freight turnover increased 2.5% to 170.1 billion tonne-kilometres, accounting for 57% of total freight turnover.

The combination of lower volumes and higher turnover may indicate that goods are being transported over longer distances. Pipeline transportation recorded a 2.6% decline in freight volumes, to 148.5 million tonnes, while freight turnover decreased 2.9%.

According to Rysmambetov, however, comparing the performance of different transport modes too directly can be misleading.

“The figures for different transportation means should be compared very cautiously. For example, a 2.6% decline in pipeline transportation reflects changes in oil production and export schedules rather than the same cargo, oil in this case, simply being moved to trucks, ships or rivers,” he said, noting that different modes serve different parts of the economy.

This distinction is important for interpreting the latest statistics. The decline in pipeline transportation coincides with an 8.9% year-on-year decrease in Kazakhstan’s oil production during the first seven months of 2026, meaning that lower pipeline volumes cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence that oil cargo is shifting to alternative modes.

Diversification rather than replacement

The strong growth recorded by maritime and inland waterway transportation nevertheless raises questions about the changing role of alternative logistics routes. Rysmambetov cautioned that the particularly high growth rates in Caspian shipping and inland waterway transportation also partly reflect a low comparison base.

“In general, the country is building diversified transportation options rather than replacing its traditional routes. Railways and pipelines will stay the backbone of the system, while road, maritime and river transport are becoming more and more important as complementary channels,” Rysmambetov said.

This distinction could be important for Kazakhstan’s long-term transport strategy. A more diversified system would not necessarily mean moving away from railways or pipelines, which remain critical for large-scale freight and energy exports. Instead, it would give businesses additional options for moving goods and accessing different markets.

Warehousing emerges as a critical part of the logistics system

The development of transport infrastructure is also creating demand for another part of the logistics chain: warehousing. Evgeny Vinokurov, chief economist of the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), said the bank’s research has identified warehousing infrastructure as a major structural issue for Eurasia.

“One of EDB’s flagship studies last year focused on warehousing infrastructure, which the Bank describes as a turning point for Eurasia this decade,” Vinokurov said.

He noted that warehouses should no longer be viewed simply as storage facilities, but as an increasingly sophisticated component of modern logistics. He also identified Almaty, Astana and Shymkent as three major logistics nodes with strong potential for warehouse development.

The development of these nodes could become increasingly important as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its role as a regional transit and distribution hub. Greater cargo flows alone, however, do not guarantee greater economic benefits. The country needs sufficient infrastructure to store, process and redistribute goods efficiently.

Growth is becoming more diversified

The passenger segment also remained broadly positive. Road passenger transportation increased 4.6% year on year, with 1.11 billion passengers transported during the period. Passenger turnover grew 6.8%.

Air passenger transportation increased 2.8%, with 9.2 million passengers transported and passenger turnover rising 8.1%. Maritime passenger transportation increased 138.3%, while inland waterway passenger transportation grew 7.0%.

Railway passenger transportation, meanwhile, declined 3.5% to 11.1 million passengers, although passenger turnover edged up 0.1%. The decline was less pronounced than the 6.3% decrease recorded during the same period last year.

The mixed performance reinforces the broader pattern: Kazakhstan’s transport sector is not moving uniformly in one direction.

For now, experts caution against interpreting the latest figures as a wholesale transformation of the transport system. The data instead point to a sector that is continuing to grow while gradually developing a broader range of logistics channels and infrastructure around its traditional backbone.

World.title: Tokayev Meets US Congressional Delegation in Astana: What Deeper US Engagement Means for Kazakhstan?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is becoming increasingly important to Washington not only as a source of energy and critical minerals, but also as a key partner in developing alternative trade routes and strengthening U.S. engagement across Central Asia. A meeting between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and a delegation of the U.S. House of Representatives on Aug. 25 highlighted the expanding scope of that relationship, as both sides emphasized economic cooperation ahead of Tokayev’s planned participation in the G20 summit in Miami.

The delegation was led by Jason Smith, chairman of the U.S. House Committee on the Budget and Taxation, and included Congress members Greg Murphy, Carol Miller, Ronny Jackson, Wesley Bell and Edward Case.

Tokayev highlighted the timing of the delegation’s visit, which came shortly after Kazakhstan’s first elections to the new unicameral Kurultai. According to him, parliamentary diplomacy would become an important area of activity for the new legislature.

“Constructive and meaningful dialogue between members of the U.S. Congress and the Kurultai is important for further deepening mutual understanding, promoting common priorities and strengthening the Kazakhstan-U.S. partnership,” Tokayev said.

The meeting also comes ahead of Tokayev’s planned visit to Miami for the G20 summit, following an invitation from U.S. President Donald Trump.

From political dialogue to economic interests

The discussion reflects a broader expansion of the Kazakhstan-U.S. relationship, which increasingly extends beyond traditional diplomatic cooperation. Tokayev briefed the delegation on Kazakhstan’s political and socioeconomic reforms and outlined the country’s modernization priorities.

Smith emphasized the economic dimension of the delegation’s visit. According to him, Trump asked to convey his warmest greetings and expressed his appreciation for the trusting and constructive relationship that has developed between both leaders.

“He also said that he looks forward to your visit to Miami to participate in the G20 summit,” Smith said.

“One of the main goals of our visit is to explore opportunities for further expanding economic ties between the U.S. and your wonderful country. We are firmly committed to meaningful dialogue on strengthening bilateral cooperation,” Smith added.

This emphasis is significant because the relationship is increasingly being driven by practical economic interests rather than diplomacy alone.

Kazakhstan’s strategic position

The growing U.S. interest in Kazakhstan also reflects the country’s position within a rapidly changing Eurasian environment. A discussion held Aug. 21 by the CFive Intellectual Platform and the Hudson Institute brought together experts from the U.S., Kazakhstan and Switzerland to examine the changing dynamics across Eurasia.

The discussion highlighted different interpretations of Kazakhstan’s emerging role. Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and an expert on Greater Asia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, described Kazakhstan as the “most important swing state in the world.”

His argument places Kazakhstan within the broader competition between the U.S. and China. He said Central Asia, the Caucasus and Türkiye could become increasingly important in that competition.

His framing, however, raises a broader question: should Kazakhstan’s importance primarily be understood through the competition between larger powers?

The growing U.S. engagement therefore does not necessarily indicate a shift away from a balanced foreign policy. Instead, it could strengthen Kazakhstan’s ability to maintain a diversified network of international partnerships.

The G20 invitation

Tokayev’s upcoming participation in the G20 summit in Miami provides a particularly visible example of this expanding engagement. The latest invitation is significant because it comes from Washington at a time when the U.S. is showing greater interest in Central Asia and the wider Trans-Caspian region.

Iskander Akylbayev, CEO of Xander Group and chairman of CFive, described the upcoming summit as a practical opportunity for Kazakhstan.

“My expectation is that the Miami G20 will be highly pragmatic and transaction-driven,” he said, identifying economic growth, secure energy supply chains and technological innovation as likely priorities.

The invitations extended to Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan can be also an evidence that Washington’s engagement extends beyond Kazakhstan. Thus, Kazakhstan’s growing importance to the U.S. can be viewed both as recognition of its individual economic and strategic weight and as part of a broader American effort to strengthen ties across the Trans-Caspian region.

A partnership with room for expansion

During the Aug. 25 meeting, Tokayev also emphasized cooperation between Kazakhstan and the U.S. in multilateral formats, including efforts to promote global and regional stability. He highlighted Kazakhstan’s support for U.S. initiatives, including the Board of Peace and the Abraham Accords, as well as cooperation on nuclear security and non-proliferation.

Smith, for his part, said Trump had expressed appreciation for the relationship and looked forward to Tokayev’s participation in the G20 summit. The upcoming meeting in Miami could therefore provide an opportunity to translate the growing political relationship into concrete economic agreements.

But the long-term significance of the partnership will depend on whether increased diplomatic attention results in sustained investment, technology cooperation, expanded trade and infrastructure development.

The latest meeting in Astana, the upcoming G20 summit and the expanding focus on economic cooperation suggest that Kazakhstan-U.S. relations are entering a more pragmatic phase – one in which the strength of the partnership will increasingly be measured by concrete economic outcomes rather than diplomatic rhetoric alone.

World.title: Experts: Kurultai Results Put Political Parties’ Ability to Deliver to Test
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s first Kurultai election has shifted the focus from winning votes to how effectively political parties can represent voters, develop clear political agendas and deliver results in parliament, experts said following the Aug. 23 vote.

The Central Election Commission (СEC) confirmed final results on Aug. 25. Five parties entered the 145-seat Kurultai after clearing the 5% threshold, with Adilet securing three-quarters of the seats. The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 3.11% and Baytaq 1.07%, while 2.51% of voters selected “against all.”

Dominant majority, higher responsibility

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the scale of Adilet’s majority places greater responsibility on the party to deliver results in Kurultai’s inaugural term.

“In other words, everything that will be done by the Kurultai and the institutions stemming from it during its first convocation will rest fully with the Adilet party and its leadership, given the vertical nature of management in Parliament,” Abishev wrote in his Telegram channel.

In his remarks to Kazakhstanskaya Pravda newspaper, Kazakh statesman Yerlan Koshanov said the campaign showed voters increasingly assessing parties by the substance of their programs and proposals rather than slogans alone. He said the first Kurultai’s lawmakers would be responsible for translating the new Constitution’s principles into legislation.

“Party programs became a subject of comparison and analysis, rather than simply a backdrop to the election campaign. People began to understand more deeply the role and place of such an important political institution as a party and to view it as a pillar of civil society,” said Koshanov.

Turnout rises, voter preferences consolidate

Participation was one of the clearest differences from the previous parliamentary election. Turnout in 2023 stood at 54.19%, compared with 74.08% in the first Kurultai election. Turnout was also close to the 73.12% recorded during the March referendum on the new Constitution.

Marian Abisheva, deputy director of the Presidential Center of Kazakhstan, said pre-election polling consistently pointed to high participation, with different surveys generally placing potential turnout between 70% and 76%.

“The March referendum and the August elections form a single political sequence. First, citizens participated in determining the state’s new constitutional architecture. Then, several months later, they came to the polling stations to form the first representative institution that will operate within that architecture,” Abisheva said at an expert meeting on Aug. 25.

She also pointed to a sharp decline in the share of undecided voters during the campaign. One early survey put the figure at 23.6%, while a later poll showed 3.9%.

“The reduction in uncertainty did not occur through growth in the protest electorate. The ‘against all’ option remained stable throughout the pre-election polling, with sociological studies showing it at between 1.5% and 2.6%. According to the final results, 2.51% of voters chose ‘against all,’” said Abisheva.

Political scientist Daniyar Ashimbayev contrasted the strong turnout with earlier expectations of voter fatigue after repeated nationwide votes in recent years.

“There is no clear algorithm in voter behavior. At the end of last year, some expressed the view that voters were tired of voting. But this year, according to the CEC, turnout reached 73-74%, and it seems no one was tired after all,” Ashimbayev wrote in his Telegram channel on Aug. 24.

Why Adilet converted recognition into votes

Serik Zhusupov, head of the Department of Comparative Studies and Scientific-Theoretical Analysis at the Eurasian Integration Institute, said party recognition alone was not enough if voters could not identify what a party stood for.

He said surveys in late 2025 and early 2026 had registered broad demand for political and institutional change, with the new Constitution and Kurultai election forming successive stages of that process.

“When we talk about party recognition, most people say that they have heard of the parties, but they do not understand their ideological positions. Adilet adopted a fairly simple and clear construct for everyone – the concept of justice. In all opinion polls, the theme of justice has always been one of society’s demands,” said Zhusupov.

He said Adilet built practical proposals around that concept and competed across several electoral groups rather than relying on a narrow base. By contrast, he said Respublica and Aq Zhol competed for overlapping business-oriented voters, while left-wing parties struggled to consolidate their potential electorate.

“As for Baytaq, I understand that the environmental agenda is quite relevant, but this ideology itself is vague, not clearly oriented and it is unclear which electoral niches it targets,” said Zhusupov.

Parties become central to representation

Zhandos Aktayev, a member of the Youth Policy Council, said the move to a fully proportional system places political parties at the center of parliamentary representation.

“People who want to engage in political activity and participate in politics, that is, to represent the country in the Kurultai, need to join parties and represent their interests through those parties. If we, as citizens, want to see ourselves represented in one party or another, or more precisely in the Kurultai, we need to go into that party. Most likely, we will also need to change its political discourse and its program from within in order to form the agenda that matters to citizens,” Aktayev told the press on Aug. 25.

Zhusupov said polling also showed expectations about deputies’ professional backgrounds. In one survey, approximately 30% of respondents favored a legal background, while others emphasized public-service experience, communication skills and strong professional and social reputations.

Election ends, inter-election competition begins

For political parties, experts said the more challenging phase begins after the campaign. According to Zhusupov, their performance would depend largely on what they do between elections.

“The parties that are working now and will continue working should not operate from one campaign to another. The inter-election cycle is very important,” said the expert.

“This is when they can promote not simply their recognition, but their ideology. Taking into account the mistakes that were made, many parties simply need to reconsider their ideology. If you are trying to build a more or less sizable faction in Parliament, you need to work with much broader electoral niches and expand them in order to receive more votes,” he said.

Abishev said the focus would now shift from electoral competition to legislative work.

“After the distribution of mandates and the annual address, the real work will begin. Inside the chamber, party division is no longer felt as strongly. Laws need to be adopted, and the best ideas from all programs need to be put into practice. It is important that new faces have the opportunity to make their contribution,” he wrote.

EU notes election process, urges further reforms

Anouar El Anouni, spokesperson for EU foreign affairs and security policy, said the European Union acknowledged Kazakhstan’s efforts to organize the election in a “well-prepared and orderly manner” despite the short period between calling and holding the vote.

“The EU strongly encourages Kazakhstan to continue its work on democratic reforms, and reaffirms its commitment to supporting Kazakhstan’s reform agenda, including in the areas of human rights, rule of law, and democratic governance. We stand ready to continue our cooperation with Kazakhstan to further strengthen our strategic partnership, based on shared values and mutual respect,” said El Anouni.

World.title: Tokayev to Convene First Session of Kazakhstan’s Kurultai on Aug. 28
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has signed a decree convening the first session of Kazakhstan’s elected Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral legislature, for Aug. 28 at 11 a.m., according to the Akorda press service.

The session will mark the start of work for the 145-member Kurultai, established under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which took effect on July 1.

The first parliamentary election under the new constitutional system was held on Aug. 23. According to the final results, five political parties cleared the statutory 5% threshold required to secure seats in the Kurultai.

The Adilet Party secured the largest share of the vote and will hold 110 seats. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party will have 10 seats, while Respublica will hold nine seats. The Aq Zhol Democratic Party and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party will each have eight seats.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 285,395 votes, or 3.11%, while the Baytaq Green Party received 97,751 votes, or 1.07%, falling below the 5% threshold. A total of 2.51% of voters selected the “against all” option.

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary election conducted under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework. The Kurultai replaced the country’s former bicameral Parliament and consists of 145 deputies elected through proportional representation from party lists in a single nationwide constituency.

The opening of the first session will formally launch the new legislature’s work and mark the next stage in implementing the institutional changes introduced by the new Constitution.

World.title: Payment Without Plastic: How Smartphones Are Reshaping Kazakhstan’s Cashless Economy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s cashless economy is entering a new stage as virtual cards become more common among active users and QR payments overtake bank cards at point-of-sale terminals. The shift suggests that digitalization is no longer simply about replacing cash with cards, but increasingly about replacing the physical card itself with a smartphone-based payment interface.

According to payment card statistics updated by the National Bank on July 31, Kazakhstan had 83.6 million payment cards in circulation as of July 1. However, only 41.9 million cards were actively used, or about half of the total. Among active cards, virtual cards accounted for 53%, compared with 47% for physical cards. That means that, among cards that are actually being used, digital versions have already overtaken plastic.

The way consumers pay at retail outlets is changing at the same time. During the first half of 2026, QR payments accounted for 58% of transactions conducted through point-of-sale infrastructure, compared with 42% for bank cards. QR payments also accounted for 53% of transaction value, compared with 47% for card payments. The number of QR transactions was 38% higher than card transactions through POS terminals, while their total value was 13% higher.

On average, Kazakh citizens made around 11 million QR payments worth 57.3 billion tenge (US$122 million) every day during the first half of the year. Card payments through POS terminals averaged about eight million transactions worth 50.8 billion tenge (US$108 million) per day. The difference is particularly visible in the average transaction size. A QR payment averaged 5,200 tenge (US$11), compared with 6,400 tenge (US$14) for a card payment through a POS terminal, suggesting QR is becoming especially prominent for routine, lower-value purchases.

From cashless to cardless

The broader trend is visible in the National Bank’s payment statistics. In June 2026, internet and mobile banking accounted for 79.5% of non-cash transactions by number and 90.2% by value. In the first half of 2026, Kazakhstan recorded around 7.1 billion cashless transactions worth 92.1 trillion tenge — data that points to the growing role of digital channels in everyday payments.

According to Ruslan Sultanov, author of Tengenomika, an analytical channel covering Kazakhstan’s macroeconomy, the tenge exchange rate and broader economic issues, the figures mark a new stage in the country’s payment digitalization.

“Earlier, the key change was the shift from cash to bank cards. Now the cashless payment itself is changing, as the physical payment instrument increasingly gives way to a digital interface,” Sultanov said.

For banks, this also changes the logic of competition. Kazakhstan has 83.6 million cards in circulation, but only about half are actively used. As Sultanov notes, the number of cards issued therefore says less about a bank’s relationship with its customers than which banking product becomes a customer’s primary one, which application they use for everyday transactions and where their payment activity is concentrated. Virtual cards can further lower the barrier to competition. Customers no longer necessarily need a physical card to use a banking product. This makes it easier to hold products from several banks, while competition increasingly moves from the physical wallet into the smartphone.

Competition moves to the smartphone

The shift also changes the infrastructure businesses use to accept cashless payments. The traditional combination of a plastic card and POS terminal is no longer the only familiar interface for a digital payment. For consumers, the change is even more visible: the bank account remains, and the card can still exist as a payment instrument, but the physical card is increasingly unnecessary at the moment of purchase.

The trend is also consistent with Kazakhstan’s broader push to build a more interoperable digital financial system. In July 2026, the country launched the nationwide Interbank Mobile Payment System, allowing customers of participating banks to make transfers by phone number and pay through a single interoperable QR code regardless of which bank they and the merchant use.

What QR means for everyday payments

The growth of QR payments does not mean bank cards are disappearing. Instead, it shows that the payment process is becoming increasingly detached from the physical card. For consumers, the change may be barely noticeable: the money remains in a bank account, while the smartphone becomes the interface through which they access and spend it. For merchants, meanwhile, QR payments provide an alternative to the traditional card-and-POS model.

Sultanov also cautions that the latest figures should not be interpreted as a complete replacement of card payments by QR. Rather, they point to a broader structural shift in which the payment itself is becoming less dependent on a physical carrier.

For banks, the main asset is increasingly the digital contact with the customer, the application through which people access their money, choose how to pay and conduct everyday transactions. Kazakhstan’s payment market is therefore moving beyond the familiar idea of a “cashless economy.” The more significant transformation may be toward a cardless economy, where the payment instrument remains digital, and the physical card becomes optional.

World.title: Why Kazakhstan’s Aviation Hub Ambitions Could Generate More Than Transit Revenue
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is investing heavily in airports, cargo infrastructure and international connectivity. But the bigger economic question is whether a growing aviation network can generate more than transit income – and become a platform for logistics, exports and higher-value economic activity.

Building the infrastructure for a regional hub

The government is upgrading aviation infrastructure as part of efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s role in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, and as a major Eurasian transit hub. From January to July, the country’s airports handled 102,500 tons of cargo, up 10% year on year. Almaty accounted for 66,100 tons, or more than 64% of the total.

Passenger traffic is also growing. In January-June, Kazakhstan’s airlines carried 7.4 million passengers, up 2.6% compared with the same period last year.

The country is also expanding passenger infrastructure. New terminals in Almaty, Kyzylorda and Shymkent have increased combined annual capacity from 3.5 million to 23 million passengers. Three new airports are being built in the resort areas of Katon-Karagay, Zaisan and Kenderli, with completion planned by the end of this year.

International connectivity is expanding alongside this infrastructure. Under the open skies regime, Kazakhstan now has 135 international routes connecting it with 30 countries. Cargo operators including Cargolux and Cathay Pacific Cargo have expanded operations through Astana, strengthening the country’s position in international freight networks.

Infrastructure alone is not enough

But infrastructure and rising traffic alone do not automatically create a successful aviation hub.

As Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva told The Astana Times in March, “the long-term sustainability of a hub depends on trust in the system: trust in safety, regulation and predictable rules.” She identified Kazakhstan’s high level of flight safety as a key competitive advantage.

International audits cited by the committee show 82% effective implementation of aviation safety oversight standards and 95.7% compliance with aviation security standards. These institutional conditions matter because airlines and cargo operators need more than runways and terminals. They need predictable regulation, reliable operations and confidence that a transit point can function consistently over time.

From transit flows to domestic value creation

The economic opportunity, however, extends beyond aviation itself.

Financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov notes that an aviation hub should be understood as a broader economic system, linking airports with roads, railways, warehouses and industries that can add value to goods before they reach export markets.

“The aviation hub is not simply the transportation of someone else’s cargo through Kazakhstan with refueling,” he told The Astana Times, stressing that the main goal should be to create additional value domestically.

For example, agricultural and food products could be processed, packaged or prepared for export near airports, allowing Kazakhstan to capture more of the value generated along the supply chain rather than simply moving foreign goods through the country.

The next test: economic integration

The next stage, therefore, is integration. New terminals, runways and cargo facilities provide the physical foundation, while safety and predictable regulation provide the institutional one. The larger economic payoff will depend on whether these assets attract logistics companies, processors, exporters and related services.

The key indicator will not only be how many passengers and tons of cargo Kazakhstan handles, but how much additional value that traffic creates.

If aviation can be integrated with rail, roads, logistics and domestic production, Kazakhstan’s emerging hubs could evolve from transit facilities into engines of export growth and broader economic development.

World.title: Kazakhstan Aims for 5% Growth, Expert Says Productive Capacity Is Key
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government has approved the Forecast of Socio-Economic Development and draft national budget for 2027-2029, targeting annual economic growth of more than 5% through 2029 while reducing the budget deficit to 0.4% of GDP. Financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov says the targets are achievable, but only if Kazakhstan expands its productive capacity through greater electricity generation, industrial development and deeper processing.

Under the baseline scenario, real GDP growth is projected to average more than 5% annually, while the national budget deficit is expected to decline from 2.3% of GDP in 2027 to 0.4% in 2029. Inflation is projected at 7.5-9.5% in 2027, before moderating to 6-8% in 2028-2029.

Kazakhstan’s economy grew by 4.1% in January-July, while the government expects full-year GDP growth of at least 5%. The framework focuses on expanding non-oil sectors, improving public spending efficiency and maintaining macroeconomic stability.

Non-oil sectors to drive growth

The government expects manufacturing, agriculture, construction and services to provide the main contribution to growth.

Nominal GDP is projected to increase from 199.3 trillion tenge (US$436.2 billion) in 2027 to 245 trillion tenge (US$536.3 billion) in 2029. Manufacturing is expected to outpace mining, led by metallurgy, machinery, construction materials, chemicals and food production.

Agriculture is forecast to grow by at least 5% annually, while construction growth is projected to rise from 16% in 2027 to 17.3% in 2029. Transport and warehousing and information and communications are expected to grow by 10.4% and 9.2%, respectively.

Inflation remains an important assumption

The projected inflation path is an important part of the macroeconomic framework. Inflation is expected to remain relatively high in 2027 before declining in the following two years.

Its trajectory will affect household purchasing power, business costs, investment decisions and the government’s fiscal position. Keeping inflation on the projected path will also affect the sustainability of planned economic growth.

Reducing the deficit while maintaining investment

The government projects budget revenues of 19.9 trillion tenge (US$43.5 billion) in 2027, rising to 23.4 trillion tenge (US$51.2 billion) in 2029. Expenditures are planned at 30.2 trillion tenge (US$66.1 billion) in 2027, 29.4 trillion tenge (US$64.3 billion) in 2028 and 29.6 trillion tenge (US$64.8 billion) in 2029.

The non-oil deficit is expected to decline from 5.3% of GDP to 2.5% over the same period.

At the same time, the 2027 budget allocates 10.5 trillion tenge (US$23 billion) to the social sector and 3.8 trillion tenge (US$8.3 billion) to the real economy. Targeted transfers from the National Fund will provide 2 trillion tenge (US$4.3 billion) in 2027 and 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3.2 billion) annually in 2028-2029 for critical infrastructure and nationwide projects.

Can Kazakhstan deliver growth while tightening its budget?

The government’s targets raise a broader question: can Kazakhstan sustain annual GDP growth of more than 5% while reducing the budget deficit to 0.4% of GDP by 2029?

According to financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov, the target is realistic, but achieving it will require increasing the economy’s productive capacity.

“In general, it is realistic. I would say a range of 4.5-5.5% is achievable. By then, we need to increase our economy’s potential by around 1.5%, meaning our productive capacity. This would require somewhat greater electricity generation, more factories and better processing. These are the key factors: productive capacity.

Right now, for example, you could build all the roads in Kazakhstan and increase GDP by 15%, but that would cost $20 billion, and this is not sustainable. GDP should grow healthily in line with the economy’s potential, not at any cost, but gradually. So, overall, 5% growth in 2029 is quite realistic,” he told The Astana Times.

Rysmambetov’s assessment points to productive capacity as a key condition for sustaining growth. Additional electricity generation, industrial capacity and deeper processing could allow the economy to expand without relying excessively on higher government spending.

This makes the composition of investment as important as its volume. Infrastructure spending can support growth by removing constraints on businesses and improving connectivity, but its longer-term effect will depend on whether investment creates new productive capacity and supports private-sector activity.

Indicators to watch

The government expects goods exports to rise from $82.8 billion in 2027 to $88.5 billion in 2029, while the National Fund’s foreign-currency assets are projected to increase from $65.2 billion to $70.6 billion.

Progress will depend on whether economic growth, inflation, budget revenues and productivity develop in line with the forecast while infrastructure and social investment are maintained.

Non-oil sector growth, private investment, export performance, inflation, tax revenues and the pace of deficit reduction will provide key indicators of how closely actual outcomes follow the 2027-2029 framework.

World.title: Azerbaijan confiscates cryptocurrency in favour of state for first time
World.content:
Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

The Yasamal District Court in Baku has sentenced two people arrested by the State Security Service, B.H.R. and I.R.F., and ordered the confiscation by the state of virtual assets identified as the proceeds or subject of the crime.

Details of the case

The defendants were found guilty under Article 206-1.3 of the Criminal Code. The article provides for criminal liability for organising the illegal covert transfer of particularly large sums of money out of Azerbaijan or into the country using set-offs and other forms of settlement.

According to the court’s ruling:

B.H.R. received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of 3,623,568 manats (about $2.13 million);

received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of (about $2.13 million); I.R.F. received a three-year restriction of liberty and a fine of 31,399,709 manats (about $18.47 million).

The court also ordered the state to confiscate 830 units of cryptocurrency held in an account on the international virtual-asset platform Binance. Investigators had frozen the assets during the preliminary investigation.

Official reports do not specify which cryptocurrency was involved, whether Bitcoin, Ethereum or another asset.

Legal basis

Under Article 99-1 of the Criminal Code, special confiscation involves the compulsory and free transfer to the state of tools and means used to commit a crime, as well as property obtained through criminal activity.

The Law on Combating the Legalisation of Property Obtained through Crime and the Financing of Terrorism also classifies virtual assets as property obtained through criminal activity.

The court has therefore applied the same legal regime to digital assets as it does to physical property for the first time in practice.

Context and significance

In 2025, the State Security Service had already secured a court order to freeze cryptocurrency in a similar criminal case. At the time, Baku’s Sabail District Court ordered the assets to be frozen. On 24 August, the process moved to the next stage: the authorities confiscated the assets.

Azerbaijan does not yet have a separate law governing virtual assets. The Central Bank previously said it expected the relevant draft law to be adopted by the end of 2026. Against this backdrop, the court ruling shows how authorities are addressing the existing legal gap in practice and could set a precedent for future regulation.

Experts note that international exchanges generally comply with court orders promptly. However, the authorities have not yet disclosed what will happen to the confiscated assets, including whether they could be sold at auction, transferred to state reserves or used in another way.

The case marks a new stage in Azerbaijan’s fight against digital crime and expands law enforcement agencies’ ability to track and confiscate virtual assets. At the same time, it highlights the real risks faced by people operating in the unregulated cryptocurrency market.

World.title: Is Georgia expecting a new wave of migrants from Russia?
World.content:
Upper Lars checkpoint, 2022. Photo: Mediazona

While rumours of a possible mobilisation circulate in Russia, Georgia is bracing for a new wave of Russian migrants. However, current data from the Upper Lars checkpoint on the Russian-Georgian border do not yet indicate a mass exodus from Russia.

In mid-August, Russia’s Customs Service said that Upper Lars had seen a “record flow” of travellers. The agency said more than 20,000 people crossed the border in passenger cars on 18 August.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry disputed the Russian figures. According to its data, 7,880 citizens of various countries entered Georgia from Russia between 8 and 19 August, while 8,406 people left Georgia for Russia. In total, 16,286 people crossed the border in both directions.

Russia’s customs authorities later clarified their figures, also saying that more than 16,000 people had crossed the border in both directions. This time, however, they did not describe the figure as “record-breaking”. They noted that more people were travelling towards Russia as the tourist season came to an end.

The figures nevertheless caused concern in Georgia. Many people remembered September 2022, when tens of thousands of Russians entered Georgia after Moscow announced a partial mobilisation.

That large influx drove up property prices significantly. Many people in Georgia now fear that the situation could happen again.

Why are people expecting a new wave of migrants?

Reports of a new mobilisation in Russia remain unconfirmed, but they are spreading widely. The reports claim that mobilisation could be announced after September’s State Duma elections. The Russian authorities have made no official statements to that effect.

Nikoloz Urushadze, managing partner at the consulting company G. Miller International Georgia, says that even these rumours could prompt some Russian citizens to leave the country.

“Even if Russia ultimately does not announce mobilisation, the expectation of it still affects people. They are afraid, and fear is often a powerful factor driving people to move,” he told BusinessPressNews.

Urushadze believes Georgia remains one of the most accessible destinations for Russian citizens and could face a new influx of migrants if Russia announces mobilisation.

The experience of 2022

In September 2022, immediately after Russia announced its partial mobilisation, the queue at the Upper Lars checkpoint stretched for 20-30 kilometres on the Russian side. Around 5,500 cars were waiting at the border. Authorities even set up a mobile military recruitment office in North Ossetia, where the checkpoint is located.

According to Georgia’s then-interior minister, Vakhtang Gomelauri, around 10,000 people crossed the border each day. Before the mobilisation announcement, the figure stood at about 6,000.

As a result of the influx, around 100,000 Russian citizens lived in Georgia for a period. Some local residents called on the authorities to introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens.

How could a new influx affect property prices in Georgia?

According to Nikoloz Urushadze, a new wave of Russian migrants would primarily affect the property market. Increased demand would push up rental prices again. Georgia experienced this in 2022-2023, when the arrival of large numbers of Russian citizens sharply increased rental costs in Tbilisi and Batumi.

Russian citizens, along with Ukrainians and Belarusians, are also actively buying property in Georgia. In the first half of 2026, they accounted for 18% of all buyers. A year earlier, their share stood at 13%. During the same period, the share of Georgian citizens among apartment buyers in the resort city of Batumi fell from 43% to 33%.

Urushadze points to another problem. In his view, some Russian citizens do not integrate into local society and the economy. Instead, they create their own closed infrastructure.

“Georgia is a country where 300,000 Russians could come and create a little Russia here, with their own schools and universities. They would not need the Georgian language or anything else at all,” he says.

At this stage, the situation on the Russian-Georgian border does not resemble the mass exodus of 2022. The queues in August were mainly linked to the tourist season and a temporary border closure due to bad weather. Many people were leaving Georgia rather than entering it, returning to Russia.

The real scale of any new influx will become clearer later. The decisive factor will be whether the Russian leadership officially announces mobilisation.

Russian migrants in Georgia

World.title: ‘Ice cream’ and cold showers: Keeping cool on hot days at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
As summer temperatures rise, Tbilisi Zoo switches to a special routine. The keepers’ main task is to help the animals cope with the heat and protect them from overheating.

A range of measures is used, from cooling the enclosures to providing special diets. The first and most important rule is to ensure that all the animals have a constant supply of clean, cool drinking water.

The water is refreshed several times a day, while keepers provide additional ways for the animals to cool down in their enclosures when needed. One method is to spray the enclosures with water. Zoo staff regularly hose down the floors and surrounding areas to maintain humidity and lower the temperature.

Large animals require particular attention. For elephants, for example, water treatments are a real treat. Keepers hose them down all over their bodies, helping them cool off quickly.

The zoo also creates mud wallows specifically for the elephants and the rhinoceros. As the mud dries on the animals’ skin, it forms a protective layer against strong sunlight, possible sunburn and insects. The layer also helps keep their bodies cool.

Summer heat also affects the animals’ daily care. Keepers adjust feeding methods so that the animals receive both physical and mental stimulation. Seasonal juicy fruits are added to their diets, providing another way to help them cool down.

For primates and herbivores, keepers freeze fruit and vegetables. For the animals, this is a kind of “ice cream”, but it serves more than just a cooling purpose. The animals have to make an effort to get to the frozen food, providing both physical and mental stimulation. It also allows them to display natural behaviour.

The same principle applies to predators, for which keepers freeze meat. “Meat ice cream” helps lions and tigers cool down while also providing sensory enrichment.

It is also important that the doors to indoor enclosures, where temperatures are lower and it is cooler, remain open at all times. This allows the animals to choose where they want to stay.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

The heat at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: South Ossetia residents name region’s main problems ahead of presidential election
World.content:
South Ossetia presidential election

South Ossetia election. Illustration created by Caucasian Knot using AI

A report by Caucasian Knot

Population decline, low wages, unemployment, queues at the customs checkpoint and poor public transport. Residents of South Ossetia named these as the main problems ahead of the snap presidential election.

Murad Valiev, Kazbek Kodoev, Marat Kambolov and Zurab Kokoev have been cleared to stand in the election. The Central Election Commission plans to print 40,000 ballot papers. Khokh Chochiev, leader of the Iry Farn party, who was denied registration, called the election a sham.

On 23 August, a Caucasian Knot correspondent spoke to residents of the region. The survey is not representative and reflects individual views.

“There is no trust left in anyone”

Fatima, 45, works as a kindergarten teacher in Tskhinval. She sees the lack of jobs as the main reason people are leaving the region.

“Young people mostly leave because of this. Graduates of Russian universities return home but cannot find work. If jobs become available here, they will come back,” she says.

Fatima also wants to see higher wages. She says incomes remain low while prices continue to rise. She also names queues at the customs checkpoint as another major problem.

“They said the situation improved after Kambolov visited the customs checkpoint. But there are still queues. I am not following the campaign. There is no trust left in anyone. I have not come across any campaigning either,” she said.

Karina, 23, is unemployed and lives in Dzau. She lists wages, unemployment, environmental problems and the state of agriculture among the region’s main challenges.

Public transport is a particular concern for her. The last bus leaves Dzau at 17:00, while the last bus from Tskhinval leaves at 18:00.

“I would like buses to run at least until eight or nine in the evening. I do not have a car and cannot afford to buy one. It is also practically impossible to get a loan or mortgage in South Ossetia,” Karina says.

In her view, unless these problems are addressed, the population decline will become irreversible.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions”

Karina is not following the election campaign and believes the outcome has already been decided.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions. They would benefit from making Kambolov president. The election is just window dressing. People have not had a choice for a long time,” she said.

Karina says she has not seen campaign posters or activists in Dzau or Tskhinval.
