World.title: Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes
World.content:
Exclusive NationalInsects Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes Angus Dalton August 26, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Australian scientists have created insect-robot hybrids for search-and-rescue missions.

The cockroach cyborgs are designed to find people trapped in areas human rescuers can’t reach.

The cyborgs can fire syringes from their backs for emergency treatment.

Other teams have made diving suits for cockroaches so they can operate during floods.

The concept has been trialled in the aftermath of a deadly earthquake in Myanmar.

If you ever find yourself buried beneath the rubble of an earthquake’s aftermath or expiring in a remote cave, salvation may not arrive in the form of a dashing rescuer or detection dog, but of a hulking, hissing, spiky-legged cockroach. Scientists are developing cyborg paramedic cockroaches designed to find people trapped in places human rescuers can’t reach, with the latest recruits capable of delivering medicine by firing syringes from a harpoon system on their backs. A cyborg cockroach armed with a syringe-firing backpack. The University of Queensland The “paraborg” (a portmanteau of paramedic and cyborg) insects are made from giant burrowing cockroaches, which are the world’s heaviest cockroach species and native to north Queensland. “It’s not for everyone,” biorobotics specialist and cyborg creator Dr T. Thang Vo-Doan, from the University of Queensland, said of working with the cockroaches. “But we have very good relationship with them in the lab.”



The glossy arthropods are fashioned into cyborgs by the insertion of electrodes into their antennae, so the cockroaches can be remote-controlled with a joystick. Antennae detect obstacles, so when the left one is stimulated, the cockroaches bear right, and vice versa. Other electrodes in the “cerci” – sensory appendages at the back of the insect – allow researchers to accelerate or stop the cyborg roaches. Scientists eventually want to make fully robotic, insect-inspired rescue devices but Vo-Doan said robots aren’t small, agile or efficient enough yet to operate in disaster zones. Cockroaches, however, are ready to rumble.



“The insect can climb and run, even carry heavy loads in different orientations in a complex environment,” Vo-Doan said. “You already have everything from nature. It simplifies our system a lot in terms of design and engineering.” PhD student Hai Nhan Le remotely controls “paraborg” cockroaches. The University of Queensland He believes more lives can be saved now by harnessing the insects, with agility and efficiency honed by evolution, to carry devices including cameras and sensors into collapsed buildings. While small robots are restricted by limited battery life, cockroaches can go for days, powered simply by gum leaves and apple slices. There’s no requirement for scientists to obtain ethical approval for research with insects. But the cockroaches are anaesthetised for the insertion of electrodes, and electronic systems are carefully removed after experiments.



Vo-Doan said the cyborg recruits seem to live as long and well as their civilian counterparts. The latest study, published in Advanced Science, focused on the “rescue” part of search and rescue. If a swarm of cyborg cockroaches discovered a victim buried beneath rubble who was suffering from sepsis, what happens next? Cyborg cockroaches can traverse complex, rubble-strewn environments better than robots. The University of Queensland Enter the medic class. The researchers created and tested needle-firing cyborgs and showed they could successfully navigate to a target and deliver a jab in 72 per cent of proof-of-concept trials. When cockroaches came within 15 centimetres of a mock target, the hit rate was 95 per cent.



“A lot of people might not like the sight of a giant cockroach scurrying towards them,” said PhD candidate and first author of the research Hai Nhan Le. “But if you’re trapped in rubble or stuck in a cave and need help, it could make a real difference between life and death.” The idea, eventually, is to create a “fully autonomous paramedic team composed of terrestrial cyborg insects” that can independently search for victims, relay information and deliver medication, the researchers write. The concept might seem far-fetched but other international teams are taking the same approach and have been trialling it in the field.



Ten cyborg Madagascan hissing cockroaches fitted with infrared cameras and sensors were deployed alongside Singapore’s Operation Lionheart rescue team in the aftermath of a 2025 earthquake in Myanmar that killed at least 3600 people. (The cockroach squad didn’t detect any survivors but researchers said the mission yielded valuable lessons to improve the cyborgs.) Other researchers have made 3D-printed diving suits for cyborg cockroaches that could help in flood rescues. NTU Singapore Meanwhile, in June, another team of researchers introduced the aquatic class. They designed flexible cockroach diving suits 3D-printed from resin. Cockroaches wearing the suits could operate underwater for three hours despite being a terrestrial species, the researchers reported in Nature. The amphibious cyborgs could one day carry out missions in flooded areas or help explore the deep ocean – or other planets. “The ultimate goal is to [take this technology to] space,” lead author Professor Hirotaka Sato told New Scientist. “Exploration over the Mars surface, for example.”



Related Article Analysis

China relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics So when might we see cyborg cockroaches rolled out to disaster zones? Perhaps five years, perhaps 20, depending on the level of support the idea gains, Vo-Doan said. Experts such as Superintendent Tim Hassiotis, from Fire & Rescue NSW, are open to the concept if the cyborgs prove effective in real emergencies. “If cyborg insects can safely enter spaces we can’t, locate casualties and ultimately help deliver emergency care, they could become another valuable tool in the future of urban search and rescue,” Hassiotis said. Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday. Sign up to get the whole newsletter in your inbox.

World.title: Police probe link between Fadi Haddara shooting and Tassie tobacco operation
World.content:
Police are investigating if the near-fatal shooting of crime figure Fadi Haddara is linked to his crime network’s alleged involvement in a multimillion-dollar tobacco and money laundering operation in Tasmania. Haddara’s targeting by a hit team was the first of three shootings targeting associates, the latest on Wednesday when a 37-year-old man was shot on a property in broad daylight in Heidelberg West. Fadi Haddara is recovering after being shot in his driveway. Jason South Haddara himself was nearly killed after being gunned down in the driveway of his family home in Altona North on August 16. He was released from hospital this week, but doctors are waiting to attempt to remove one bullet still lodged near his jawline.



“He’s up walking around, speaking properly. Friends couldn’t believe it,” an associate said. A week after the failed hit, a known Haddara associate was shot in the arm while sitting in a cafe in Altona North’s Borrack Square commonly frequented by figures linked to the clan. On Wednesday afternoon, Victoria Police said a victim had been left suffering from serious injuries after being shot outside a property on Malacca Street in Heidelberg West. A spokesperson said the unknown offenders fled in a car, and the incident is being treated as targeted. Two sources, who have knowledge of the incident but spoke anonymously for their safety, identified the 37-year-old as an associate of the Haddara patriarch.



Organised crime gang The Commission is the prime suspect behind the attacks, which signals a renewal of the hostilities that first ignited Melbourne’s tobacco wars. Related Article Organised crime He lived like a man with nothing to fear. His shooting has left even the underworld shocked The Commission, also known as the 313, is the transnational crime gang established by exiled gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2023 that has created a nationwide illicit tobacco cartel after waging a campaign of firebombings and shootings. They had reached an uneasy truce with Haddara who had stepped back from active involvement in the family’s activities after he “surrendered” to Hamad in early 2024 in exchange for an end to a campaign of fire bombings targeting family businesses and a $1 million hit contract put on his head. However, there have been a number of branches of the extended Haddara family that have allegedly continued to operate in the illicit tobacco market. Some even switched sides and were absorbed into The Commission.



The shootings started just days after the federal and state Joint Organised Crime Taskforce took down a money-laundering syndicate operating between Tasmania and Victoria. “It is alleged they facilitated the movement of criminal proceeds in cash from Tasmania and Victoria using hire cars and a commercial passenger and freight vessel,” the Australian Federal Police, Australian Border Force and Tasmanian and Victorian police announced. Loading The operation on August 12 uncovered more than $2.5 million worth of tobacco, over $1 million in cash and $34,000 in silver and gold in raids in Melbourne and near Hobart and Devonport. A 33-year-old from Hoppers Crossing and a 22-year-old Tasmanian, arrested in Melbourne, have been charged with knowingly dealing with the proceeds of crime and recklessly dealing with proceeds of crime.

World.title: Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them?
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them? Dream sequences are a lazy storytelling device. The only place they belong is the cutting room floor. John Bailey August 26, 2026 — 7:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

How good is that bit in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey where Matt Damon skydives naked with the sexy chimp who talks just like his Grade 6 English teacher? No, wait, that’s a dream I had, and I won’t bore anyone further with the grubby details. Nobody likes to hear another person’s dream, especially my partner and children. Jeff Bridges dreaming of flying (among other things) in The Big Lebowski. YouTube Christopher Nolan knows that dream sequences are the worst, which is why the director famous for his flashbacks and flash-forwards and all sorts of timey-wimey shenanigans generally steers clear of sleepytime nonsense. He even directed an entire film set within dreams that strenuously avoided surrealist imagery or flights of fancy. The “dreams” in Inception were closer to your daily commute than a nude plummet with a primate playmate. This is the storytelling equivalent of waving your palms and pleading, “No, no, I take it all back!” There’s a piece of writing advice sometimes attributed to the novelist Henry James: tell a dream, lose a reader. The irony here is that James himself could really knock out a killer dream story. He wrote in an autobiography of “the most appalling yet most admirable nightmare of my life,” in which he was chased through The Louvre by a terrible creature, the whole affair lit only by lightning. But James would agree with Nolan, who recently argued that audiences “devalue” dream sequences.



How many times does a film or TV show just start to become interesting before our protagonist bolts upright amid a snarl of bedsheets, panting with relief that none of what they’ve just experienced really happened? This is the storytelling equivalent of waving your palms and pleading, “No, no, I take it all back!” It’s like ending a chapter of your book with the line “haha not really, lol”. It’s a failure of commitment, undoing the very thing that is likely the dramatic highlight of your tale. Rather than escalating tension and ratcheting up the stakes, it deflates whatever energy the dream sequence was supposed to generate. There’s also the sorry tendency to treat dreams as perfectly legible pieces of code. Thanks to Freud and Jung, storytellers feel justified in treating our complex and jumbled inner worlds as if they were simple ciphers describing our fears and desires. Yawn. Not everything that appears in our dreams represents something at the core of our psyche. Freud was forced to remind us that sometimes a cigar is just a cigar, just as I’ve been forced to remind my partner and children that sometimes a naked skydive with your Grade 6 English teacher is perfectly innocent.



I can already hear the cinephiles unsheathing their poison pens, so let me issue a caveat: I’m not against stories that are dream-like. In fact, they’re some of the best. Think of Picnic at Hanging Rock, a gossamer dream of the Australian landscape as shared by young white women under an oppressive colonial regime. The films of directors as diverse as Yasujiro Ozu, Ingmar Bergman, Sofia Coppola and Lynne Ramsay all possess a dreamlike weightlessness, even though they’re grounded in the waking world. Henry James himself pulled off the same trick with his classic The Turn of the Screw, in which the boundary between the real and the imagined is never resolved. Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Enough with the boring alpha men – I can’t get enough of this TV trend Paul Kalina Contributor Then there’s David Lynch, whose art was almost entirely defined by dream logic but who rarely stooped to anything as low as an actual dream sequence. From Twin Peaks to Mulholland Drive, dreams and reality overlap to the point that there’s little difference. Lynch often said that our partial, fragmented perception of existence means that we all essentially live inside our own private dream. His films, then, were dreams within a dream, and that’s a phrase that a whole bunch of his characters would repeat across his work. If a film is already a fantasy, then why not go the whole hog and commit? How much more compelling is it to happen upon the moment in a story that has you thinking, “This can’t be happening, not really”, only to gradually realise that yes, we’re going there, and you won’t believe what happens next, too. Take this alluring primate by the hand and leap out into that wide blue sky. No need to tell us it was just a dream all along.

World.title: Andrew lost his son to cannabis. A landmark study helps us understand why
World.content:
NationalNSWMedicine Andrew lost his son to cannabis. A landmark study helps us understand why Rachel Rasker August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Patrick Leunig finished high school with a great ATAR and a coveted spot in a law degree, his father assumed he was on the path to success. “It looked like he had his whole future in front of him,” Patrick’s father, Andrew Leunig, said. Andrew Leunig said his son was a “happy, healthy kid” before his illness. “We later found out he started smoking cannabis in Year 11, when he was 16.” Patrick dropped out of university inside a year. By the time he was 21, he was hospitalised against his will for the first time, when the delusions and conspiracies of drug-induced psychosis made it clear he needed help.



In April 2024, Patrick was found dead of a methamphetamine overdose. It was two days before his 26th birthday. Patrick Leunig had “his whole future ahead of him”. “If he had never smoked cannabis, would he have had a mental illness? I don’t know the answer,” Leunig said. A landmark Australian-led global study found cannabis users develop psychosis an average two-and-a-half years earlier than non-users who experience psychosis. The largest study of its kind, published in Biological Psychiatry, involving 149 studies with data from more than 70,000 individuals, found that the younger people started smoking cannabis, the worse the clinical outcomes. They lost years of healthy life and incurred greater healthcare and societal costs.



Cannabis users in their early 20s developed psychosis 1.6 years earlier than non-users, while those over 30 developed psychoses about 6.3 years earlier, the analysis found. Related Article Drugs ‘Took control of my life’: Teens banned from buying popular Sydney party drug University of NSW professor of psychiatry Matthew Large, one of the study’s co-authors, said the most plausible explanation is the increased years of exposure. The cumulative toxicity of cannabis was comparable to lung cancer and tobacco – the longer someone smokes, the higher their risk, Large said. Co-author Carly Stevens said there was a prevailing myth that “you’ll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s,” once your brain had developed.



“What we’ve found challenges the assumption,” she said. “There’s been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone … no one is really safe when it comes to trying cannabis.” Cannabis users are two to five times more likely to develop schizophrenia, with a six-year average delay between initial cannabis use and the onset of psychosis. Medicinal cannabis has surged in popularity since its introduction in 2016, as outlined by Penington Institute reports. In 2025, 6.35 million units of the prescription drug were sold in Australia, a 279 per cent increase in three years, with 1.68 million units sold in 2022. Medicinal cannabis is essentially identical to illicit cannabis, Large said, and carries the same or greater risk, given it tends to have a higher concentration of THC. “I think we have effectively legalised cannabis already, but we’ve given it a halo of a medicine that has meant that it’s very difficult to talk about its harms,” he said.



Related Article Mental health The $300 a week medicine Daniel feels better without “You can buy it with almost no information about how bad it may be for you. I think we’ve just ended up with the worst of both worlds.” Studies have found no evidence that medicinal cannabis is effective for treating anxiety, depression and PTSD. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s 2022–‍2023 National Drug Strategy Household Survey found 3 per cent of Australians had used cannabis for medical purposes in the previous 12 months, equating to about 700,000 people. Dr Pramudie Gunaratne, CEO of the Australian Society of Psychiatrists, said prescribing doctors had a responsibility to ensure patients understand the risks of psychosis: “The growth of medicinal cannabis has been incredibly rapid, but our understanding and communication of the psychiatric risks hasn’t kept pace.



“Cannabis has become increasingly normalised as both a recreational drug and a medicine. This study is an important reminder that normalisation doesn’t make it harmless,” she said. Andrew Leunig said Patrick was “on the launchpad” to success. Leunig said there was no known history of psychosis in his family, and Patrick’s “rolling chaos” was eventually diagnosed as schizoaffective disorder, with his initial cannabis dependency a clear “gateway drug” to meth use. “Patrick was generally a pretty happy, healthy kid … to then become very unwell and continue to be unwell, it was just horrible.” Leunig can’t help thinking that Patrick’s life would have been different had he developed psychosis later in life.



Related Article Legal Cannabis Cannabis companies caught allegedly making false promises “If you’re a bit older and more established, you have more resilience, you’d have some experience of being an adult, before the onset of illness,” he said. “I certainly underappreciated the risks of cannabis, [and] I think most people would not be aware of how dangerous it can be for vulnerable people.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Swedes seize Russian tycoon’s island home over security fears
World.content:
WorldEuropeSweden Swedes seize Russian tycoon’s island home over security fears David Crowe August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A Russian businessman planning a luxury home on a beautiful Swedish island will have his property seized by the state in a dramatic move to protect a nearby naval base, highlighting European concerns about conflict with Moscow. The Swedish Defence Ministry ordered the forced sale of the waterside holiday home to ensure the security of an underground base with docks, tunnels and a shipyard built into caverns on the Baltic Sea. A Swedish Navy patrol boat operates near the base on Musko Island near Stockholm. Alamy Stock Photo Once likened to a hidden lair from a James Bond film, the base at Musko Island is now the subject of serious debate about the risks to Sweden of “hybrid” attacks from Russia, including drone incursions near airports and military facilities. German investigators have found three drones and suspected explosives near Leipzig airport in recent weeks, while Romanian forces destroyed a marine drone near a gas project in the Black Sea last Thursday, and Poland experienced two instances of sabotage on its rail lines last year.



‘We are in the most serious security situation since the end of World War II.’ Carl-Johan Edstrom, Swedish chief of defence staff The concern about Musko Island, about 40 kilometres south of Stockholm, centres on the Russian businessman’s plan to build a prestige home, up to 600 square metres in size, for himself and his wife, who has Russian and Swedish citizenship. The Swedish government did not name the couple. Swedish Defence Minister Pal Jonson said on Tuesday morning in Stockholm (late Tuesday night, AEST) that the National Fortifications Administration had taken steps to expropriate a property near the naval base. “The Swedish Armed Forces state that they have an immediate need for this property for military defence purposes,” he said.



“The security situation has deteriorated in recent years, and the threat landscape facing Sweden and Swedish interests has become increasingly complex. Consequently, a massive expansion of the total defence system is under way. “This also entails an increased need for access to sites where operations can be conducted during peacetime and which offer strategic advantages in the event of war.” Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Who started the fire?’ UK backs Ukraine with seismic deal on AI weapons Jonson said the state had the power to compulsorily acquire property for military defence, although he did not elaborate on how the purchase price might be decided. The base on Musko Island was built in the 1960s and used at the height of the Cold War, but it was decommissioned after the fall of the Berlin Wall and was only put to military use again in a major construction project over the past nine years.



Swedish newspaper Expressen reported on Tuesday that the property was owned by Stanislav Aleshchenko, a businessman with ties to the regime of Russian President Vladimir Putin. It said the property was purchased in 2017 for 18 million Swedish kronor (about $2.6 million), and the new home was being partly dug into the rock. The newspaper said the Russian’s wife, Tatiana Sazonova, was the formal owner of the property. She had previously denied knowing the site was near a military base, telling Expressen: “I didn’t know that when I bought it. I was looking everywhere. And it just turned out that way by chance. An unfortunate, unfortunate coincidence.” Russian incursions increase Sweden began rebuilding the Musko Island base after Russian forces seized control of the Crimea in 2014 and a series of incidents around that time, including the sighting of a Russian mini-submarine in Swedish waters that year.

World.title: Royal commission has created the best record of antisemitism since World War II
World.content:
NationalAntisemitism royal commission Opinion Royal commission has created the best record of antisemitism since World War II Philip Crutchfield Barrister August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professor Steven Prawer walked into his office at the University of Melbourne and found around 20 people waiting for him, most with their faces covered by keffiyehs. He had spent untroubled years running a physics research collaboration with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Other senior staff were involved in the collaboration, but Prawer, who wears a kippah, was the only one visibly Jewish. He told the people in his office that they were trespassing and asked them to leave. They refused, and as he tried to reach a secure part of the building, two of them followed him and wedged a foot in the door to stop him closing it, chanting, “Prawer, Prawer, you can’t hide, you’re guilty of genocide.” When he returned to his office later that day, a photograph of him had been vandalised and symbols associated with Hamas had been stuck to his walls. Commissioner Virginia Bell on the bench. ABC News Accounts like this are now part of the public record of this country, permanently, because a royal commission compelled them.



I made a submission to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. My submission is principally about the malevolent power of the herd and the damage it wrought to a country’s society and democracy. I wrote my submission because I cannot countenance any minority group in this country having to send their children to school under armed guard. I would feel the same whatever group was in that situation. Over recent weeks, the royal commission has attracted criticism. Some have expressed concern that certain witnesses have not been called to give evidence. Others have argued that some of the loudest antisemites and supporters of proscribed terrorist groups who have done so much damage to our country have not been made to answer publicly for what they have said and done. The disgraceful events at the Sydney Opera House on October 9, 2023, have not been fully examined. Those grievances are real and they must not be dismissed. But taken on their own, they understate what the commission set out to achieve and what it has already achieved. Its single greatest feat has been to create an extraordinary truth-telling process. Truth-telling processes are incredibly important and cathartic. I have seen this with my own eyes, in the area of sexual abuse of children, through an organisation I chair. In this commission, more than 20,000 submissions were made before a single public hearing began – the largest response of its kind in Australian history. Commissioner Virginia Bell, the highly respected former High Court judge, opened each hearing with the lived experience of Jewish and other Australians before institutions were questioned. Ordinary Australians, many of them frightened and previously without a platform, were heard with empathy, care and respect. If the personal accounts established the human cost, the institutional evidence has been just as pointed. The vice-chancellors of ANU and the Universities of Sydney and Melbourne answered for their institutions. The University of Melbourne confirmed that the university had chosen not to name the students disciplined over the occupation of Professor Prawer’s office.



Related Article Antisemitism royal commission ‘TikTok dances in the car parks of Auschwitz’: Universities slammed at royal commission There is now no more complete public record of contemporary antisemitism, perhaps since World War II. Once evidence like this sits on the record, it becomes very hard to pretend it does not exist. Some want the commission to do more than build a record. They want it to name every person, leader and institution that turned away while this hatred grew and to see them held to account. I understand that wish and the raw anger that sits behind it. It is true that another commission may have been conducted in that way, allowing the performative evisceration of bad actors and institutional leaders who enabled them. However, and having regard to the terms of reference, this commission was never going to disembowel protagonists or terrify witnesses into submission. Systemic and meaningful change requires real listening, education and empathy, of the kind being displayed by this commission. This commissioner seems to understand that history shows that punishment and retribution need to be balanced with education and understanding.



The commission has done an extraordinary job to date and should be trusted to finish its work in the best way Commissioner Bell thinks fit. Forensic criticisms of the commission at this stage can only give those resistant to change an opportunity to dismiss the commission as partisan. The success of the commission should be judged by the degree of cultural and institutional change it effects, and by the recommendations that are made and implemented. A commission that delivers instant gratification but compounds fractures to social cohesion is ripe for politicisation and harms our chances of real change. The report Commissioner Bell writes by December will have an impact, and so will what the government will assuredly have to do with it. But the evidence that got us there already exists and cannot be undone and Australians can see what antisemitism looks like. We, as a community, can no longer deny or ignore it and are duty-bound to confront it. Only then can we be satisfied that we took the steps that needed to be taken to reveal, recognise and confront the abhorrent disease of antisemitism – a disease which is anathema to a country that is world-famous for giving everyone a fair go. Philip Crutchfield is a Melbourne barrister

World.title: Our five favourite luxury homes that offer a holiday aura
World.content:
PropertyLivingLuxury property Our five favourite luxury homes that offer a holiday aura Shona Hendley August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

From outdoor amenities and lush gardens to luxurious en suites and entertainment zones, there are many features that can make your home feel like a five-star resort. Here are our five favourite luxury homes on the market that make you feel like you’re on holiday. 13 Elwood Street, Brighton, VIC Who needs to leave the house when you have a host of resort-style amenities at your fingertips in your backyard?



Set on a 1183-square-metre allotment, the property features private grounds with a full north-south tennis court, a shingled al fresco pavilion with a kitchenette and en suite, and a Magna magnesium pool and spa. Stirling Manor, a short walk from North Point Beach, was designed by Jon Friedrich and has recently been transformed. The property features internal spaces that complement the resort feel of the exterior, including a lower-ground wellness retreat with a display wine cellar, bar, gym, infrared sauna, bathroom, and a secluded lightwell courtyard. 11 Pearl Bay Avenue, Mosman, NSW Backing onto Pearl Bay Reserve and a short walk to the waterfront, this Mosman property offers a perfect opportunity to enjoy the outdoors, or you could sit back and relax with your own Middle Harbour views.



This updated six-bedroom, four-bathroom home is set over two levels, offering flexible family living. The home prioritises indoor-outdoor connection, with a second kitchen on the lower level that opens to a sun deck surrounding the mosaic-tiled pool. Bifold doors connect the primary living space to a north-facing al fresco area with lounge, dining and barbecue, while the open-plan living area features a wood-burning fireplace. 422E Sandy Road, St Andrews Beach, VIC Designed by architect Hugh Feggans, this residence offers a coastal sanctuary on a 10,000-square-metre allotment near St Andrews Beach and The Dunes Golf Links.



Connected to the natural environment, the home utilises timber and a natural palette, with floor-to-ceiling windows and a central courtyard that brings natural light throughout the interior. Outside, there is a custom pool with a swim turbine, plus an al fresco zone featuring an ice machine, a Gozney pizza oven and a built-in Weber barbecue. 7 Dudley Avenue, Roseville, NSW Strathmore is a renovated period home with a long list of features to keep every family member entertained.



For wine lovers, there is a climate-controlled wine cellar, while entertainers can enjoy the covered terrace overlooking the gardens and the fully tiled, heated pool. The property also includes a synthetic grass basketball and netball court, a home gym, a Sonos-integrated surround-sound system and a large deck that can be used as a games room. 23 River Crescent, Broadbeach Waters, QLD This brand-new waterfront residence, designed by Jayson Pate, is set on a north-eastern point position with water and city views from Broadbeach to the Surfers Paradise skyline.



The home features a media lounge that opens to a central courtyard and rear terrace, which is fitted with an outdoor kitchen, an Artusi barbecue, a rangehood, a sink and a Vintec drinks fridge. Outside, there is a hot rock sauna and a sunken terrace with a tiled pool and a fire pit area with built-in bench seating.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
PoliticsNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 8:03pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown in a critical condition to Royal North Shore Hospital, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young people’s understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Consent education advocate Chanel Contos said she was devastated by news of the teen’s death: “This just feels insanely preventable.” “There is no safe way to engage in strangulation during sex, and unfortunately, mainly because of pornography, where young people are learning and mimicking scripts from that, this act that was traditionally on the fringes of kink culture has made it way into the mainstream,” the Teach Us Consent founder said. “We need to seriously investigate the impact that pornography is having on shaping the sexual scripts and behaviours of young people.” Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely.



“And there’s really no reason to think that the effects of strangulation would be any different if the strangulation was consensual or otherwise,” the study’s lead author, University of Melbourne Professor Heather Douglas, said. “Even lower levels of strangulation, it can result in brain injuries like problem-solving difficulties, memory issues, and so on, and that’s without even being made unconscious, so it’s a really serious thing to do.” “There’s such a range of injuries associated with strangulation. Some are permanent, some are fleeting … it doesn’t take much pressure, and it doesn’t take very long, to have really terrible consequences.” Douglas said there were no safe ways to undertake strangulation, and she questioned aspects of consent surrounding it. Among the almost 5000 people aged between 18 and 35 surveyed in the research were reports of consent having been assumed from previous instances of strangulation, consent without an understanding of the risks, and consent influenced by pressure or power differentials, Douglas said.



“A lot of people just want to be normal … and doing normal things in their sex life. “And I think there is a bit of a normalisation of strangulation in many young people’s sex lives,” Douglas said. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Federal independent MP Zali Steggall, from the neighbouring electorate of Warringah, said the teenager’s death underscored the need for a national education campaign to tackle misogyny and teach respectful relationships.



“My thoughts are with her family, friends and community at this incredibly difficult time,” she said. “Police are investigating the circumstances of the girl’s death and no charges have been laid. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising. “The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732).

World.title: Dolly Parton, singer, songwriter, humanitarian, loved by all
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Dolly Parton, singer, songwriter, humanitarian, loved by all August 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. A bright light has gone out with the sad news of the death of one-of-a-kind exemplary musician and humanitarian Dolly Parton. And like many of her adoring fans worldwide, I have my favourite Parton tunes that thrum in my head when they’re played on the radio.

Notably, Parton leaves behind more than her formidable legacy of musicianship (and leading by example musical genre crossover for other musicians to follow her path), but what she gave back to her beloved community of humble origin, children (ie reading books) and to marginalised communities (ie LGBQTI and black) through some of the profits she turned with her hits.

Not to mention that Parton was one of the early atypical feminist role models in life, as in in fiction (9 to 5), demonstrating that women can be many things and need not ever ″⁣shrink″⁣ themselves to fit in any one prescribed box.

Needless to say, many people worldwide will always love Dolly Parton, as do I.

Jelena Rosic, Mornington Joining the great gig in the sky

Dolly Parton, you were the greatest. The essence of country music is ″⁣the cry in the voice″⁣, and you had it to perfection. Enjoy your reunion with all the other greats in Heaven. What a gig that will be.

Robert Scheffer, Bayswater North She was the real thing

In a world of egos and celebrities who are manufactured, Dolly Parton’s authenticity, philanthropy and, more importantly, her music and extraordinary songwriting united everyone.

Pam Papadopoulos, South Yarra



A light has faded in the world

I never thought that I would ever agree with a Donald Trump directive, but I stand corrected. I can certainly get behind his order for the American flag to be lowered across the United States for the next week in honour of Dolly Parton. There is a little less shine in the world now the legendary musician, singer, songwriter, actor, author and philanthropist has left us.

Rest in power, Dolly Parton. We shall not see the likes of you again.

Caryn Auld, Point Cook Inspiration for children to read

Dolly Parton was not just a great singer. She also helped children’s education and inspired millions to read with her book program. What an inspiration.

Peta Colebatch, Hawthorn Success is measured in what is given back

It is difficult to think of many people who have combined extraordinary musical talent with such genuine generosity and humanity as Dolly Parton.

From humble beginnings, she built a remarkable career, yet fame and fortune have never seemed to diminish her warmth nor her concern for others.

Through her philanthropy, most notably her Imagination Library, Parton has helped put books into the hands of millions of children, quietly demonstrating that giving can be every bit as powerful as performing.

Her songs have touched generations. 9 to 5 gave working people an anthem with a smile, while Coat of Many Colours offered something far more profound – a reminder that love, dignity and family can be worth more than material wealth.

Dolly Parton has given us music, laughter and countless reasons to smile, but perhaps her greatest legacy is the goodness she has spread beyond the stage. In an age when celebrity can too often be measured in wealth, outrage and self-promotion, she reminds us that success is better measured by what we give back.

Long may she sing, and long may her generosity inspire us all.

Darren Grindrod, Glenroy THE FORUM Simply, madness

After five Sydney Swans players were stood down for the rest of the AFL season, one would have thought that ″⁣mad Monday″⁣ shenanigans would be suitably modified.

Unfortunately, it seems that was a false hope. Now there have been Richmond players behaving in a disgraceful way in public, including ″⁣appearing to urinate″⁣ against a fence (″⁣Tigers deny antics referenced Swans″⁣, 26/8).

But, hey, they’re footballers, so the commentary will no doubt be along the lines of ″⁣boys will be boys″⁣. Trouble is, they are not boys, they are adults who must know that their actions on this day, would be seen.

Columnist Jenna Price (Comment, 26/8) writes it always seems to be women who have to point out bad behaviour, and men who fail to recognise that there is any kind of problem. Sadly, it seems that not much has changed.

Ruth Hudspeth, Burwood



Not so wise

The Richmond Tigers players’ actions on “mad Monday” remind me of Lord Chesterfield’s statement to his son: “Young men are apt to think themselves wise enough; just as drunken men are apt to think themselves sober enough.“

Howard Hutchins, Wantirna Unreal v real

Reported experiences such as “melding”, “embeddedness”, “boundlessness” of people taking hallucinogens such as psilocybin are not new (“What brain does on magic mushrooms”, 26/8). But they should be reminders these types of mind-altering drugs don’t play well in the real world.

In the real world, psychological and physical boundaries exist between oneself and other people and other objects and for very good reason.

To fail to adhere to the many boundaries that exist can lead to harm (for example, physical such as not keeping to the speed limit when driving a car) or other potential offences (psychological such as various forms of disinhibited behaviours or “boundary violations” in social or intimate settings).

So while medical researchers continue to explore potential therapeutic benefits of hallucinogens, their dangers in real world usage should not be minimised at all or overlooked.

Dr Larry Hermann, consultant psychiatrist, South Yarra Wrong housing approach

I generally admire Shane Wright’s economic analyses. However, his news article, “Warning slump in house prices will drag on until 2028” (26/8), says everything about what’s wrong with our current approach to housing.

Surely, the best thing for correcting the current inequity in access to housing – a basic human right – would be if the current “slump” continued for some time.

Perhaps a better headline would be, “Lower house prices to persist until at least 2028”, with an article highlighting the benefits of lower prices for social cohesion to follow. Vivienne Kane, Hawthorn

Queue around the bloc

I don’t know anyone my age (60+) who would be happy waiting in a long queue to buy something or wait for a restaurant table. This is a generational trait. However, the article, “Brands tap into psychology of queue culture” (24/8), took me back to a very different time and place in communist Hungary when queueing, shortages and black markets were a normal part of life. When visiting, I, too, jumped in queues for who knows what?

On one occasion, word had got out that Cuban oranges had arrived in the small country town I was in and so it was queue to buy this rarity or go without.

In those days, consumer sovereignty didn’t rule and there wasn’t an abundance of popular, trendy goods, except in the Dollar shops.

So, while queueing today is seen as social, fun and on trend by some, back then in Eastern bloc countries, it was one of the few ways (other than black markets) to get necessities and desirable goods in short supply. Queues draw us in, but in a different time and place, for very different reasons.

Marg Wilson, Brighton Help the birds more

As Cathy Wilcox’s cartoon powerfully demonstrates (25/8), it is distressing to see wild birds and a seal already dead from bird flu (“First mainland mammal dies from bird flu”, 24/8). This virus has devastated wildlife across the globe, wiping out more than 50 per cent of some bird populations and hundreds of thousands of marine mammals.

Here in Australia, where BirdLife Australia reports that one in six bird species are threatened, scientists warn that H5N1 could have extinction-level impacts.

We have known for years that the H5N1 virus would eventually reach our shores (“Bird flu threat sparks urgent wildlife vaccine push as virus keeps spreading”, 16/8). And our wildlife is already under pressure from habitat destruction and climate change.

Could the Albanese government be investing more to give our precious wildlife a fighting chance?

Karin Ruff, Yanakie Right to protest

Melbourne Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece is worried that people aren’t coming into the city because of protest activity (″⁣Lord Mayor says one in three graffiti reports ‘antisemitic’ ″⁣, 25/8) . He is no doubt concerned about lost revenue to business. We need to remember that the protests are peaceful, and, importantly, people have the right to protest in a democracy.

And we need to remember the reasons for these protests. The people who turn out to support Palestine are protesting against civilian deaths, crimes against humanity, the deplorable treatment of prisoners and the destruction of homes, olive groves and hospitals. How can we weigh people’s right to shop against the fact that according to the Gaza Ministry of Health, Israeli operations in Gaza have killed 1286 people since the so-called ceasefire began in October last year?

Elizabeth O’Connor, Ivanhoe East



China shows off

I fail to grasp the point of the so-called robot humanoid ″⁣Games″⁣ in Beijing other than an opportunity for China to display to the world how incredibly advanced their freaky robots have become.

That one of them ran 100 metres faster than Olympic champion Usain Bolt is just China showing-off. Bolt shouldn’t feel badly; he’s still got his gold medals.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris Trade off and lose

Ross Gittins explains, in an understandable way, something many of us thought was always suspect (“Labor’s carbon credit scheme fails to stack up”, 26/8). Allowing firms to obtain carbon credits was probably well intentioned, but was always going to be open to self-interested manipulation by business.

Similarly, “safeguard mechanisms” which cap emissions of large polluters: If they breach these, they have to buy a “carbon offset” to compensate.

What all this means, of course, is that polluting emissions can continue if you have enough wealth to buy credits.

This is not a meaningful way to reduce emissions.

This trade-off is now even more important to consider, given that we are witnessing firms jostling to build data centres, usually in areas too close to populations (“Environmental watchdog challenges data centre over noise fears”, 26/8). Apart from noise pollution, these centres consume huge amounts of electricity and water. Once again, there are meant to be safeguards, but already citizen rights are being ignored because the Planning Minister, Sonya Kilkenny, makes the ultimate decision without having to take account of bodies such as the Environment Protection Authority. What sort of world are we entering into?

Jan Marshall, Brighton Obstacle to progress

Columnist Ross Gittins’ critique of carbon credit and offset systems is on the money (“Labor’s carbon credit scheme fails to stack up”, 26/8). Real climate action requires slashing pollution from coal, oil and gas, ending land clearing, and restoring carbon-rich ecosystems — all at the same time.

Offsetting burnt coal and gas by protecting a tree is at best problematic and at worst a dangerous crutch undermining progress. When will the Albanese government strengthen the Safeguard Mechanism climate policy and ensure carbon accounting reflects reality rather than wishful thinking?

Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn Assumptions made

Ross Gittins’ column reminds me of a joke my mother used to tell about an engineer and an economist who fall down a mine shaft. The engineer fossicks around for materials to build a ladder. The economist says: “Let’s assume there is a ladder.“

Sarah Russell, Mt Martha An elongated idea

A great idea from your correspondent that if Elon Musk invented a car that returned itself to its owner after it’s been stolen, it could be called “the Homer” (Letters, 26/8). And if it took a really, really, really long time to find its way back, it could be called “the Odysseus”.

Deborah Morrison, Malvern East



Decentralise option

Building up or out should not be the question. Whatever happened to decentralisation? Regional cities have decent public transport to Melbourne. Bendigo, Ballarat and Geelong, for example, have better access to the airport than many suburbs. Good planning for industry, education, immigration, health and other infrastructure ought to include the rest of Victoria, not just Melbourne.

Pete Dunne, Highett Such iconography

Thanks to your correspondent (Letters, 26/8) for his iconic letter bemoaning the fact that he cannot find anything that is not iconic. It’s certainly a legendary observation – quintessential, really.

Geoff Allen, Parkdale Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Data

As the world warms, increasing the demands on water and power, who or what gets priority access

to cooling: people or data centres (″⁣EPA’s data centre warning″⁣, 26/8)?

Jenny Bone, Surrey Hills



Be it a gold rush or data centre rush, it’s a sure thing the environment comes out worse. More power to the Environment Protection Authority’s arm.

Jenny Smithers, Ashburton I don’t understand what artificial intelligence is and what data centres do. I do, though, have a bad feeling about all of it.

John Rawson, Mernda I asked AI whether huge data centres would create environmental problems but was reassured all would be OK.

Bryan Fraser, St Kilda West Robot games! What next, Russian robot soldiers, fighting Ukrainian robot soldiers? Hang on, that might not be such a bad thing.

Myra Fisher, Brighton East AFL

That’s it for me. Swans, now Tiges. No more interest in the AFL. I’ll follow and watch the women’s competition, but not the men’s games. Bonus is that I’ll have less gambling promos to ignore.

Barry Greer, Balnarring Beach



Mark McVeigh proposes to get all the Essendon supporters – an ″⁣armada″⁣ – behind the club. I thought a group of a ships is an armada whereas a group of bombers is a squadron?

Lindsay Donahoo, Wattle Glen Furthermore

Bravo Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney (″⁣Trump’s bulldozer approach no match for Canada’s stance″⁣, 25/8). Give Carney a special peace prize for anti-bullying.

Alan McLean, Queenscliff I have been a rusted-on Labor supporter since the Vietnam War days. The proposal to reduce the rebate on private health insurance cover for over-65s means my vote will be going elsewhere for the first time in 60 years. Kevin Drinan, Bentleigh A song lyric goes, ″⁣Well, hello, Dolly″⁣. Sadly, it is now ″⁣goodbye, Dolly″⁣.

Gerry Lonergan, Reservoir

World.title: Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes
World.content:
Exclusive NationalInsects Scientists make giant cyborg cockroaches that can fire drug-filled syringes Angus Dalton August 26, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Australian scientists have created insect-robot hybrids for search-and-rescue missions.

The cockroach cyborgs are designed to find people trapped in areas human rescuers can’t reach.

The cyborgs can fire syringes from their backs for emergency treatment.

Other teams have made diving suits for cockroaches so they can operate during floods.

The concept has been trialled in the aftermath of a deadly earthquake in Myanmar.

If you ever find yourself buried beneath the rubble of an earthquake’s aftermath or expiring in a remote cave, salvation may not arrive in the form of a dashing rescuer or detection dog, but of a hulking, hissing, spiky-legged cockroach. Scientists are developing cyborg paramedic cockroaches designed to find people trapped in places human rescuers can’t reach, with the latest recruits capable of delivering medicine by firing syringes from a harpoon system on their backs. A cyborg cockroach armed with a syringe-firing backpack. The University of Queensland The “paraborg” (a portmanteau of paramedic and cyborg) insects are made from giant burrowing cockroaches, which are the world’s heaviest cockroach species and native to north Queensland. “It’s not for everyone,” biorobotics specialist and cyborg creator Dr T. Thang Vo-Doan, from the University of Queensland, said of working with the cockroaches. “But we have very good relationship with them in the lab.”



The glossy arthropods are fashioned into cyborgs by the insertion of electrodes into their antennae, so the cockroaches can be remote-controlled with a joystick. Antennae detect obstacles, so when the left one is stimulated, the cockroaches bear right, and vice versa. Other electrodes in the “cerci” – sensory appendages at the back of the insect – allow researchers to accelerate or stop the cyborg roaches. Scientists eventually want to make fully robotic, insect-inspired rescue devices but Vo-Doan said robots aren’t small, agile or efficient enough yet to operate in disaster zones. Cockroaches, however, are ready to rumble.



“The insect can climb and run, even carry heavy loads in different orientations in a complex environment,” Vo-Doan said. “You already have everything from nature. It simplifies our system a lot in terms of design and engineering.” PhD student Hai Nhan Le remotely controls “paraborg” cockroaches. The University of Queensland He believes more lives can be saved now by harnessing the insects, with agility and efficiency honed by evolution, to carry devices including cameras and sensors into collapsed buildings. While small robots are restricted by limited battery life, cockroaches can go for days, powered simply by gum leaves and apple slices. There’s no requirement for scientists to obtain ethical approval for research with insects. But the cockroaches are anaesthetised for the insertion of electrodes, and electronic systems are carefully removed after experiments.



Vo-Doan said the cyborg recruits seem to live as long and well as their civilian counterparts. The latest study, published in Advanced Science, focused on the “rescue” part of search and rescue. If a swarm of cyborg cockroaches discovered a victim buried beneath rubble who was suffering from sepsis, what happens next? Cyborg cockroaches can traverse complex, rubble-strewn environments better than robots. The University of Queensland Enter the medic class. The researchers created and tested needle-firing cyborgs and showed they could successfully navigate to a target and deliver a jab in 72 per cent of proof-of-concept trials. When cockroaches came within 15 centimetres of a mock target, the hit rate was 95 per cent.



“A lot of people might not like the sight of a giant cockroach scurrying towards them,” said PhD candidate and first author of the research Hai Nhan Le. “But if you’re trapped in rubble or stuck in a cave and need help, it could make a real difference between life and death.” The idea, eventually, is to create a “fully autonomous paramedic team composed of terrestrial cyborg insects” that can independently search for victims, relay information and deliver medication, the researchers write. The concept might seem far-fetched but other international teams are taking the same approach and have been trialling it in the field.



Ten cyborg Madagascan hissing cockroaches fitted with infrared cameras and sensors were deployed alongside Singapore’s Operation Lionheart rescue team in the aftermath of a 2025 earthquake in Myanmar that killed at least 3600 people. (The cockroach squad didn’t detect any survivors but researchers said the mission yielded valuable lessons to improve the cyborgs.) Other researchers have made 3D-printed diving suits for cyborg cockroaches that could help in flood rescues. NTU Singapore Meanwhile, in June, another team of researchers introduced the aquatic class. They designed flexible cockroach diving suits 3D-printed from resin. Cockroaches wearing the suits could operate underwater for three hours despite being a terrestrial species, the researchers reported in Nature. The amphibious cyborgs could one day carry out missions in flooded areas or help explore the deep ocean – or other planets. “The ultimate goal is to [take this technology to] space,” lead author Professor Hirotaka Sato told New Scientist. “Exploration over the Mars surface, for example.”



Related Article Analysis

China relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics So when might we see cyborg cockroaches rolled out to disaster zones? Perhaps five years, perhaps 20, depending on the level of support the idea gains, Vo-Doan said. Experts such as Superintendent Tim Hassiotis, from Fire & Rescue NSW, are open to the concept if the cyborgs prove effective in real emergencies. “If cyborg insects can safely enter spaces we can’t, locate casualties and ultimately help deliver emergency care, they could become another valuable tool in the future of urban search and rescue,” Hassiotis said. World.title: Police probe link between Fadi Haddara shooting and Tassie tobacco operation
World.content:
Police are investigating if the near-fatal shooting of crime figure Fadi Haddara is linked to his crime network’s alleged involvement in a multimillion-dollar tobacco and money laundering operation in Tasmania. Haddara’s targeting by a hit team was the first of three shootings targeting associates, the latest on Wednesday when a 37-year-old man was shot on a property in broad daylight in Heidelberg West. Fadi Haddara is recovering after being shot in his driveway. Jason South Haddara himself was nearly killed after being gunned down in the driveway of his family home in Altona North on August 16. He was released from hospital this week, but doctors are waiting to attempt to remove one bullet still lodged near his jawline.



“He’s up walking around, speaking properly. Friends couldn’t believe it,” an associate said. A week after the failed hit, a known Haddara associate was shot in the arm while sitting in a cafe in Altona North’s Borrack Square commonly frequented by figures linked to the clan. On Wednesday afternoon, Victoria Police said a victim had been left suffering from serious injuries after being shot outside a property on Malacca Street in Heidelberg West. A spokesperson said the unknown offenders fled in a car, and the incident is being treated as targeted. Two sources, who have knowledge of the incident but spoke anonymously for their safety, identified the 37-year-old as an associate of the Haddara patriarch.



Organised crime gang The Commission is the prime suspect behind the attacks, which signals a renewal of the hostilities that first ignited Melbourne’s tobacco wars. Related Article Organised crime He lived like a man with nothing to fear. His shooting has left even the underworld shocked The Commission, also known as the 313, is the transnational crime gang established by exiled gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2023 that has created a nationwide illicit tobacco cartel after waging a campaign of firebombings and shootings. They had reached an uneasy truce with Haddara who had stepped back from active involvement in the family’s activities after he “surrendered” to Hamad in early 2024 in exchange for an end to a campaign of fire bombings targeting family businesses and a $1 million hit contract put on his head. However, there have been a number of branches of the extended Haddara family that have allegedly continued to operate in the illicit tobacco market. Some even switched sides and were absorbed into The Commission.



The shootings started just days after the federal and state Joint Organised Crime Taskforce took down a money-laundering syndicate operating between Tasmania and Victoria. “It is alleged they facilitated the movement of criminal proceeds in cash from Tasmania and Victoria using hire cars and a commercial passenger and freight vessel,” the Australian Federal Police, Australian Border Force and Tasmanian and Victorian police announced. Loading The operation on August 12 uncovered more than $2.5 million worth of tobacco, over $1 million in cash and $34,000 in silver and gold in raids in Melbourne and near Hobart and Devonport. A 33-year-old from Hoppers Crossing and a 22-year-old Tasmanian, arrested in Melbourne, have been charged with knowingly dealing with the proceeds of crime and recklessly dealing with proceeds of crime.

World.title: Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them?
World.content:
CultureMoviesThe Verdict Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them? Dream sequences are a lazy storytelling device. The only place they belong is the cutting room floor. John Bailey August 26, 2026 — 7:35pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

How good is that bit in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey where Matt Damon skydives naked with the sexy chimp who talks just like his Grade 6 English teacher? No, wait, that’s a dream I had, and I won’t bore anyone further with the grubby details. Nobody likes to hear another person’s dream, especially my partner and children. Jeff Bridges dreaming of flying (among other things) in The Big Lebowski. YouTube Christopher Nolan knows that dream sequences are the worst, which is why the director famous for his flashbacks and flash-forwards and all sorts of timey-wimey shenanigans generally steers clear of sleepytime nonsense. He even directed an entire film set within dreams that strenuously avoided surrealist imagery or flights of fancy. The “dreams” in Inception were closer to your daily commute than a nude plummet with a primate playmate. This is the storytelling equivalent of waving your palms and pleading, “No, no, I take it all back!” There’s a piece of writing advice sometimes attributed to the novelist Henry James: tell a dream, lose a reader. The irony here is that James himself could really knock out a killer dream story. He wrote in an autobiography of “the most appalling yet most admirable nightmare of my life,” in which he was chased through The Louvre by a terrible creature, the whole affair lit only by lightning. But James would agree with Nolan, who recently argued that audiences “devalue” dream sequences.



How many times does a film or TV show just start to become interesting before our protagonist bolts upright amid a snarl of bedsheets, panting with relief that none of what they’ve just experienced really happened? This is the storytelling equivalent of waving your palms and pleading, “No, no, I take it all back!” It’s like ending a chapter of your book with the line “haha not really, lol”. It’s a failure of commitment, undoing the very thing that is likely the dramatic highlight of your tale. Rather than escalating tension and ratcheting up the stakes, it deflates whatever energy the dream sequence was supposed to generate. There’s also the sorry tendency to treat dreams as perfectly legible pieces of code. Thanks to Freud and Jung, storytellers feel justified in treating our complex and jumbled inner worlds as if they were simple ciphers describing our fears and desires. Yawn. Not everything that appears in our dreams represents something at the core of our psyche. Freud was forced to remind us that sometimes a cigar is just a cigar, just as I’ve been forced to remind my partner and children that sometimes a naked skydive with your Grade 6 English teacher is perfectly innocent.



I can already hear the cinephiles unsheathing their poison pens, so let me issue a caveat: I’m not against stories that are dream-like. In fact, they’re some of the best. Think of Picnic at Hanging Rock, a gossamer dream of the Australian landscape as shared by young white women under an oppressive colonial regime. The films of directors as diverse as Yasujiro Ozu, Ingmar Bergman, Sofia Coppola and Lynne Ramsay all possess a dreamlike weightlessness, even though they’re grounded in the waking world. Henry James himself pulled off the same trick with his classic The Turn of the Screw, in which the boundary between the real and the imagined is never resolved. Related Article Opinion

The Verdict Enough with the boring alpha men – I can’t get enough of this TV trend Paul Kalina Contributor Then there’s David Lynch, whose art was almost entirely defined by dream logic but who rarely stooped to anything as low as an actual dream sequence. From Twin Peaks to Mulholland Drive, dreams and reality overlap to the point that there’s little difference. Lynch often said that our partial, fragmented perception of existence means that we all essentially live inside our own private dream. His films, then, were dreams within a dream, and that’s a phrase that a whole bunch of his characters would repeat across his work. If a film is already a fantasy, then why not go the whole hog and commit? How much more compelling is it to happen upon the moment in a story that has you thinking, “This can’t be happening, not really”, only to gradually realise that yes, we’re going there, and you won’t believe what happens next, too. Take this alluring primate by the hand and leap out into that wide blue sky. No need to tell us it was just a dream all along.

World.title: Andrew lost his son to cannabis. A landmark study helps us understand why
World.content:
NationalNSWMedicine Andrew lost his son to cannabis. A landmark study helps us understand why Rachel Rasker August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Patrick Leunig finished high school with a great ATAR and a coveted spot in a law degree, his father assumed he was on the path to success. “It looked like he had his whole future in front of him,” Patrick’s father, Andrew Leunig, said. Andrew Leunig said his son was a “happy, healthy kid” before his illness. “We later found out he started smoking cannabis in Year 11, when he was 16.” Patrick dropped out of university inside a year. By the time he was 21, he was hospitalised against his will for the first time, when the delusions and conspiracies of drug-induced psychosis made it clear he needed help.



In April 2024, Patrick was found dead of a methamphetamine overdose. It was two days before his 26th birthday. Patrick Leunig had “his whole future ahead of him”. “If he had never smoked cannabis, would he have had a mental illness? I don’t know the answer,” Leunig said. A landmark Australian-led global study found cannabis users develop psychosis an average two-and-a-half years earlier than non-users who experience psychosis. The largest study of its kind, published in Biological Psychiatry, involving 149 studies with data from more than 70,000 individuals, found that the younger people started smoking cannabis, the worse the clinical outcomes. They lost years of healthy life and incurred greater healthcare and societal costs.



Cannabis users in their early 20s developed psychosis 1.6 years earlier than non-users, while those over 30 developed psychoses about 6.3 years earlier, the analysis found. Related Article Drugs ‘Took control of my life’: Teens banned from buying popular Sydney party drug University of NSW professor of psychiatry Matthew Large, one of the study’s co-authors, said the most plausible explanation is the increased years of exposure. The cumulative toxicity of cannabis was comparable to lung cancer and tobacco – the longer someone smokes, the higher their risk, Large said. Co-author Carly Stevens said there was a prevailing myth that “you’ll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s,” once your brain had developed.



“What we’ve found challenges the assumption,” she said. “There’s been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone … no one is really safe when it comes to trying cannabis.” Cannabis users are two to five times more likely to develop schizophrenia, with a six-year average delay between initial cannabis use and the onset of psychosis. Medicinal cannabis has surged in popularity since its introduction in 2016, as outlined by Penington Institute reports. In 2025, 6.35 million units of the prescription drug were sold in Australia, a 279 per cent increase in three years, with 1.68 million units sold in 2022. Medicinal cannabis is essentially identical to illicit cannabis, Large said, and carries the same or greater risk, given it tends to have a higher concentration of THC. “I think we have effectively legalised cannabis already, but we’ve given it a halo of a medicine that has meant that it’s very difficult to talk about its harms,” he said.



Related Article Mental health The $300 a week medicine Daniel feels better without “You can buy it with almost no information about how bad it may be for you. I think we’ve just ended up with the worst of both worlds.” Studies have found no evidence that medicinal cannabis is effective for treating anxiety, depression and PTSD. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s 2022–‍2023 National Drug Strategy Household Survey found 3 per cent of Australians had used cannabis for medical purposes in the previous 12 months, equating to about 700,000 people. Dr Pramudie Gunaratne, CEO of the Australian Society of Psychiatrists, said prescribing doctors had a responsibility to ensure patients understand the risks of psychosis: “The growth of medicinal cannabis has been incredibly rapid, but our understanding and communication of the psychiatric risks hasn’t kept pace.



“Cannabis has become increasingly normalised as both a recreational drug and a medicine. This study is an important reminder that normalisation doesn’t make it harmless,” she said. Andrew Leunig said Patrick was “on the launchpad” to success. Leunig said there was no known history of psychosis in his family, and Patrick’s “rolling chaos” was eventually diagnosed as schizoaffective disorder, with his initial cannabis dependency a clear “gateway drug” to meth use. “Patrick was generally a pretty happy, healthy kid … to then become very unwell and continue to be unwell, it was just horrible.” Leunig can’t help thinking that Patrick’s life would have been different had he developed psychosis later in life.



Related Article Legal Cannabis Cannabis companies caught allegedly making false promises “If you’re a bit older and more established, you have more resilience, you’d have some experience of being an adult, before the onset of illness,” he said. “I certainly underappreciated the risks of cannabis, [and] I think most people would not be aware of how dangerous it can be for vulnerable people.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Swedes seize Russian tycoon’s island home over security fears
World.content:
WorldEuropeSweden Swedes seize Russian tycoon’s island home over security fears David Crowe August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A Russian businessman planning a luxury home on a beautiful Swedish island will have his property seized by the state in a dramatic move to protect a nearby naval base, highlighting European concerns about conflict with Moscow. The Swedish Defence Ministry ordered the forced sale of the waterside holiday home to ensure the security of an underground base with docks, tunnels and a shipyard built into caverns on the Baltic Sea. A Swedish Navy patrol boat operates near the base on Musko Island near Stockholm. Alamy Stock Photo Once likened to a hidden lair from a James Bond film, the base at Musko Island is now the subject of serious debate about the risks to Sweden of “hybrid” attacks from Russia, including drone incursions near airports and military facilities. German investigators have found three drones and suspected explosives near Leipzig airport in recent weeks, while Romanian forces destroyed a marine drone near a gas project in the Black Sea last Thursday, and Poland experienced two instances of sabotage on its rail lines last year.



‘We are in the most serious security situation since the end of World War II.’ Carl-Johan Edstrom, Swedish chief of defence staff The concern about Musko Island, about 40 kilometres south of Stockholm, centres on the Russian businessman’s plan to build a prestige home, up to 600 square metres in size, for himself and his wife, who has Russian and Swedish citizenship. The Swedish government did not name the couple. Swedish Defence Minister Pal Jonson said on Tuesday morning in Stockholm (late Tuesday night, AEST) that the National Fortifications Administration had taken steps to expropriate a property near the naval base. “The Swedish Armed Forces state that they have an immediate need for this property for military defence purposes,” he said.



“The security situation has deteriorated in recent years, and the threat landscape facing Sweden and Swedish interests has become increasingly complex. Consequently, a massive expansion of the total defence system is under way. “This also entails an increased need for access to sites where operations can be conducted during peacetime and which offer strategic advantages in the event of war.” Related Article Russia-Ukraine war ‘Who started the fire?’ UK backs Ukraine with seismic deal on AI weapons Jonson said the state had the power to compulsorily acquire property for military defence, although he did not elaborate on how the purchase price might be decided. The base on Musko Island was built in the 1960s and used at the height of the Cold War, but it was decommissioned after the fall of the Berlin Wall and was only put to military use again in a major construction project over the past nine years.



Swedish newspaper Expressen reported on Tuesday that the property was owned by Stanislav Aleshchenko, a businessman with ties to the regime of Russian President Vladimir Putin. It said the property was purchased in 2017 for 18 million Swedish kronor (about $2.6 million), and the new home was being partly dug into the rock. The newspaper said the Russian’s wife, Tatiana Sazonova, was the formal owner of the property. She had previously denied knowing the site was near a military base, telling Expressen: “I didn’t know that when I bought it. I was looking everywhere. And it just turned out that way by chance. An unfortunate, unfortunate coincidence.” Russian incursions increase Sweden began rebuilding the Musko Island base after Russian forces seized control of the Crimea in 2014 and a series of incidents around that time, including the sighting of a Russian mini-submarine in Swedish waters that year.

World.title: Royal commission has created the best record of antisemitism since World War II
World.content:
NationalAntisemitism royal commission Opinion Royal commission has created the best record of antisemitism since World War II Philip Crutchfield Barrister August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 26, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professor Steven Prawer walked into his office at the University of Melbourne and found around 20 people waiting for him, most with their faces covered by keffiyehs. He had spent untroubled years running a physics research collaboration with the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Other senior staff were involved in the collaboration, but Prawer, who wears a kippah, was the only one visibly Jewish. He told the people in his office that they were trespassing and asked them to leave. They refused, and as he tried to reach a secure part of the building, two of them followed him and wedged a foot in the door to stop him closing it, chanting, “Prawer, Prawer, you can’t hide, you’re guilty of genocide.” When he returned to his office later that day, a photograph of him had been vandalised and symbols associated with Hamas had been stuck to his walls. Commissioner Virginia Bell on the bench. ABC News Accounts like this are now part of the public record of this country, permanently, because a royal commission compelled them.



I made a submission to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. My submission is principally about the malevolent power of the herd and the damage it wrought to a country’s society and democracy. I wrote my submission because I cannot countenance any minority group in this country having to send their children to school under armed guard. I would feel the same whatever group was in that situation. Over recent weeks, the royal commission has attracted criticism. Some have expressed concern that certain witnesses have not been called to give evidence. Others have argued that some of the loudest antisemites and supporters of proscribed terrorist groups who have done so much damage to our country have not been made to answer publicly for what they have said and done.
